﴿Ṭa-Ha﴾. These two letters are among the disjoined letters (al-ḥurūf al-fawātiḥ, the letters that open some surahs), like ﴿Alif-Lam-Mim﴾ and ﴿Ya-Sin﴾. They are written in the Mushaf in the form of the letter names that are called ṭā and hā, just as all the surahs opened with disjoined letters are written. Both are recited by all the reciters, just as the rest of the opening letters of surahs are recited. The discussion of them is the same as the preferred view regarding the opening letters of those surahs, which was discussed at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah and Surat al-A'raf.

It has also been said that they are two letters clipped from the words ṭāhir ("pure") and hādin ("guide"), and that they have the meaning of a vocative with the vocative particle omitted.

[Page 183]

The reason for the elongation (madd, the lengthening of a vowel) in ṭā and hā was discussed at the beginning of Surat Yunus.

It has also been said that they are clipped from the verb ṭa’ (an imperative from waṭ’, "to tread"), and that the hā is the pronoun of the feminine third person, referring to the earth. It has been explained that the Prophet ﷺ, at the beginning of his affair, when he stood in the night prayer, stood on one foot, so God commanded him with this verse to tread the earth with his other foot. But this is not authentically transmitted.

It has also been said that (ṭāhā) is a single word, and that its origin is from Abyssinian (Ethiopic). Its meaning is "man," and the tribe of ʿAkk or ʿUkl used it. They recited for Yazid ibn Muhalhil:

"Indeed foolishness, ṭāhā, is from your character;
May God not bless the accursed people."

Some exegetes went to regard them as a word in the language of ʿAkk or ʿUkl, or as a word from Abyssinian or Nabataean, and that its meaning in the language of ʿAkk is "O man" or "O sir," and in other languages "O my beloved." It has also been said: it is a name that God named His Prophet ﷺ with, and it is in the sense of a vocative; or it is an oath by it. It has been said: it is one of God's names, in the sense of an oath, and reports and traditions were transmitted concerning this, some of which ʿIyad mentioned in al-Shifa' (the book of Qadi ʿIyad). The view of whoever made all these letters united in their purpose applies to it, like the view of whoever said they are names of the surahs in which they occur, and similar views that were mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. They were only misled by this because of similarity in pronunciation, so we will not lengthen the refutation. Likewise, there is no regard for the view of those who claimed that it is one of the names of the Prophet ﷺ.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 2–6:

[Page 184]
﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you that you may be distressed.﴾ ﴿But as a reminder to those who fear.﴾ ﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful, who is established above the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾

The surah opens with a gentle address to the Prophet ﷺ, informing him that Allah did not intend, by sending him and sending down the Qur'an to him, that he should be distressed by it. That is, that hardship should afflict him and fatigue should overwhelm him. Rather, He intended that he should remind by the Qur'an those who fear its threat. In this there is also an honouring of the believers, who are described as people of fear (khashyah), for without that they would not have taken heed from the Qur'an.

In this opening there is a preparation for what follows concerning the command to the Messenger ﷺ to undertake the task of conveyance (al-tabligh). It also points to his being among the Ulu al-'Azm (the resolute messengers), like Musa (peace be upon him), and that he should not be negligent in resolve as Adam (peace be upon him) was before his descent to the earth. Included in this is an honouring of the Qur'an, because within it is an honouring of the one to whom it was sent down and who brought it. Al-Shaqa' (distress) is the excess of fatigue through labour or grief in the soul. Al-Nabigha said:

"Except the speech of people by whom I was made wretched; their speech was a striking upon my liver."

The hamza in al-shaqa' is substituted from a waw. It is said: shaqa' and shaqawah with a fatha on the shin, and shiqwah with a kasra.

The occurrence of the verb anzalna in the context of negation requires the generality of its meaning, because a verb in the context of negation has the status of an indefinite noun in such a context. The generality of the verb necessitates the generality of its complements, objects and prepositional phrases, so that it encompasses the negation of every kind of sending down of the Qur'an in which there is distress for him, and the negation of every distress connected with that sending down; that is, all types of distress. Thus the sending down of the Qur'an is not a cause of any distress for the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 185]
The first thing intended here is the Prophet's ﷺ grief at his people's turning away from belief in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this message, in sorrow﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]).

It is also possible that the meaning is: We did not send you to be disappointed, but rather to support you, and that the final outcome will be yours.

His saying "But as a reminder" is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from omitted circumstances of the Qur'an, meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an to you in any state except the state of being a reminder. Thus the meaning becomes: We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you be distressed, and We did not send it down in any condition other than as a reminder. This is supported by its being followed by His saying (﴿A revelation from He who created the earth﴾), which is undoubtedly a circumstance (hal) of the Qur'an. So the verb anzalna governs li-tashqa through the particle of the preposition, and governs tadhkirah through the circumstance's bearer. By this you understand that the exception is not from the negated cause expressed in li-tashqa, so that you would be perplexed in determining the sense of the exception and resort to making it disconnected (munqati') and fall into strain to correct the structure.

Al-Wahidi said in Asbab al-Nuzul, citing Muqatil: "Abu Jahl, al-Nadr ibn al-Harith, and – other than al-Wahidi added – al-Walid ibn al-Mughirah and al-Mut'im ibn 'Adi said to the Prophet ﷺ: 'You are indeed distressed by abandoning our religion,' when they saw his prolonged worship and striving. So Allah the Exalted revealed (﴿Ta-Ha. We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 1–2]) the verse." There is no chain of transmission for it.

Tadhkirah is the recollection of something forgotten to the mind, for monotheism is firmly established in the innate nature (fitrah), and polytheism contradicts it. Therefore the call to Islam is a reminder of what is in the innate nature, or a reminder of the religion of Ibrahim (peace be upon him).

[Page 186]
As for (﴿those who fear﴾ [al-A'la: 10]), it refers to one who is prepared to reflect and consider the soundness of the religion, and it is everyone who thinks about salvation in the final outcome. Thus khashyah here is used in its original Arabic meaning. It is also possible that the Islamic meaning is intended, which is fear of Allah, so that the intended sense of the verb is its outcome, that is, whose affair results in khashyah by Allah's facilitating piety for him, as in His saying: "guidance for the God-fearing," meaning those who arrive at piety.

Tanzilan is a second circumstance (hal) of the Qur'an.

Its purpose is to honour the Qur'an and to show concern for it, so that from this one moves to the implication that He who sent it down to you in this station will not abandon your support and reinforcement.

The shift from the name of Majesty (Allah) or from its pronoun to the relative form, because of what the relative clause signifies of the necessity of singling Him out for worship, is because He is the Creator of those addressed by the Qur'an and of others who are greater than them in creation. For this reason He described the heavens with "the high" as a clarifying attribute, to add to the affirmation of the meaning of the greatness of their Creator. Also, since this is the character of the one who sent down the Qur'an, it is inevitable that the Qur'an is something great, as al-Farazdaq said:

"Indeed He who raised the heaven built for us a house whose pillars are mightier and loftier."

Al-Rahman may be the predicate of an omitted subject which must be omitted according to the established usage of the subject it is attributed to, as al-Sakkaki named it, or it may be the subject. The attribute al-Rahman was chosen to teach people by it, because the polytheists denied His being named al-Rahman (﴿And when it is said to them, "Prostrate to the Most Merciful," they say, "And what is the Most Merciful?"﴾ [al-Furqan: 60]). In its mention here and the frequency of reminding by it in the Qur'an, there is an incitement to单独 worship Him in gratitude for His immense mercy in kindness.

The clause (﴿established above the Throne﴾) is a circumstance (hal) of al-Rahman, or a second predicate of the omitted subject.

[Page 187]
Al-istiwa' is settling and being established. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Then when you and those with you are settled upon the ship﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 28]), the verse. And He said: (﴿And it settled upon al-Judi﴾ [Hud: 44]).

Al-'Arsh is a great world among the higher worlds; it is said that it is the highest and greatest of the heavens. It is said otherwise. It is also called al-Kursi according to the correct view. It is said: al-Kursi is other than al-'Arsh.

Whichever is the case, mentioning settling upon it adds to depicting the greatness of Allah the Exalted and the vastness of His dominion after His saying (﴿of He who created the earth and the high heavens﴾).

As for the mention of istiwa', its interpretation is that it is a figurative representation (tamthil) of the greatness of Allah by the greatness of the greatest kings who sit upon thrones; the Arabs knew of such kings the kings of Persia and the kings of Rome, and these were the paradigm of greatness in their eyes.

What made the expression with istiwa' appropriate is its being paired with the Throne, which is among the things one settles upon in common usage. Thus the mention of istiwa' serves as a complement (tarshih) to the application of the term 'Arsh to the greatest heaven. The verse is among the clearly ambiguous (al-mutashabih al-bayyin), whose interpretation is by Arab usage and by what is established in creed: that there is nothing like unto Him.

It is said: istiwa' is used in the sense of istila' (seizing power). They cited the verse of al-Akhtal:

"Bishr has seized Iraq without sword or spilled blood."

It is a later (muwallad) usage. It is possible that it is a figurative representation like the verse. Perhaps he derived it from this verse.

What has been said about this was previously mentioned at His saying (﴿Then He established Himself above the Throne﴾ [al-A'raf: 54]) in Surah al-A'raf. We have repeated some of it here only because this verse is the best known among our Ash'ari colleagues.

[Page 188]
In al-Abbi's annotation on the tafsir of Ibn 'Arafah:
"'Izz al-Din ibn 'Abd al-Salam chose not to declare takfir upon one who says [God is] in a direction (al-jihah). It was said to Ibn 'Arafah: 'Your habit is to speak on the ambiguous expressions found in the hadith, as in the hadith of the slave-girl and others, so the Prophet's ﷺ mention [of it] is evidence for not declaring takfir upon one who says [God is] corporeal (al-tajsim).' He said: 'This is difficult, but I dared to say it following Shaykh 'Izz al-Din, because he preceded me in that.'"

He followed what indicates the greatness of His dominion, the Exalted, with what further establishes it, which is the clause (﴿To Him belongs what is in the heavens﴾), etc. It is an explanation of the clause (﴿The Most Merciful, who is established above the Throne﴾).

Both clauses indicate His immense power, because that is what is intended by the vastness of dominion.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying (﴿To Him belongs what is in the heavens﴾) is for restriction (qasr), in refutation of the claim of the polytheists that their gods have powers over the earth and that the jinn have access to the unseen. To establish the refutation, the kinds of existents were mentioned: the heavens, the earth, what is between them, and what is beneath the soil.

Al-thara is dust; and what is beneath it is the entire interior of the earth.

The clause (﴿To Him belongs what is in the heavens﴾) is conjoined (ʿatf) to the clause (﴿established above the Throne﴾).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 2–6:

[Page 184]
﴿We have not sent down the Qur'an to you that you may be distressed.﴾ ﴿But as a reminder to those who fear.﴾ ﴿A revelation from He who created the earth and the high heavens.﴾ ﴿The Most Merciful, who is established above the Throne.﴾ ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth and whatever is between them and whatever is beneath the soil.﴾

The surah opens with a gentle address to the Prophet ﷺ, informing him that Allah did not intend, by sending him and sending down the Qur'an to him, that he should be distressed by it. That is, that hardship should afflict him and fatigue should overwhelm him. Rather, He intended that he should remind by the Qur'an those who fear its threat. In this there is also an honouring of the believers, who are described as people of fear (khashyah), for without that they would not have taken heed from the Qur'an.

In this opening there is a preparation for what follows concerning the command to the Messenger ﷺ to undertake the task of conveyance (al-tabligh). It also points to his being among the Ulu al-'Azm (the resolute messengers), like Musa (peace be upon him), and that he should not be negligent in resolve as Adam (peace be upon him) was before his descent to the earth. Included in this is an honouring of the Qur'an, because within it is an honouring of the one to whom it was sent down and who brought it. Al-Shaqa' (distress) is the excess of fatigue through labour or grief in the soul. Al-Nabigha said:

"Except the speech of people by whom I was made wretched; their speech was a striking upon my liver."

The hamza in al-shaqa' is substituted from a waw. It is said: shaqa' and shaqawah with a fatha on the shin, and shiqwah with a kasra.

The occurrence of the verb anzalna in the context of negation requires the generality of its meaning, because a verb in the context of negation has the status of an indefinite noun in such a context. The generality of the verb necessitates the generality of its complements, objects and prepositional phrases, so that it encompasses the negation of every kind of sending down of the Qur'an in which there is distress for him, and the negation of every distress connected with that sending down; that is, all types of distress. Thus the sending down of the Qur'an is not a cause of any distress for the Messenger ﷺ.

[Page 185]
The first thing intended here is the Prophet's ﷺ grief at his people's turning away from belief in the Qur'an. Allah the Exalted said: (﴿Then perhaps you would kill yourself with grief over their traces, if they do not believe in this message, in sorrow﴾ [al-Kahf: 6]).

It is also possible that the meaning is: We did not send you to be disappointed, but rather to support you, and that the final outcome will be yours.

His saying "But as a reminder" is an exceptive construction (istithna' mufarragh) from omitted circumstances of the Qur'an, meaning: We did not send down the Qur'an to you in any state except the state of being a reminder. Thus the meaning becomes: We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you be distressed, and We did not send it down in any condition other than as a reminder. This is supported by its being followed by His saying (﴿A revelation from He who created the earth﴾), which is undoubtedly a circumstance (hal) of the Qur'an. So the verb anzalna governs li-tashqa through the particle of the preposition, and governs tadhkirah through the circumstance's bearer. By this you understand that the exception is not from the negated cause expressed in li-tashqa, so that you would be perplexed in determining the sense of the exception and resort to making it disconnected (munqati') and fall into strain to correct the structure.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 7:**

﴿And if you speak aloud, then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden.﴾

This is a conjunction (*'atf*) on the clause ﴿To Him belongs whatever is in the heavens and whatever is on the earth﴾ [Ta-Ha: 6]. The purpose of this clause is to show the breadth of God's knowledge, just as the clause it is conjoined to shows the greatness of His dominion and power.

The underlying arrangement of the wording is: "He knows the secret and what is more hidden if you speak aloud."

[Page 189]

Here, the phrase ﴿if you speak aloud with speech﴾ has the position of a parenthetical insertion (*i'tiraD*) between the clause ﴿He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾ and the clause ﴿God, there is no god but Him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 8]. The wording is therefore cast in the form of a conditional and its consequent, to strengthen the affirmation of its occurrence, following the method known as *al-madhhab al-kalami* (the theological method), which is to present a statement in the form of a proof in order to affirm its occurrence.

The meaning is: He knows the secret and what is more hidden than the secret, in the circumstances in which the speaker raises his voice with speech so that his addressee may hear. That is, He has no need of the raising of the voice, because He knows the secret and what is more hidden.

This is a style followed by eloquent speakers and common in their speech in many forms: it occurs in every conditional that is not intended to express contingency but to express certainty, such as the words of Abu Kabir al-Hudhali:

*"She brought him, a heart-sore, wakeful one with a hidden grief, whenever the night of the one who is anxious sleeps."*

That is: wakeful at every time, when others, who are anxious, sleep.

And the words of Bashama ibn Hazn al-Nahshali:

*"When the warriors withdraw lest the edge of the swords' points reach them, we reach them with our hands."*

And the words of Ibrahim ibn Kunayf al-Nabhani:

*"If the days have turned their vicissitudes, with misfortune and ease, and calamities do what they do,*
*they have not softened from us a firm spear, nor have they made us submissive to what is not becoming."*

And the words of al-Qatami:

*"Whoever is captivated by civilization, then what men of the desert are we who see you!"*

The address in His words ﴿and if you speak aloud﴾ may be an address to the Prophet ﷺ while including others besides him. It may also be addressed to an unspecified person, so as to include every addressee.

[Page 190]

In establishing the breadth of God's knowledge, His knowledge of audible things was singled out, because the secret is, in ordinary custom, the most hidden of things from people's knowledge.

When the Qur'an came reminding of God's knowledge, the gaze of the polytheists turned to knowing the extent of God's knowledge, and they debated this in their gatherings.

In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, it is related from Abdullah ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Two men from Thaqif and a man from Quraysh, or two men from Quraysh and a man from Thaqif, gathered near the House. Much fat was in their bellies, and little understanding in their hearts. One of them said: 'Do you think that God hears what we say?' The other said: 'He hears if we speak aloud, and does not hear if we conceal.' Another said: 'If He hears when we speak aloud, [although He is far from us], then He hears when we conceal.' So God revealed (﴿You did not conceal yourselves lest your hearing and your sight and your skins testify against you, but you thought that God does not know much of what you do﴾ [Fussilat: 22])."

It has been much stated in the Qur'an that God knows what people keep secret and what they make public, and I do not think this verse is intended except in the same direction as the verse just mentioned.

And God, the Exalted, said: ﴿Certainly they fold their breasts to hide from Him. Unquestionably, when they cover themselves with their garments, He knows what they conceal and what they make public. Indeed, He is Knower of what is within the breasts﴾ [Hud: 5].

There remains the consideration of why this condition is introduced as a parenthetical insertion, and why the supposition of the condition is taken as the case of speaking aloud rather than the case of secrecy, although what appears to the observer is that the case of secrecy is more fitting to mention in the context of informing that God's knowledge encompasses what people's knowledge does not encompass, as is mentioned in the report transmitted from Ibn Mas'ud concerning the verse just mentioned.

I think the supposition of the condition in the case of speaking aloud with speech has a particular relevance to this context, required by the Prophet's ﷺ effort in reciting the Qur'an aloud in prayer or other than it. Thus the occasion of this verse is like the occasion of His words: ﴿And remember your Lord within yourself, humbly and with fear, and without loudness of speech﴾ [al-A'raf: 205].

[Page 191]

This is what was abrogated (*naskh*) by His words: ﴿So proclaim what you are commanded﴾ [al-Hijr: 94]. It also serves as an instruction to the Muslims that raising the voice and keeping it low are equal in supplication, and as a refutation of the delusion of the polytheists that raising the voice is closer to God's knowledge than secrecy, as indicated by the report transmitted from Abu Mas'ud mentioned above.

*Al-qawl* (speech) is a verbal noun, meaning a person's pronunciation of words. It includes recitation, supplication and conversation. What is intended here is what has greater relevance to His words ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2] and the verses following it.

The answer to the conditional ﴿and if you speak aloud with speech﴾ is omitted, indicated by His words ﴿then indeed He knows the secret and what is more hidden﴾. The implied sense is: "Do not burden yourself, for indeed God knows the secret and what is more hidden." That is, there is no merit in raising the voice with it.

From this you know that the purpose of the verse is not to teach people the manner of supplication, for raising the voice in supplication and remembrance is established in the Sunnah. So it is not correct to raise that question here except in the sense of an allusion.

*Akhfa* (more hidden) is an elative form (*ism tafdil*), and the thing it is compared to is omitted, because the context indicates it. The sense is: "and more hidden than the secret." What is meant by "more hidden than it" is what the tongue utters of inner speech and the like, of sounds that are more hidden than the speech of the secret.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 8:

﴿Allah—there is no god but Him. To Him belong the Most Beautiful Names.﴾

This is a concluding statement (tadhyil) to what precedes it, because what precedes it included attributes concerning Allah's action, His creation, and His greatness. So this concluding statement came with what encompasses His attributes.

The Name of Majesty (ism al-jalalah, "Allah") is the predicate of an omitted subject. The estimated form is: "He is Allah," following what was mentioned before in His saying (﴿The Most Merciful, established upon the Throne﴾ [Taha: 5]).

The clause ﴿there is no god but Him﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) of the Name of Majesty. Likewise the clause ﴿to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾.

The "names" (asma') are the words that denote being characterized by realities. With regard to Allah, they are either a proper name, which is the Name of Majesty alone, or a descriptive name, such as al-Rahman, al-Jabbar, and the rest of the Most Beautiful Names.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿to Him belong the Most Beautiful Names﴾ is for exclusivity (ikhtisas), meaning: not to anyone else. This is because anything other than Him either has a name stripped of the meanings that names denote, such as idols; or its realities are present in it without reaching the full perfection of their reality, such as humans being characterized by mercy and dominion; or its characterization by them is false rather than real, such as humans being characterized by pride, since he is not fit for pride, tyranny, or might.

The names are described as ﴿the Most Beautiful﴾ because they denote perfect realities with respect to the One they name, exalted and sanctified is He. This is evident in names other than the Name of Majesty. As for the Name of Majesty, which is the proper name, it is because it differs from proper names in that, originally, it is a descriptive term denoting exclusivity in divinity, since it denotes "the god" (al-ilah), and it is defined by the article (al-), which denotes that the reality is restricted to Him. Thus it comprised the meaning of necessary existence, and it deserves worship because the causes of deserving it are present in Him.

Some of this has already been mentioned at His saying ﴿To Allah belong the Most Beautiful Names, so call upon Him by them﴾ [al-A'raf: 180] in Surah al-A'raf.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 9–10:

Page 193
﴿Has the story of Moses reached you? When he saw a fire and said to his family, "Stay here; I have perceived a fire. Perhaps I will bring you a burning brand from it, or find at the fire some guidance."﴾

This follows the affirmation of the Messenger in conveying the message and in exalting the Qur'an with regard to the One who sent it down and the one to whom it was sent down, by mentioning the story of Moses, peace be upon him, so that he might take him as an example in patience in bearing the burdens of the message and enduring its hardships. It is also a consolation to him, that those who denied him will receive the same recompense as the deniers before them. For this reason, following the story of Moses, Allah the Exalted says: ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder. Whoever turns away from it will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden, abiding therein﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. It also comes after the mention of the story of Adam, who had no resolve: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130] and the verses that follow.

The clause ﴿Has the story of Moses reached you?﴾ is a conjunction (ʿatf) upon the clause ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an to you that you should be distressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 2]. The purpose is the connection of the conjunction, as has been mentioned just above. This story has been partly mentioned in Surat al-A'raf and Surat Yunus.

The interrogative is used to arouse curiosity about the news, metaphorically, and is not used in its literal sense, whether this story had been related to the Prophet ﷺ before or whether this was the first time it was related to him. The phrase ﴿when he saw a fire﴾ adds to the arousal of curiosity, as will come shortly.

The particle (hal) is chosen in this context because of what it contains of the meaning of confirmation, since (hal) in interrogation is like (qad) in declarative statements.

Al-hadith (the news/report) means the account. It is a term for the speech by which something that happened in reality is related. Its plural is ahadith, contrary to analogy. Al-Farra' said: "The singular of al-ahadith is uhdutha, then they made it a plural of al-hadith." End of quote. He means that they dispensed with the pattern fa'ala'.
(Idha) is an adverb modifying al-hadith, and its similar cases have already been mentioned. This adverb was singled out for mention because it increases curiosity to learn the reality of the news, since seeing a fire admits of many states. Seeing a fire indicates that it was at night, and that he was in need of the fire; hence it is followed by: ﴿So he said to his family, "Stay here"﴾ etc.

Al-ahl means the wife and children. They were with him, as indicated by the plural in his words "Stay here." In the Book of Exodus of the Torah: "Moses took his wife and his sons, set them upon donkeys, and returned to the land of Egypt."

The majority read the hā' of the pronoun in ahlihi with a kasra, according to the original form. Hamza and Khalaf read it with a damma, following the damma of the hamzat al-wasl in (imkuthu).

Al-iynas (perceiving) is clear sight in which there is no doubt.

The emphasis of the news with inna is for the purpose of expressing concern for it, as good news to his family, since they were in darkness.

Al-qabas is that which is taken from the ignition of something and is kindled, like an ember taken from a mass of embers and a wick and the like. This implies that he was in darkness and did not find anything with which to strike a spark. It has been said: he struck his firestarter and it did not spark, i.e., it did not give fire.

The meaning of ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾: or I may arrive at someone knowing the way, intending to travel in the direction I am travelling, so that he guides me to the path. It has been said: Moses had lost the way because of the intensity of the darkness, and he loved to travel at night.

Page 195
Here (aw) is for choice, because bringing a brand is a certain matter; so he will either take the brand only, or he will go further and find the owner of the fire, who is heading to the same road as he, and accompany him.

The particle (ʿala) in His words ﴿or find at the fire some guidance﴾ is used in a metaphorical sense of elevation, meaning extreme closeness to the fire, a closeness resembling elevation above it, since one who kindles a fire draws near to it in order to be lit by its light or to warm himself by it. Al-A'sha said:

"And the dew and the one who shaves his head spent the night at the fire."

By "guidance" he meant the one who gives guidance. Allah caused the meaning of this word to pass over Moses' tongue by inspiring him that he would find at that fire great guidance, and would convey to his people from it what would benefit them.

The manifestation of the fire to Moses is a subtle divine symbol, since making his approach to receive revelation by a summons with light in darkness is a symbol that he would receive that by which people would be illuminated with a correct religion after the darkness of misguidance and bad belief.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 11–13:

﴿So when he came to it, he was called: "O Moses!"﴾ ﴿"Indeed, I am your Lord, so take off your sandals; indeed you are in the sacred valley of Tuwa."﴾ ﴿"And I have chosen you, so listen to what is being revealed."﴾

The verb of calling (fi'l al-nida') is put in the passive form to add to the suspense about the story: the anonymity of the caller makes the hearer of the verse eager to know who he is, and when it surprises him with (﴿"Indeed, I am your Lord"﴾), he knows that the caller is God, Exalted, and it settles in the soul with complete firmness. Also, it is more effective in depicting that state, that Moses was called by a caller unknown to him, so his calling is related with the passive verb.

The clause (﴿"Indeed, I am your Lord"﴾) is an explanation (bayan) of the clause (nudiya, "he was called"). By this call Moses knew that the speech was directed to him from God, Exalted, because it is unusual speech, and God, Exalted, does not change the customs He has established in the cosmos except to indicate that He has a special care for the one who is singled out by the change. So God created sounds in an unusual way, not issuing from a visible person, nor addressed to him through an angel who himself conveys the speech, because his saying (﴿"Indeed, I am your Lord"﴾) is evident that this was not conveyed to him through the angels. Therefore God, Exalted, said (﴿"And God spoke to Moses directly"﴾ [al-Nisa': 164]), since Moses knew that those sounds indicated the will of God, Exalted. The meaning that those extraordinary sounds indicate is what we call the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi). The inner speech is not what Moses heard, because the inner speech is an attribute subsisting in the Essence of God, Exalted, free from letters, sounds, and being an object of hearing.

The reporting about the speaker's pronoun as "the Lord of the one addressed" is to calm the fear of his soul from an address whose speaker he cannot see, for the nature of the Lord is gentleness towards the one who is nurtured.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle (inna) is to confirm it because of its strangeness, to repel the doubt that might occur to Moses about the source of this speech.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read (anni) with a fatha on the hamza, by deleting the preposition ba' (of the genitive). The estimate is: "he was called with [the words] that I am your Lord." The emphasis is achieved in both readings.

The branching of the command to take off the two sandals from the information that He is his Lord is an indication that that place has been made sacred by the existence of a speech from God in it.

Al-khal' (taking off) is the separation of one thing from another that was connected to it.

Al-na'lan (the two sandals) are two thick hides placed under the foot and fastened with a strap of leather to protect the foot from the pain of walking on dust and pebbles; the sandal was made in the shape of the foot.

God only commanded him to take off his sandals as a glorification of that place in which he would hear the divine speech.

At-Tirmidhi reported from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "His sandals were made of the skin of a dead donkey." I say: In this there is also an addition of humility (khushu'). Both meanings are required by His saying (﴿"Indeed you are in the sacred valley"﴾). So the particle of emphasis here indicates causation, as is its role in every context that does not require emphasis. This is a particular feature from certain aspects, so a ruling requiring the removal of the sandal during prayer should not be derived from it.

Al-wad: the open space between mountains and hills. Its original form has a ya' at its end. It is commonly shortened by dropping the ya', as in this verse; but when dualized the ya' is obligatory: one says wadiyan, not wadan; and likewise when made an annexed noun: one says biwadiyika, not biwadika.

Al-muqaddas: the purified, the exalted. It was discussed in His saying (﴿"and we glorify You"﴾) at the beginning of al-Baqarah. The sanctification of places occurs through what dwells in them of exalted matters, and here it is the descent of the speech directed from God, Exalted.

The commentators differed about the meaning of Tuwa, which is pronounced with a damma or a kasra on the ta', but in the well-known reading only the damma was read. It was said: it is the name of that place. It was said: it is a verbal noun like huda, described by a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "that Moses traversed (tawahu) by walking during that night," as if it were said to him: "Indeed you are in the sacred valley which you traversed by walking," so the meaning is specifying that this is that valley.

Better than this in this view is to say that it is a command to Moses to traverse the valley and ascend to its top to receive the revelation. It has been said that Moses ascended to the top of the valley. It was also said: it means "sanctified twice," because tay is placing a garment in two halves. On this view you may take the dualness as a metaphor for repetition and doubling, like (﴿"Then return the gaze twice"﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]). The meaning then is: sanctified intensely. The verbal noun is then an absolute object specifying the number, i.e., sanctified in a doubled way.

My own view is that Tuwa is the name of a kind of valley that is narrow, like a folded garment, or deep, like a folded well; a well is called tawiyy. A valley in the outskirts of Mecca is called (Dhu Tuwa), with the ta' having three vowels, and it is a place where it is recommended for the pilgrim or the one performing 'umrah arriving at Mecca to bathe.

There is disagreement about whether Tuwa is declined or not, based on whether it is a foreign name, or because it is derived by alteration from tawin, like 'Umar from 'Amir.

The majority read (Tuwa) without tanwin, treating it as not declined. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with tanwin, because it is the name of a masculine valley.

As for His saying (﴿"And I have chosen you"﴾), it informs about God's choosing of Moses by way of the verbal predicate, which conveys strengthening the judgment, because the context is not one of restriction, i.e., exclusivity, like: "I strove for your need," and he gives abundantly. The motive for strengthening is the strangeness of the information and the surprise of it, to repel the doubt that might occur to his soul.

Al-ikhtiyar (choosing): seeking what is good with effort. The form of effort (tafa''ul) is used in the sense of excelling in seeking good.

Branching upon the information about His choosing him, he was commanded to listen to the revelation, because it is the effect of the choosing; there is no meaning to choosing except his being chosen to receive what God will reveal.

The meaning is what is revealed to him at that time of speech. As for what will be revealed to him in the future, his being commanded to listen to it is known all the more.

Hamzah alone read (wa-anna ikhtarnaka) with the pronouns of majesty.

The lam in (li-ma yuha) is for strengthening the transitivity of the verb "listen" to its object; it may be connected to "I have chosen you," i.e., "I have chosen you for the revelation, so listen," placed as a parenthesis between the verb and what is connected to it. It may also be that "listen" is construed with the meaning of "give ear."

The reporting about the speaker's pronoun as "the Lord of the one addressed" is to calm the fear of his soul from an address whose speaker he cannot see, for the nature of the Lord is gentleness towards the one who is nurtured.

The emphasis of the statement with the particle (inna) is to confirm it because of its strangeness, to repel the doubt that might occur to Moses about the source of this speech.

Abu 'Amr and Ibn Kathir read (anni) with a fatha on the hamza, by deleting the preposition ba' (of the genitive). The estimate is: "he was called with [the words] that I am your Lord." The emphasis is achieved in both readings.

The branching of the command to take off the two sandals from the information that He is his Lord is an indication that that place has been made sacred by the existence of a speech from God in it.

Al-khal' (taking off) is the separation of one thing from another that was connected to it.

Al-na'lan (the two sandals) are two thick hides placed under the foot and fastened with a strap of leather to protect the foot from the pain of walking on dust and pebbles; the sandal was made in the shape of the foot.

God only commanded him to take off his sandals as a glorification of that place in which he would hear the divine speech.

At-Tirmidhi reported from Ibn Mas'ud, from the Prophet (ﷺ), who said: "His sandals were made of the skin of a dead donkey." I say: In this there is also an addition of humility (khushu'). Both meanings are required by His saying (﴿"Indeed you are in the sacred valley"﴾). So the particle of emphasis here indicates causation, as is its role in every context that does not require emphasis. This is a particular feature from certain aspects, so a ruling requiring the removal of the sandal during prayer should not be derived from it.

Al-wad: the open space between mountains and hills. Its original form has a ya' at its end. It is commonly shortened by dropping the ya', as in this verse; but when dualized the ya' is obligatory: one says wadiyan, not wadan; and likewise when made an annexed noun: one says biwadiyika, not biwadika.

Al-muqaddas: the purified, the exalted. It was discussed in His saying (﴿"and we glorify You"﴾) at the beginning of al-Baqarah. The sanctification of places occurs through what dwells in them of exalted matters, and here it is the descent of the speech directed from God, Exalted.

The commentators differed about the meaning of Tuwa, which is pronounced with a damma or a kasra on the ta', but in the well-known reading only the damma was read. It was said: it is the name of that place. It was said: it is a verbal noun like huda, described by a verbal noun in the sense of the passive participle, i.e., "that Moses traversed (tawahu) by walking during that night," as if it were said to him: "Indeed you are in the sacred valley which you traversed by walking," so the meaning is specifying that this is that valley.

Better than this in this view is to say that it is a command to Moses to traverse the valley and ascend to its top to receive the revelation. It has been said that Moses ascended to the top of the valley. It was also said: it means "sanctified twice," because tay is placing a garment in two halves. On this view you may take the dualness as a metaphor for repetition and doubling, like (﴿"Then return the gaze twice"﴾ [al-Mulk: 4]). The meaning then is: sanctified intensely. The verbal noun is then an absolute object specifying the number, i.e., sanctified in a doubled way.

My own view is that Tuwa is the name of a kind of valley that is narrow, like a folded garment, or deep, like a folded well; a well is called tawiyy. A valley in the outskirts of Mecca is called (Dhu Tuwa), with the ta' having three vowels, and it is a place where it is recommended for the pilgrim or the one performing 'umrah arriving at Mecca to bathe.

There is disagreement about whether Tuwa is declined or not, based on whether it is a foreign name, or because it is derived by alteration from tawin, like 'Umar from 'Amir.

The majority read (Tuwa) without tanwin, treating it as not declined. Ibn 'Amir, 'Asim, Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, and Khalaf read it with tanwin, because it is the name of a masculine valley.

As for His saying (﴿"And I have chosen you"﴾), it informs about God's choosing of Moses by way of the verbal predicate, which conveys strengthening the judgment, because the context is not one of restriction, i.e., exclusivity, like: "I strove for your need," and he gives abundantly. The motive for strengthening is the strangeness of the information and the surprise of it, to repel the doubt that might occur to his soul.

Al-ikhtiyar (choosing): seeking what is good with effort. The form of effort (tafa''ul) is used in the sense of excelling in seeking good.

Branching upon the information about His choosing him, he was commanded to listen to the revelation, because it is the effect of the choosing; there is no meaning to choosing except his being chosen to receive what God will reveal.

The meaning is what is revealed to him at that time of speech. As for what will be revealed to him in the future, his being commanded to listen to it is known all the more.

Hamzah alone read (wa-anna ikhtarnaka) with the pronouns of majesty.

The lam in (li-ma yuha) is for strengthening the transitivity of the verb "listen" to its object; it may be connected to "I have chosen you," i.e., "I have chosen you for the revelation, so listen," placed as a parenthesis between the verb and what is connected to it. It may also be that "listen" is construed with the meaning of "give ear."

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 14–16:

﴿Indeed, I am Allah; there is no deity except Me, so worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance.﴾ ﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming; I am almost concealing it, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives.﴾ ﴿So let not one who does not believe in it and follows his desire avert you from it, lest you perish.﴾

This is "that which is revealed" (ma yuha) which he was commanded to listen to. The sentence is therefore an exact apposition (badal mutabiq) for "ma yuha". The predicate is stated about the first-person pronoun by its proper name, which signifies the Essence that necessarily exists and deserves all praises. This is the first thing that must be known of the matters of divinity: that one knows the name which Allah made a proper name for Himself, because that is the basis for all the rulings he will be addressed with, conveyed from his Lord.

In this is an indication that the first thing by which those who meet get acquainted is that they know one another's names. So Allah indicated that He knows the name of His interlocutor, and taught His interlocutor His name, which is Allah.

Page 200

This name is the proper name of the Lord in the Arabic language. His name, exalted is He, in the Hebrew language is (Yahweh) or (Ehyeh), mentioned in chapter three of the Book of Exodus in the Torah, and in chapter six. The name of Allah is mentioned in several places in the Torah, such as chapter thirty-one of the Book of Exodus, verse sixteen. Perhaps this is from the expression of the translators; most of the Torah's expression is only "the Lord" or "the God".
The word (Ehyeh) or (Yahweh) is close in letters to the word ilah (god) in Arabic.

It is said that the name of majesty in Hebrew is (Lahm). Perhaps the mim at its end is the origin of the tanwin in ilah.

The emphasis of the sentence with a particle of emphasis is to remove doubt from Musa; he was treated as one who doubts, because the strangeness of the report exposes the listener to doubt about it.

The insertion of the separating pronoun in his saying (﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾) is to add strength to the report, and it does not serve restriction (qasr), since there is no requirement for it here, because the intent is to report that the speaker is the one named Allah; so the predication is one of identity (haml mu'awata), not of derivation (haml ishtiqaq). It is like His saying, exalted is He (﴿Certainly have those disbelieved who said, "Indeed, Allah is the Messiah, son of Mary"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 17]).

The clause (﴿there is no deity except Me﴾) is a second predicate of the subject of inna. Its intent is that Musa attain knowledge of the oneness of Allah, exalted is He.

Then, as a consequence of that, comes the command to worship Him. Worship (ibadah) combines the meaning of action indicating glorification, through speech, deed and sincerity of heart. The reason for the consequence is that His exclusive divinity requires that He alone be worthy of being worshipped.

Among the acts of worship, establishing prayer is singled out for mention, because prayer combines the states of worship. Establishing prayer means maintaining it, i.e., not being heedless of it.

Page 201

Remembrance (dhikr) may be remembrance by the intellect, and it may be remembrance by the tongue.
The lam in (li-dhikri, "for My remembrance") denotes causation: establish prayer for the sake of your remembering Me, because prayer reminds the servant of his Creator, as he senses that he stands before Allah to commune with Him. In this statement there is an allusion to the wisdom behind prescribing prayer. Combined with His saying, exalted is He (﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]), it becomes apparent that piety is among the wisdoms of prescribing prayer, because when the responsible person remembers Allah's command and prohibition, he does what He commanded and avoids what He forbade. Allah informed Musa of the wisdom of prayer in summary, and informed Muhammad (ﷺ) of it in detail.

The lam may also denote a time: establish prayer at the time that I have appointed for My remembrance. Remembrance may also be the remembrance by the tongue, because remembrance by the tongue stirs remembrance of the heart and includes praise of Allah and acknowledgment of His right, i.e., that which I have specified for you. In the statement there is an allusion to the wisdom in the times of prayer. There is an ellipsis in the statement that is known from the context.

The clause (﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾) is a resumptive sentence (mustanifah), beginning the announcement of a second principle of the foundations of religion after the principle of monotheism, namely the affirmation of recompense. "As-Sa'ah" (the Hour) is a term become predominant for the Hour of Resurrection or the Hour of Reckoning.

The clause (﴿I am almost concealing it﴾) is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to "the Hour", or a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) between a sentence and its cause.

Ikhfa' (concealment) is covering and non-disclosure, and what is intended here is the metaphorical sense of not informing. The well-known usage is that kada indicates the closeness of the occurrence of the action reported about it, so the verb after it falls within the scope of negation. His saying, exalted is He (﴿They nearly became around him a compacted mass﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]), indicates that their becoming a compacted mass has not occurred, but it has drawn near to occurring. Since the Hour is concealed in its occurrence, i.e., concealed in its time, the saying (﴿I am almost concealing it﴾) was not clear in its intent, so they differed in its interpretation in many ways, the most plausible of which are three. It was said: the intent is concealing the mention of it, i.e., from the intensity of the desire to conceal its time, meaning that mention of it is to be left out; perhaps the reason for this is that those who deny the Hour were only increased in obstinate denial by the repeated mention of it in the Qur'an.
It was said: "akad" is here an extra particle, in the position of the extra "kana" in some places, as emphasis for the concealment. The meaning is: I conceal it, so it will come only suddenly. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi interpreted the meaning of "ukhfiha" as "ut'hiruha" (I reveal it), and said: the hamzah in "ukhfiha" is for removal, like the hamzah in "a'jama al-kitab" (he made the book unclear) and "ashka Zaydan" (he complained about Zayd), i.e., I remove its concealment. Khafa' is a cloth in which a water-skin is wrapped, used metaphorically for covering.

So the meaning is: I almost reveal it, i.e., I reveal its occurrence, meaning its occurrence is near. This verse is among the strange uses of kada, to be added to its negated usage in His saying (﴿And they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]) in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying (li-tujza, "so that it may be recompensed") relates to "coming" (atiyah), and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. This is an instruction in the wisdom of appointing a day for recompense. The lam in (﴿so that every soul may be recompensed﴾) is related to "atiyah". The meaning of (bima tas'a, "for what it strives") is "for what it does"; the use of "sa'y" (striving) for action is a general metonymy (majaz mursal), as mentioned previously in His saying (﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19]) in Surah al-Isra'.

Page 203

Consequent upon its being coming and its being concealed is the warning against a people who do not believe in its occurrence, deceived by the delay of its appearance, averting him from belief in it. The consequence following (﴿I am almost concealing it﴾) is more fitting, because that concealment is what the deniers of resurrection are compared to among people. He, exalted is He, said (﴿So they will shake their heads at you and say, "When is it?" Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ [al-Isra': 51]) and said (﴿And when it was said, "Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and the Hour, there is no doubt about it," you said, "We do not know what the Hour is; we only think it is conjecture, and we are not certain."﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32]).

The prohibition to Musa against being averted from it was phrased as the prohibition addressed to one who does not believe in the Hour, against averting Musa from belief in it, as an intensification of the prohibition to Musa against even the slightest thing that would stand between him and belief in the Hour. Since the address was directed to him, and the prohibition was of the non-believer against averting Musa, it is known that the intent is the prohibition to Musa from engaging in the averting of the disbeliever from belief in the Hour; i.e., do not be soft-natured toward one who would avert you, and do not give ear to him, lest your gentleness toward him embolden him to avert you. Thus the prohibition fell upon the result, while the intent is the prohibition of the cause. This style is of the kind of saying: "I will not find you doing such-and-such, nor see you here."

The addition (﴿and follows his desire﴾) is to indicate, through the relative clause, the reason for the averting: i.e., they have no motive for averting from belief in the Hour except following desire, without proof or doubt; rather, the proof requires belief in the Hour, as indicated by His saying (﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾). As a consequence of the prohibition, it is stated that if he is averted from belief in the Hour, he will perish, i.e., be ruined. "Perish" (rada) is used metaphorically for the worst condition, as in His saying, exalted is He (﴿they destroy themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42]) in Surah al-Tawbah.

The consequence arises from committing the forbidden act, not from the prohibition itself. For this reason the consequence was introduced with the fa' (then), and not as a conditional response in the jussive form; so it did not say "tarda" (you would perish), because "in" cannot validly replace the conditional with "la" [in the prohibition]. That is the criterion for the validity of jussive conditional response after a prohibition.

Remembrance (dhikr) may be remembrance by the intellect, and it may be remembrance by the tongue.
The lam in (li-dhikri, "for My remembrance") denotes causation: establish prayer for the sake of your remembering Me, because prayer reminds the servant of his Creator, as he senses that he stands before Allah to commune with Him. In this statement there is an allusion to the wisdom behind prescribing prayer. Combined with His saying, exalted is He (﴿Indeed, prayer prohibits immorality and wrongdoing﴾ [al-'Ankabut: 45]), it becomes apparent that piety is among the wisdoms of prescribing prayer, because when the responsible person remembers Allah's command and prohibition, he does what He commanded and avoids what He forbade. Allah informed Musa of the wisdom of prayer in summary, and informed Muhammad (ﷺ) of it in detail.

The lam may also denote a time: establish prayer at the time that I have appointed for My remembrance. Remembrance may also be the remembrance by the tongue, because remembrance by the tongue stirs remembrance of the heart and includes praise of Allah and acknowledgment of His right, i.e., that which I have specified for you. In the statement there is an allusion to the wisdom in the times of prayer. There is an ellipsis in the statement that is known from the context.

The clause (﴿Indeed, the Hour is coming﴾) is a resumptive sentence (mustanifah), beginning the announcement of a second principle of the foundations of religion after the principle of monotheism, namely the affirmation of recompense. "As-Sa'ah" (the Hour) is a term become predominant for the Hour of Resurrection or the Hour of Reckoning.

The clause (﴿I am almost concealing it﴾) is either in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal) relative to "the Hour", or a parenthetical clause (mu'taridah) between a sentence and its cause.

Ikhfa' (concealment) is covering and non-disclosure, and what is intended here is the metaphorical sense of not informing. The well-known usage is that kada indicates the closeness of the occurrence of the action reported about it, so the verb after it falls within the scope of negation. His saying, exalted is He (﴿They nearly became around him a compacted mass﴾ [al-Jinn: 19]), indicates that their becoming a compacted mass has not occurred, but it has drawn near to occurring. Since the Hour is concealed in its occurrence, i.e., concealed in its time, the saying (﴿I am almost concealing it﴾) was not clear in its intent, so they differed in its interpretation in many ways, the most plausible of which are three. It was said: the intent is concealing the mention of it, i.e., from the intensity of the desire to conceal its time, meaning that mention of it is to be left out; perhaps the reason for this is that those who deny the Hour were only increased in obstinate denial by the repeated mention of it in the Qur'an.
It was said: "akad" is here an extra particle, in the position of the extra "kana" in some places, as emphasis for the concealment. The meaning is: I conceal it, so it will come only suddenly. Abu 'Ali al-Farisi interpreted the meaning of "ukhfiha" as "ut'hiruha" (I reveal it), and said: the hamzah in "ukhfiha" is for removal, like the hamzah in "a'jama al-kitab" (he made the book unclear) and "ashka Zaydan" (he complained about Zayd), i.e., I remove its concealment. Khafa' is a cloth in which a water-skin is wrapped, used metaphorically for covering.

So the meaning is: I almost reveal it, i.e., I reveal its occurrence, meaning its occurrence is near. This verse is among the strange uses of kada, to be added to its negated usage in His saying (﴿And they almost did not do it﴾ [al-Baqarah: 71]) in Surah al-Baqarah.

His saying (li-tujza, "so that it may be recompensed") relates to "coming" (atiyah), and what lies between them is a parenthetical insertion. This is an instruction in the wisdom of appointing a day for recompense. The lam in (﴿so that every soul may be recompensed﴾) is related to "atiyah". The meaning of (bima tas'a, "for what it strives") is "for what it does"; the use of "sa'y" (striving) for action is a general metonymy (majaz mursal), as mentioned previously in His saying (﴿And whoever desires the Hereafter and strives for it its striving﴾ [al-Isra': 19]) in Surah al-Isra'.

Page 203

Consequent upon its being coming and its being concealed is the warning against a people who do not believe in its occurrence, deceived by the delay of its appearance, averting him from belief in it. The consequence following (﴿I am almost concealing it﴾) is more fitting, because that concealment is what the deniers of resurrection are compared to among people. He, exalted is He, said (﴿So they will shake their heads at you and say, "When is it?" Say, "Perhaps it is near."﴾ [al-Isra': 51]) and said (﴿And when it was said, "Indeed, the promise of Allah is true, and the Hour, there is no doubt about it," you said, "We do not know what the Hour is; we only think it is conjecture, and we are not certain."﴾ [al-Jathiyah: 32]).

The prohibition to Musa against being averted from it was phrased as the prohibition addressed to one who does not believe in the Hour, against averting Musa from belief in it, as an intensification of the prohibition to Musa against even the slightest thing that would stand between him and belief in the Hour. Since the address was directed to him, and the prohibition was of the non-believer against averting Musa, it is known that the intent is the prohibition to Musa from engaging in the averting of the disbeliever from belief in the Hour; i.e., do not be soft-natured toward one who would avert you, and do not give ear to him, lest your gentleness toward him embolden him to avert you. Thus the prohibition fell upon the result, while the intent is the prohibition of the cause. This style is of the kind of saying: "I will not find you doing such-and-such, nor see you here."

The addition (﴿and follows his desire﴾) is to indicate, through the relative clause, the reason for the averting: i.e., they have no motive for averting from belief in the Hour except following desire, without proof or doubt; rather, the proof requires belief in the Hour, as indicated by His saying (﴿so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives﴾). As a consequence of the prohibition, it is stated that if he is averted from belief in the Hour, he will perish, i.e., be ruined. "Perish" (rada) is used metaphorically for the worst condition, as in His saying, exalted is He (﴿they destroy themselves﴾ [al-Tawbah: 42]) in Surah al-Tawbah.

The consequence arises from committing the forbidden act, not from the prohibition itself. For this reason the consequence was introduced with the fa' (then), and not as a conditional response in the jussive form; so it did not say "tarda" (you would perish), because "in" cannot validly replace the conditional with "la" [in the prohibition]. That is the criterion for the validity of jussive conditional response after a prohibition.

Page 204

Allah's address to Musa, peace be upon him, came by way of reasoning for every ruling, command or prohibition. He began with informing him that the One speaking to him is Allah, and that there is no deity except Him; then He made the command a consequence of that, in His saying (﴿So worship Me and establish prayer for My remembrance﴾); then He followed with the affirmation of the Hour, and gave as reason that it is so that every soul may be recompensed for what it strives; then He made the prohibition a consequence of it, against being averted from it by one who does not believe in it; then He made a consequence of the prohibition that if he commits what he was forbidden, he will perish and lose.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 20, verses 17–21:**

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said, "It is my staff. I lean on it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa."﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ ﴿He said, "Take it and do not fear. We will return it to its original form."﴾

This is the remainder of what Musa was addressed with. The verse is conjoined to the sentences before it as a transition to a dialogue through which Allah intended to show Musa how to argue for the one sent to his people by means of the great miracle, namely the transformation of the staff into a snake that devours the snakes they produce.

The display of the staff's transformation into a snake within the dialogue serves to strengthen Musa and to remove any doubt that might occur to him had he been commanded to do this without a test. Sights of extraordinary events quickly lead the soul, at first glance, to interpret them, and introduce doubt about whether the familiar thing could be concealed by a hidden covering or by imagination. Therefore he began by asking him about what was in his hand, so that he would be certain that he was holding his staff, so that when it turned into a snake he would not doubt that this snake was the very staff he had been holding.

So the interrogative here is used to establish the reality of the thing asked about. The purpose of this is to increase the tranquility of his heart, that he is in a station of chosen prophethood, and that the speech he heard was speech from Allah without the intermediary of a familiar speaker, nor in the form of something familiar, as indicated by His saying after this, ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ (Q. 20:23).

The outward meaning of the interrogative is that it is a question about something that had been pointed to, and the pointing was clarified by the stative adverbial phrase *bi-yaminika* (in your right hand), which occurs as a circumstantial qualifier of the demonstrative. That is, "What is that in the state of being in your right hand?"

In this there is a hint that the question concerns a matter that is strange in its nature. For this reason, Musa answered the question by stating the quiddity of what was asked about, following the apparent sense, and by mentioning some of its benefits, to fully satisfy the questioner's intent, since he may have been asking about the reason for his holding the staff in his hand. The rule for obvious matters is that one does not ask about them unless the questioner wants something not apparent from the question. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ said in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon, "What day is this?", the people fell silent, thinking that he would name it by another name. In another narration, they said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said, "Is it not the Day of Jumu'ah?" … and so on to its end.

Thus Musa began by stating the quiddity in a manner that signals the unveiling of the reality of what was asked about, and he anticipated that the question about it was a means to seek an explanation beyond it. So he said, "It is my staff," mentioning the subject explicitly, although the usual usage in the context of a question is to omit it, since it is not necessary to mention it in the answer when it is itself the object of the question. So brevity would require him to say, "My staff." When he said, "It is my staff," the style became that of one who marvels at the need to give information, just as a questioner who sees a man he knows with another man he does not know says, "Who is this with you?" and he replies, "So-and-so." If he meets them again and asks, "Who is this with you?", he is answered, "He is so-and-so."

For this reason, Musa followed his answer with a statement of the purpose of holding it, perhaps this being the questioner's aim. He said, ﴿I lean on it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it.﴾ He gave the details and then summarized, in order to see how far the questioner is convinced, so that if he asks for more explanation, he would give more.

The *ba'* in *bi-yaminika* is either for location (*zarfiyyah*) or for association (*mulabasah*).

*Al-tawakku'* means relying upon something of one's possessions for support, and leaning in the same way. One does not say *tawakka'a 'ala al-ha'it* (he leaned on the wall), but one says *tawakka'a 'ala wisadah* (he leaned on a cushion) and *tawakka'a 'ala 'asa* (he leaned on a staff).

*Al-hashsh* means striking, namely striking a tree with a stick so that its leaves fall. Its original use is transitive, with the tree as its object, which is why its middle letter is vowelled with *damma* in the present tense. Then the omission of its object became frequent, and it was extended to that for whose sake the striking is done, using *'ala* (upon), either because *uhushshu* (I beat down) is taken to include the sense of *usqitu* (I cause to fall) upon my sheep the leaves, which they then eat, or because *'ala* is used in the metaphorical sense of elevation, as in the saying, "He is a *wakil* (agent) 'ala (over) so-and-so."

*Ma'arib* is the plural of *ma'raba*, which may have the vowel on the *ra'* in three forms, meaning need, that is, matters I need. There are many benefits in the staff, some of which were reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Jahiz devoted a chapter in *Kitab al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin* to the benefits of the staff. Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "He is the best one from whom you part by the staff."

Among the subtle meanings of the verse is what some men of letters have pointed to, that Musa elaborated in his answer beyond what was in the question, because the context is one of honour, in which lengthy speech is appropriate. The apparent sense is that his saying ﴿other uses﴾ is a quotation of Musa's words in similar form, so it would be brevity after elaboration, and he could have added more mention of the staff's benefits. It is also possible that it is a quotation of Musa's words in their essential meaning, that is, he counted other benefits, so the brevity is from the composition of the Qur'an and not from the speech of Musa, peace be upon him.

The pronoun in ﴿He said, "Throw it down"﴾ refers to Allah, Exalted, by way of *iltifat* (shift of speaker), from the first person in His saying ﴿Indeed, I am Allah﴾ (Q. 20:14). What called for the *iltifat* is that this speech occurs as a dialogue in response to Musa's saying, "It is my staff," and so on.

His saying "Throw it down" makes clear that the question was a pretext for a purpose that will follow, and this is the indication that the interrogative in ﴿And what is that in your right hand﴾ is used to draw attention to the importance of what is asked about, like the one that occurs in His saying ﴿And what hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ (Q. 20:83).

*Al-hayyah* (the snake) is the name of a species of serpent that is deadly poisonous: when it bites with its fangs it kills the one bitten. It is also applied to the male.

Describing the snake with *tas'a* (moving swiftly) serves to show that its life was complete in its vigorous movement. *Al-sa'y* is walking that involves intensity, and for this reason it is mostly restricted to a man's walk rather than a woman's. The verb of ﴿He said, "Take it"﴾ is repeated without a conjunction because it occurs within the flow of the dialogue.

*Al-sirah* in origin means the manner of travelling, and it was applied to custom and nature. The phrase *sirataha* is in the accusative by removal of the preposition, meaning, "We will return it to its former manner, which it had before it turned into a snake," that is, "We will return it as a staff as it was the first time."

The purpose of showing this to Musa is that he should know that the staff had been naturally disposed to transform into a snake, so that he would remember this when disputing with the magicians, lest he need revelation at that time.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 20, verses 17–21:**

﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said, "It is my staff. I lean on it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it."﴾ ﴿He said, "Throw it down, O Musa."﴾ ﴿So he threw it down, and suddenly it was a snake, moving swiftly.﴾ ﴿He said, "Take it and do not fear. We will return it to its original form."﴾

This is the remainder of what Musa was addressed with. The verse is conjoined to the sentences before it as a transition to a dialogue through which Allah intended to show Musa how to argue for the one sent to his people by means of the great miracle, namely the transformation of the staff into a snake that devours the snakes they produce.

The display of the staff's transformation into a snake within the dialogue serves to strengthen Musa and to remove any doubt that might occur to him had he been commanded to do this without a test. Sights of extraordinary events quickly lead the soul, at first glance, to interpret them, and introduce doubt about whether the familiar thing could be concealed by a hidden covering or by imagination. Therefore he began by asking him about what was in his hand, so that he would be certain that he was holding his staff, so that when it turned into a snake he would not doubt that this snake was the very staff he had been holding.

So the interrogative here is used to establish the reality of the thing asked about. The purpose of this is to increase the tranquility of his heart, that he is in a station of chosen prophethood, and that the speech he heard was speech from Allah without the intermediary of a familiar speaker, nor in the form of something familiar, as indicated by His saying after this, ﴿That We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾ (Q. 20:23).

The outward meaning of the interrogative is that it is a question about something that had been pointed to, and the pointing was clarified by the stative adverbial phrase *bi-yaminika* (in your right hand), which occurs as a circumstantial qualifier of the demonstrative. That is, "What is that in the state of being in your right hand?"

In this there is a hint that the question concerns a matter that is strange in its nature. For this reason, Musa answered the question by stating the quiddity of what was asked about, following the apparent sense, and by mentioning some of its benefits, to fully satisfy the questioner's intent, since he may have been asking about the reason for his holding the staff in his hand. The rule for obvious matters is that one does not ask about them unless the questioner wants something not apparent from the question. For this reason, when the Prophet ﷺ said in the Farewell Pilgrimage sermon, "What day is this?", the people fell silent, thinking that he would name it by another name. In another narration, they said, "Allah and His Messenger know best." He said, "Is it not the Day of Jumu'ah?" … and so on to its end.

Thus Musa began by stating the quiddity in a manner that signals the unveiling of the reality of what was asked about, and he anticipated that the question about it was a means to seek an explanation beyond it. So he said, "It is my staff," mentioning the subject explicitly, although the usual usage in the context of a question is to omit it, since it is not necessary to mention it in the answer when it is itself the object of the question. So brevity would require him to say, "My staff." When he said, "It is my staff," the style became that of one who marvels at the need to give information, just as a questioner who sees a man he knows with another man he does not know says, "Who is this with you?" and he replies, "So-and-so." If he meets them again and asks, "Who is this with you?", he is answered, "He is so-and-so."

For this reason, Musa followed his answer with a statement of the purpose of holding it, perhaps this being the questioner's aim. He said, ﴿I lean on it, and I beat down [leaves] with it for my sheep, and I have other uses for it.﴾ He gave the details and then summarized, in order to see how far the questioner is convinced, so that if he asks for more explanation, he would give more.

The *ba'* in *bi-yaminika* is either for location (*zarfiyyah*) or for association (*mulabasah*).

*Al-tawakku'* means relying upon something of one's possessions for support, and leaning in the same way. One does not say *tawakka'a 'ala al-ha'it* (he leaned on the wall), but one says *tawakka'a 'ala wisadah* (he leaned on a cushion) and *tawakka'a 'ala 'asa* (he leaned on a staff).

*Al-hashsh* means striking, namely striking a tree with a stick so that its leaves fall. Its original use is transitive, with the tree as its object, which is why its middle letter is vowelled with *damma* in the present tense. Then the omission of its object became frequent, and it was extended to that for whose sake the striking is done, using *'ala* (upon), either because *uhushshu* (I beat down) is taken to include the sense of *usqitu* (I cause to fall) upon my sheep the leaves, which they then eat, or because *'ala* is used in the metaphorical sense of elevation, as in the saying, "He is a *wakil* (agent) 'ala (over) so-and-so."

*Ma'arib* is the plural of *ma'raba*, which may have the vowel on the *ra'* in three forms, meaning need, that is, matters I need. There are many benefits in the staff, some of which were reported from Ibn 'Abbas.

Al-Jahiz devoted a chapter in *Kitab al-Bayan wa al-Tabyin* to the benefits of the staff. Among the proverbs of the Arabs: "He is the best one from whom you part by the staff."

The apparent sense is that his saying ﴿other uses﴾ is a quotation of Musa's words in similar form, so it would be brevity after elaboration, and he could have added more mention of the staff's benefits. It is also possible that it is a quotation of Musa's words in their essential meaning, that is, he counted other benefits, so the brevity is from the composition of the Qur'an and not from the speech of Musa, peace be upon him.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 22–23:

[p. 208]
﴿And draw your hand in to your side; it will come out white, without disease, as another sign﴾ ﴿so that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾.

This is another miracle which Allah taught him, so that when he challenged Pharaoh and his people, he would do the same thing before the magicians. This is a training upon a second miracle, with a purpose unified with the casting of the staff.

Al-janah (the wing): the upper arm and what is below it down to the armpit; this was applied to it by way of comparison with the wing of a bird.

Al-damm (drawing in): joining, that is, join your right hand, the one in which you were holding the staff. The manner of joining it to his wing is that it touches the skin of his wing, by inserting it into the pocket of his garment until it makes contact with the skin of his side, as in the verse of Surat al-Naml (﴿And insert your hand into your pocket; it will come out white, without disease﴾ [al-Naml: 12]).

Allah made the change in the colour of the skin of his hand upon its contact with his wing an honour for the part of his body most suited to it in action and reaction.

Bayda' (white) is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in (takhruj), and min ghayr su' (without disease) is a circumstantial phrase from the pronoun in bayda'.

The meaning of (﴿without disease﴾) is without an ailment such as leprosy (al-baras) or vitiligo (al-bahaq), such that it becomes white and then returns to its colour, matching the colour of the rest of his skin. Ayatan (a sign) is in the accusative as a circumstantial state from the pronoun in (takhruj).

The causal clause in His words (﴿so that We may show you of Our greatest signs﴾) refers back to His words (﴿it will come out white﴾). The lam is connected to (takhruj), because it carries the sense of "We make it white," so that "it comes out white," or "We bring it out white for you." This causal clause refers back to the repetition of the sign:

[p. 209]
that is, We repeated the signs so that We might show you some of Our signs, and you would know Our power over other than them. It is also permissible that li-nuriyaka (so that We may show you) be connected to an elided element indicated by His words "cast it" and what branches from it. The elided element is: "His words 'and draw your hand in to your side' and what follows it; the estimate of the elided element is: We did that so that We might show you of Our signs."

Min ayatina (of Our signs) occupies the position of the second object of nurIyaka (We show you), so min in it is a noun meaning "some" according to the view of al-Taftazani. This was mentioned earlier at His words (﴿And among the people is one who says, "We believe in Allah"﴾ [al-Baqarah: 8]) in Surat al-Baqarah, and the discourse of al-Kashshaf points to it here.

Al-kubra (greatest) is an attribute of (ayatina, Our signs). Al-kibar (greatness) is used metaphorically for the strength of the reality, that is, Our signs that are strongly indicative of Our power or of the fact that We sent you.
