[p. 210]
(﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress." He said, "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing."﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:45]).

The journey commanded here is a specific journey. Moses understood it from the preliminaries of the announcement, through his being chosen and through the miracles shown to him. Or it was stated to him explicitly and its mention is omitted here for brevity, since the reason that follows indicates it.

The clause ﴿indeed he has transgressed﴾ is the reason for the command to go to him. It is suitable as a reason because the intended journey is a specific one: conveying to him what God commanded to be conveyed, namely that he change from his worship of other than God. When Moses knew this, he did not hasten to object out of fear of Pharaoh's oppression. Instead he received the command and asked God for help in carrying it out, which would result in steadiness of heart, the creation of means that assist him in conveying it, and the granting of eloquence of speech so that he could quickly persuade through proof.

Moses' reply is reported by the verb of saying without a conjunction, following the manner of dialogues.

Moses ordered the things he asked for in his speech according to their actual order, following the original arrangement of speech, unless something required departing from it.

Now, al-sharh (expansion, "opening") literally means cutting open the surface of a soft thing. It is used here metaphorically for removing from a person's soul the thoughts that distress him or make him hesitate to undertake an action, by analogy with dissecting flesh, with the common element being widening.

The qalb (heart) in their usage means the intellect. So the meaning is: remove from my mind fear and the like, of the obstacles that stand in a person's way and prevent him from benefiting from his resolve and determination, and that is a kind of hardship. So he asked that his affair be made easy, that is, that the obstacles surrounding what he was commanded to do be removed.

[p. 211]
The word amr here means "matter" or "affair". The attribution of amr to the first-person pronoun serves to indicate his greater particular association with it, and it is the matter of the mission, as in his later words ﴿and make him a partner in my affair﴾.

Taysir means making something easy, that is, possessing ease. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿God intends ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185] in al-Baqarah. Then he asked for the soundness of the instrument of conveying, which is the tongue, by granting him eloquence of expression and the capacity to render his meaning in the clearest wording. So he likened the impediment of the tongue to a knot in a rope or thread or the like, because it prevents its quick use.

Al-'uqdah is the place where part of a thread or rope is tied to another part of it. It has the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul, like qissah and ghurfah. It was applied, by way of metaphor, to difficulty in speech or in pronouncing certain letters, because the tongue does not move freely when pronouncing the word. This is an explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah), also called ḥabsah (impediment). It is said: 'aqada al-lisan (the tongue became knotted), like fariḥa, so he is a'qad when he cannot express speech clearly. For its removal he used the verb of untying, which suits a knot, in the manner of an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah).

The addition of li ("for me") after ashrah and after yassir is itnab (redundancy for emphasis), as noted by the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki), because the sentence conveys its meaning without it. However, this elaboration was adopted because of the meaning conveyed by the lam, namely "expand my breast for my sake and make my affair easy for my sake." This is the lam called lam al-tabyin (the lam of clarification), which serves to strengthen the explanation. Since it is clear that the expansion and the facilitation are connected to ṣadri and amri, the phrase li ("for me") adds further clarification, like His saying ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1]. Here it is a kind of insistence in supplication for himself. As for the fronting of this prepositional phrase before its complement, it is so that the general may come first and then the detail, which conveys the effect of emphasis because the predication is repeated.

[p. 212]
He did not use this with His saying ﴿and untie a knot from my tongue﴾, because that request concerns God's message to Pharaoh, so its benefit does not return to him, and therefore he did not bring the lam of clarification for it. The indefiniteness of 'uqdatan is for magnification, that is, a severe knot. The phrase min lisani ("from my tongue") is an adjective modifying 'uqdatan. He departed from saying 'uqdata lisani (the knot of my tongue), using the genitive construction, so that the indefiniteness could be expressed, which indicates that it is a severe knot.

The verb yafqahu is in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative, following the manner used in the Qur'an of treating the desired thing as if it were already realized right after the condition, like His saying ﴿Tell the believers to lower some of their gaze﴾ [al-Nur 24:30], meaning: if we say to them "lower," they will lower, that is, their situation is compliance. Al-fiqh means understanding.

Al-wazir is fa'il meaning fa'il (helper), from wazara, not by regular pattern, like ḥakim from aḥkama. It is derived from al-azr, which means support, and al-mu'azarah is likewise; all are derived from al-azr, meaning the back, as will come shortly. So its proper form should be azir with a hamzah, but they changed its hamzah to a waw by analogy with muwazir, which has the same meaning and whose hamzah became a waw because of the preceding ḍammah. When the forms muwazir and yuwazir with waw became common in speech, they pronounced its counterpart in meaning with a waw without any reason for the change except analogy with the counterpart in pronunciation, that is, the habit of pronouncing its hamzah as a waw. That is: make a helper from my family.

He specified Aaron because of his great trust in him, and because he was eloquent of tongue and a good speaker. His being of his family is a basis for sincere counsel to him, and his being his brother is stronger in sincere counsel, and his being the particular brother is because he was known to him for soundness of judgment.

(﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress." He said, "Do not fear. Indeed, I am with you both, hearing and seeing."﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:45]).

When Moses knew this, he did not hasten to object out of fear of Pharaoh's oppression. Instead he received the command and asked God for help in carrying it out, which would result in steadiness of heart, the creation of means that assist him in conveying it, and the granting of eloquence of speech so that he could quickly persuade through proof.

Moses' reply is reported by the verb of saying without a conjunction, following the manner of dialogues.

Moses ordered the things he asked for in his speech according to their actual order, following the original arrangement of speech, unless something required departing from it.

Now, al-sharh (expansion, "opening") literally means cutting open the surface of a soft thing. It is used here metaphorically for removing from a person's soul the thoughts that distress him or make him hesitate to undertake an action, by analogy with dissecting flesh, with the common element being widening.

The qalb (heart) in their usage means the intellect. So the meaning is: remove from my mind fear and the like, of the obstacles that stand in a person's way and prevent him from benefiting from his resolve and determination, and that is a kind of hardship. So he asked that his affair be made easy, that is, that the obstacles surrounding what he was commanded to do be removed.

[p. 211]
The word amr here means "matter" or "affair". The attribution of amr to the first-person pronoun serves to indicate his greater particular association with it, and it is the matter of the mission, as in his later words ﴿and make him a partner in my affair﴾.

Taysir means making something easy, that is, possessing ease. It was discussed earlier at His saying ﴿God intends ease for you﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:185] in al-Baqarah. Then he asked for the soundness of the instrument of conveying, which is the tongue, by granting him eloquence of expression and the capacity to render his meaning in the clearest wording. So he likened the impediment of the tongue to a knot in a rope or thread or the like, because it prevents its quick use.

Al-'uqdah is the place where part of a thread or rope is tied to another part of it. It has the form fu'lah in the sense of maf'ul, like qissah and ghurfah. It was applied, by way of metaphor, to difficulty in speech or in pronouncing certain letters, because the tongue does not move freely when pronouncing the word. This is an explicit metaphor (isti'arah musarrahah), also called ḥabsah (impediment). It is said: 'aqada al-lisan (the tongue became knotted), like fariḥa, so he is a'qad when he cannot express speech clearly. For its removal he used the verb of untying, which suits a knot, in the manner of an implicit metaphor (isti'arah makniyyah).

The addition of li ("for me") after ashrah and after yassir is itnab (redundancy for emphasis), as noted by the author of al-Miftah (al-Sakkaki), because the sentence conveys its meaning without it. However, this elaboration was adopted because of the meaning conveyed by the lam, namely "expand my breast for my sake and make my affair easy for my sake." This is the lam called lam al-tabyin (the lam of clarification), which serves to strengthen the explanation. Since it is clear that the expansion and the facilitation are connected to ṣadri and amri, the phrase li ("for me") adds further clarification, like His saying ﴿Did We not expand your breast for you?﴾ [al-Sharh 94:1]. Here it is a kind of insistence in supplication for himself. As for the fronting of this prepositional phrase before its complement, it is so that the general may come first and then the detail, which conveys the effect of emphasis because the predication is repeated.

[p. 212]
He did not use this with His saying ﴿and untie a knot from my tongue﴾, because that request concerns God's message to Pharaoh, so its benefit does not return to him, and therefore he did not bring the lam of clarification for it. The indefiniteness of 'uqdatan is for magnification, that is, a severe knot. The phrase min lisani ("from my tongue") is an adjective modifying 'uqdatan. He departed from saying 'uqdata lisani (the knot of my tongue), using the genitive construction, so that the indefiniteness could be expressed, which indicates that it is a severe knot.

The verb yafqahu is in the jussive mood as the answer to the imperative, following the manner used in the Qur'an of treating the desired thing as if it were already realized right after the condition, like His saying ﴿Tell the believers to lower some of their gaze﴾ [al-Nur 24:30], meaning: if we say to them "lower," they will lower, that is, their situation is compliance. Al-fiqh means understanding.

Al-wazir is fa'il meaning fa'il (helper), from wazara, not by regular pattern, like ḥakim from aḥkama. It is derived from al-azr, which means support, and al-mu'azarah is likewise; all are derived from al-azr, meaning the back, as will come shortly. So its proper form should be azir with a hamzah, but they changed its hamzah to a waw by analogy with muwazir, which has the same meaning and whose hamzah became a waw because of the preceding ḍammah. When the forms muwazir and yuwazir with waw became common in speech, they pronounced its counterpart in meaning with a waw without any reason for the change except analogy with the counterpart in pronunciation, that is, the habit of pronouncing its hamzah as a waw. That is: make a helper from my family.

He specified Aaron because of his great trust in him, and because he was eloquent of tongue and a good speaker. His being of his family is a basis for sincere counsel to him, and his being his brother is stronger in sincere counsel, and his being the particular brother is because he was known to him for soundness of judgment.

The clause ﴿strengthen my back through him﴾, according to the reading of the majority with the imperative form in ushdud and ashrik, explains the clause ﴿make for me a helper﴾. He asked God

[p. 213]
to make him a helper in his works, and asked Him to grant him permission to be a partner to Moses in his affair, that is, the affair of his mission.

Ibn 'Amir read it in the first-person form, with a fatḥah on the cut hamzah in ushdud and a ḍammah on the hamzah of ushrikhu. So the two verbs are in the jussive mood as answers to the supplication, just as ﴿yafqahu qawli﴾ is jussive.

Harun is the first object of the verb ij'al, and the second object was fronted before it for emphasis.

Al-shadd means holding firmly with strength.

Al-azr originally means the back. Since the back is the gathering point of the body's movement and the basis of its uprightness, its name was applied to strength in a widespread usage that is equivalent to the literal meaning, so it was said al-azr for strength.

It was said: āzarahu means he helped him and strengthened him. The waist-wrapper (izar) was named izar because the back is bound with it, and here it is intended to mean the back so as to match the binding. So the statement is a metaphor for the condition of the helper and the one helped by the condition of a back bound with a belt or the like, and the one who binds it.

Moses, peace be upon him, gave as the reason for his request, both for himself and his brother, that the two of them would glorify God much and mention God much. The reasoning is that in what he asked for himself there is facilitation of the performance of the call by making its tools abundant and the help for it present, and that is a basis for multiplying it. Also, in what he asked for his brother there is making him a partner in the call, which he had not been before, and this makes his brother a doubling of his call, and this also moves his brother to call. The call of each of them includes acquainting people with God's attributes and declaring Him free of imperfection, so it includes glorification. And in the call there is urging toward acting on God's commands to His servants, and bringing the community into the presence of faith and piety.

[p. 214]
In that there is also much mention of God by conveying His command and prohibition. Do you not see His saying after these verses ﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in My remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:42], that is, do not weaken in conveying the message. Therefore, in attaining what he prayed for there is much glorification of Him and remembrance of God by both of them. Also, in cooperating to carry out the message there is a reduction in preoccupation with the necessities of life, since they can share the necessary work for their living, so the time occupied with necessities decreases and the times for performing the message become available. That is a great benefit to both of them in conveying.

What drove Moses to ask for this was his knowledge of Pharaoh's severity, his tyranny, and his preventing the community from leaving their error. So he knew that in calling him there was a trial for the caller, and he asked for help to be freed from that trial, so that there would be ample room for much glorification and remembrance.

The clause ﴿indeed you have always been watching us﴾ is the reason for his request to expand his breast and what follows it, that is, because You know my condition and my brother's condition, and I did not call You with what I called except because we are in need of that. It also entrusts the matter to God Most High, that He knows best what their welfare lies in, and that he asked only according to what his knowledge reached.

His saying ﴿He said, "You have been granted your request, O Moses."﴾ is a promise of answer to him and a confirmation of him in what he surmised of the benefits in what he asked for himself and for his brother.

Al-su'l means the thing asked. It has the pattern fi'l in the sense of maf'ul, like al-khubz meaning the thing baked, and al-akl meaning the thing eaten. This indicates that the knot was removed from his tongue, and for this reason it is not reported afterward that he set Aaron to argue with Pharaoh. In the Torah, in the seventh chapter of the Book of Exodus, it is written: "Then the LORD said to Moses, 'See, I have made you as God to Pharaoh, and Aaron your brother shall be your prophet.'" Also: "You shall speak everything that I command you, and Aaron your brother shall speak to Pharaoh."

[Page 215]

﴿And We had already bestowed a favour upon you another time﴾ ﴿when We inspired in your mother what was inspired﴾ ﴿saying: Cast him into the chest, then cast him into the river, and the river shall throw him onto the bank, and there shall take him an enemy of Mine and an enemy of his﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 39].

The clause "And We had already bestowed a favour upon you" (﴿ولقد منَنّا عليك﴾) is coordinated with the clause "You have been granted your request" (﴿قد أوتيت سؤلك﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 36]), because the clause "You have been granted your request" includes a favour upon him. Coordinated with it is a reminder of another favour upon him, at the time of his growth, so that he knows that, since he was in the place of his Lord's care from the earliest moments of his existence, and He began with His care before he asked, His care for him after his asking is more fitting. Also, that earlier care was a preparation for what God intended for him of chosen status (iṣṭifā') and messengership (risāla). Generosity requires that beginning with kindness calls for its continuation. So this is an assurance to his heart and an expansion of his breast, so that he knows he will be supported in all his future circumstances, like the saying of the Exalted to Muḥammad (ﷺ): ﴿And your Lord is going to give you, and you will be satisfied﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 5] ﴿Did He not find you an orphan and give you refuge?﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 6] ﴿And He found you lost and guided you﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 7] ﴿And He found you poor and made you self-sufficient﴾ [al-Ḍuḥā: 8].

The emphasis of the statement by the particle of oath (lām al-qasam) and "qad" is to confirm the statement, because Mūsā (peace be upon him) already knew that, so confirming the statement to him is confirming its implied meaning, which is that God's care for him is constant and never cut off from him. It is an increase in reassuring his mind after the Exalted's saying (﴿You have been granted your request﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 36]).

"al-Marra" is a form (fa'la) from "al-murūr" (passing), which came to mean a single occurrence of a specific act known by an addition or by the context. It was discussed earlier at the Exalted's saying (﴿And they initiated [hostilities] against you the first time﴾ [al-Tawba: 13]) in the surah "Barā'a" (al-Tawba). The accusative of "marra" here is an absolute object (maf'ūl muṭlaq) of the verb "mannanā" (We bestowed a favour), meaning: one favour of bestowing. Its qualification by "another" (ukhrā) here is in consideration that it is other than this favour.

[Page 216]

"Idh" (when) is an adverb of time for the favour.

"Waḥy" (inspiration) here is the inspiration of true inspiration (waḥy al-ilhām al-ṣādiq), which is the placing of a meaning into the soul, by which the soul of the one to whom it is addressed is set at ease, so that he is certain of its success, and that is from God's success (tawfīq). It may occur by way of a good dream, which is cast into the soul of the dreamer that it is true.

"Mā yūḥā" (what is inspired) is a relative clause that indicates the importance of what was inspired to her, and indicates the emphasis that it is an inspiration from the side of the Truth.

"An" (that) is an explanation of the verb "awḥaynā" (We inspired), because it carries the meaning of speech without its letters, or it is an explanation of "yūḥā".

"Al-qadhf" originally means throwing, and here it is used for placing into the chest, as an image of the form of one who hides his action: he quickly places it from his hand, like one who throws a stone or the like.

"Al-tābūt" is the box (ṣundūq). It was discussed earlier at the Exalted's saying (﴿Indeed the sign of his kingship is that the chest will come to you﴾ [al-Baqara: 248]) in the surah "al-Baqara".

"Al-yamm" is the sea, and what is meant by it here is the Nile River.

"Al-sāḥil" is the shore. The imperative particle (lām al-amr) in the saying "falyulqihi" (let it cast him) indicates the command of creation (amr al-takwīn), meaning: We subjected the river so that it would cast him onto the shore, and not carry him away to a distant place. What is meant is a known shore, which is the one the people of Pharaoh used to head to for swimming.

The three pronouns in the accusative may refer to Mūsā, because he is the one intended, and he is present in the mind of his mother to whom it was inspired. His being placed in the chest, in the river, and his casting onto the shore are all actions related to his pronoun,

[Page 217]

since there is no difference in the act of casting between it being direct or within something else, because he is the one intended by the three actions. It is also permissible to make the last two pronouns refer to the chest, and there is no ambiguity in that.

The apocopate (jazm) of "yakhudhhu" (will take him) as the answer to the imperative follows the manner of the apocopate in the saying (﴿that they may understand my speech﴾ [Ṭā-Hā: 28]) mentioned just before.

"Al-'aduww" (the enemy) is Pharaoh. He is the enemy of God, because he claimed divinity for himself, and he is the enemy of Mūsā by estimation in the future, and he would be his enemy even if he knew that he was one of the children of Israel, because he had resolved to kill their sons.

[Page 215]

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 39:

﴿And I cast upon you love from Me﴾.

This is coordinated (*'atf*, grammatical conjunction) with the clause "We revealed," meaning: when We revealed to your mother what would secure your safety from death, and when I cast upon you love, so that the one who found you in the river would steal you away, would be eager for your life and growth, and would take you as a son, as occurs in the other verse (﴿And Pharaoh's wife said, "A comfort of the eye for me and for you. Do not kill him"﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]). This is because Pharaoh had come to think that he was one of the children of Israel and not one of the sons of the Copts, or because it occurred to him to take precaution.

The "casting of love" is a figurative usage (*majaz*) for the attachment of love to him, that is, the creation of love in the heart of the lover without an ordinary cause, as if it were placed there by hand, without any customary necessity for it.

The description of the love as being "from Allah" indicates that it was a love that broke the customary pattern, since the usual causes of love, such as familiarity and benefit, had not yet arisen. Do you not see the words of Pharaoh's wife (﴿Perhaps it will benefit us, or we may take him as a son﴾ [al-Qasas: 9]) alongside her words (﴿A comfort of the eye for me and for you﴾ [al-Qasas: 9])? So he was a comfort of the eye to her before he benefited her and before she took him as a son.

* * *

Page 218

﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾ ﴿When your sister walks and says, "Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?" So We returned you to your mother that her eye might be comforted and she would not grieve﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40].

The clause (﴿And that you might be raised under My eye﴾) is coordinated with the clause (﴿When We revealed to your mother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 38]) and so on.

The two matters are made a completion of a single favour, because his deliverance from being killed would not show its effect unless He delivered him from death by wasting away through the lack of nursing, and from neglect that leads to ruin or weakness if he were brought up by one who does not feel for him the natural compassion. The implied meaning is: "And when your sister walks and says, 'Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?' — so that you might be raised under My eye."

The verb (*sana'a*, to make/raise) is used figuratively for upbringing and nurturing, by analogy with the making of a made thing. From this comes the saying about one to whom someone has shown a great favour: "He is the *sani'ah* (creation/protégé) of so-and-so."

The sister of Musa was Maryam, daughter of 'Imran. In the Torah it is stated that she was a prophetess, as in chapter fifteen of the Book of Exodus. Maryam died in the third year after the Children of Israel left Egypt, in the wilderness of Zin, as in chapter nineteen of the Book of Numbers. That was in 1417 BC.

The majority of readers recited (*la* in *li-tuṣna'a*) with a kasra on the lam, taking it as the lam of purpose (*lam kay*), with the verb (*tuṣna'a*) in the subjunctive. Abu Ja'far recited it with a sukun on the lam, taking it as the lam of command (*lam al-amr*) and the verb in the jussive, as a creative command, meaning: "And We said: Let him be raised."

As for His words (﴿under My eye﴾), the "upon" (*'ala*) here is used for figurative elevation, meaning accompaniment with firm establishment. So "upon" here has the sense of the "bi" of accompaniment, as in the words of the Exalted (﴿Indeed you are under Our eyes﴾ [al-Tur: 48]).

Page 219

The "eye" is figurative for watchful care and observation, as in His words (﴿And build the ark under Our eyes﴾ [Hud: 37]), and in the words of al-Nabigha:

"I knew you to watch over me with a seeing eye, and to send guards and a watcher over me."

There is an abridgement in the narration of the story of his sister's walking, which is explained in detail in Surah al-Qasas.

The interrogative in (﴿Shall I direct you﴾ [al-Qasas: 12]) is for offering. By (﴿one who will nurse him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]) she meant his mother. That is why He said (﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]).

This is a favour upon him for the completion of his growth, and upon his mother for his deliverance. She was separated from her son only for a few hours, which Allah honoured her with because of her son.

The coordination of the negation of grief with the comfort of the eye is for the distribution of the favour, since her comfort of the eye was by his return to her, and the negation of her grief was by the confirmation of his safety from destruction and from drowning, and by his arrival at the best of dwellings. The mention of the comfort of the eye before the negation of grief, though it is more particular, makes mention of it sufficient in place of mention of the negation of grief. This order was observed for the sake of the harmony of the following of (﴿So We returned you to your mother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]) with what it contains of wisdom. Then the wisdom in his sister's walk was completed by her words (﴿Shall I direct you to one who will nurse him?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 40]), spoken in her own household. Such was the custom of wet-nurses who had husbands, as came in the hadith of Halima, and likewise it is established in the Torah in the Book of Exodus.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 40–41:

﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress, and We tried you with a trial. Then you remained some years among the people of Madyan. Then you came upon a decree, O Musa.﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself.﴾

The clause "and you killed a soul" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "And We had already bestowed upon you another favour" (Q. 20:37), because what is mentioned in the clause "and you killed a soul" is a third, separate favour.

The mention of his killing the soul is placed before the mention of his deliverance from distress in order to magnify the favour, since the story opens with mention of a grave offence with grave consequences, namely the killing of a soul. Thus his statement "and We saved you" carries great weight as a favour, for He delivered him from a punishment from which one like him could not normally escape. This soul was that of a Copt from the people of Pharaoh who had quarrelled with a man from the Children of Israel in the city. The Israelite sought help from Musa so that he would support him, and Musa struck the Copt and killed him, as is recounted in Surat al-Qasas.

Al-ghamm (distress) means grief. What is meant by it is the fear of retaliation that overcame Musa, for when the news reached Pharaoh, he resolved to take retaliation against Musa for the Copt, since the Copts were the masters of the Children of Israel; an assault by an Israelite upon a Copt was therefore no small matter among them. It appears that the Pharaoh who adopted Musa had died before that.

Al-futun is a verbal noun from fatana, like al-khurud, al-thubur and al-shukur, and it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) serving to emphasise its verb, which is fatannaka. Its indefiniteness is for magnification, meaning a strong, great trial.

Al-futun, like al-fitnah, is the disturbance of a person's state during a period of his life. This was discussed earlier at His saying (Q. 2:191) "And persecution is worse than killing" in Surat al-Baqarah.

It appears that al-futun is the original verbal noun of fatana in the sense of "to test", and so it may be used for evil and for good. As for al-fitnah, it is perhaps specific to testing that causes harm. It appears that the tanwin in futunan is for diminution, and the clause "and We tried you with a trial" functions as a qualification (istidrak) upon His saying "We saved you from distress", meaning: We saved you, and fear befell you, as in His saying (Q. 28:18) "So he became in the city, fearful, watchful", and that is the trial.

What is meant by this trial is Musa's fear of Pharaoh's punishment and his departure from the city mentioned, up to His saying (Q. 28:20–21) "And a man came from the farthest part of the city, running. He said, 'O Musa, the chiefs are conspiring against you to kill you, so leave; indeed, I am to you of the sincere advisers.' So he left from it, fearful and watchful. He said, 'My Lord, save me from the wrongdoing people.'"

The mention of the trial among the enumeration of favours is an inclusion (idmaj) informing that God did not neglect the blood of the Copt whom Musa killed, for he was a soul whose blood was protected, since nothing had occurred that would require his killing, as no divine call had reached them at that time. So among the trials of Musa in the matter of the Copt was that He decreed for him departure to the land of Madyan, in order that he might acquire discipline of the soul and preparation of the conscience for bearing hardships, and that he might receive refinement from his father-in-law, the Messenger Shu'ayb, peace be upon him. For this reason, after mentioning the trial, He followed it with the consequential clause (tafri') "Then you remained some years among the people of Madyan. Then you came upon a decree, O Musa," thereby explaining to him what the outcome of the trial was. Testing is a figurative depiction of the state of his being charged with the command to convey the message, in the manner of one who is being tested; and for this reason it was chosen here rather than fitnah.

The people of Madyan: they are the people of Shu'ayb. Madyan is the name of one of the sons of Ibrahim, peace be upon him, whose descendants settled in a place called al-Aykah on the shore of the Red Sea, south of 'Aqabat Ayla. The name of the tribe came to predominate over the land and became a proper name for the place, and therefore "people" (ahl) was prefixed to it. This was mentioned earlier in Surat al-A'raf.

The meaning of "ji'ta" is "you attended before Us", namely his presence at the sacred valley to receive the revelation. And "ʿalā" is for figurative elevation, in the sense of establishment (tamakkun); it made his coming at the time suitable for good as being like one who rises above that time and is firmly established in it.

Al-qadar: the determination of a thing according to a measure suited to what the determiner intends, in such a way that it was not by chance, for otherwise it would be unsuitable or its fitting would be flawed. Al-Nabigha said:

My heart was startled, though it was but a glance that appeared one day, and the success of fates matching fates.

That is, conforming to what I was desiring.

This is a specific determination, namely the care for the gradual progression of his states until he reached the place from which God spoke to him. The statement is a depiction of the manner of selection for conveying the law, in the manner of one who fashions something for the benefit of himself, devoting to it the utmost perfection of its craftsmanship.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 40–41:

﴿And you killed a soul, but We saved you from distress, and We tried you with a trial. Then you remained some years among the people of Madyan. Then you came upon a decree, O Musa.﴾ ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself.﴾

The clause "and you killed a soul" is coordinated (ʿaṭf) with the clause "And We had already bestowed upon you another favour" (Q. 20:37), because what is mentioned in the clause "and you killed a soul" is a third, separate favour.

The mention of his killing the soul is placed before the mention of his deliverance from distress in order to magnify the favour, since the story opens with mention of a grave offence with grave consequences, namely the killing of a soul. Thus his statement "and We saved you" carries great weight as a favour, for He delivered him from a punishment from which one like him could not normally escape. This soul was that of a Copt from the people of Pharaoh who had quarrelled with a man from the Children of Israel in the city. The Israelite sought help from Musa so that he would support him, and Musa struck the Copt and killed him, as is recounted in Surat al-Qasas.

Al-ghamm (distress) means grief. What is meant by it is the fear of retaliation that overcame Musa, for when the news reached Pharaoh, he resolved to take retaliation against Musa for the Copt, since the Copts were the masters of the Children of Israel; an assault by an Israelite upon a Copt was therefore no small matter among them. It appears that the Pharaoh who adopted Musa had died before that.

Al-futun is a verbal noun from fatana, like al-khurud, al-thubur and al-shukur, and it is an absolute object (maf'ul mutlaq) serving to emphasise its verb, which is fatannaka. Its indefiniteness is for magnification, meaning a strong, great trial.

Al-futun, like al-fitnah, is the disturbance of a person's state during a period of his life. This was discussed earlier at His saying (Q. 2:191) "And persecution is worse than killing" in Surat al-Baqarah.

It appears that al-futun is the original verbal noun of fatana in the sense of "to test", and so it may be used for evil and for good. As for al-fitnah, it is perhaps specific to testing that causes harm. It appears that the tanwin in futunan is for diminution, and the clause "and We tried you with a trial" functions as a qualification (istidrak) upon His saying "We saved you from distress", meaning: We saved you, and fear befell you, as in His saying (Q. 28:18) "So he became in the city, fearful, watchful", and that is the trial.

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary on Surah 20, verse 42:**

﴿Go, you and your brother, with My signs, and do not slacken in remembering Me.﴾

This is a return to the main subject after the dialogue. The sentence is an explanatory elaboration (*bayan*) of the sentence ﴿Go to Pharaoh; he has indeed transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24]. Alternatively, it is an explanatory resumption (*istinaf bayani*), because His saying ﴿And I have chosen you for Myself﴾ [Ta-Ha: 41] indicates that He selected Moses and prepared him for a great matter. The Wise does not take something for Himself except by intending to make it a manifestation of His wisdom, so the addressee awaits the specification of that matter. Here He commanded him to go to Pharaoh and to have his brother go with him. The meaning is that he conveys to his brother that God has commanded him to accompany him, because Aaron was not present when God spoke to Moses at the blessed spot by the tree. Moreover, this was not the time to set out toward Pharaoh. It is therefore determined that the command seeks the realisation of a future going, upon arriving in Egypt, Pharaoh's land, and upon meeting his brother Aaron and conveying to him God's command. Thus the indication that immediacy is not intended is present here.

The *ba'* in ﴿with My signs﴾ denotes accompaniment, with the purpose of reassuring Moses that he will be accompanied by the signs of God, that is, the proofs that attest to his truthfulness before Pharaoh.

The meaning of ﴿لا تَنِيا﴾ (*la taniya*) is "do not weaken." It is said: *wanā yanī wanan*, meaning he became weak in work. That is, "do not weaken, you; and convey to Aaron that he should not weaken." The form of prohibition is thus used in both its literal and its figurative sense.

[Page 224]

﴿Go, both of you, to Pharaoh; indeed, he has transgressed.﴾ ﴿Speak to him with gentle speech, perhaps he may be reminded or fear.﴾

It is permissible that this be a shift to addressing Musa and Harun. This implies that Harun was present for this address, and this is the apparent meaning of His saying after it: (﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear that he will hasten against us or that he will transgress."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]).

Harun's presence with Musa was by a revelation from Allah that He revealed to Harun in the land of (Jasan [Goshen]), where the dwellings of the Children of Israel were, in a land near Tiba.

The Torah says, in the fourth chapter of the Book of Exodus: "And He said: Behold, Harun is coming out to meet you, and when he sees you he will be glad in his heart. You shall speak to him, and put the words in his mouth." And in it also: "The Lord said to Harun: Go into the wilderness to meet Musa. So he went, and they met at the mountain of God, that is, the mountain of Horeb." So the events between Allah the Exalted speaking to Musa at the valley by the fire and Musa's arrival with his family at the mountain of Horeb on his way to the land of Egypt are omitted. His saying (﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear..."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]) etc. is then an answer to Allah the Exalted's saying to both of them (﴿Go to Pharaoh...﴾) etc. The separation of the clause (﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear..."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]) etc. is because it occurs in the style of dialogue (*fasl*, the disjunction of clauses).

It is also permissible that the clause (﴿Go to Pharaoh﴾) is a substitute (*badal*, apposition) for the clause (﴿Go, you and your brother﴾ [Ta-Ha: 42]), so His saying "Go" (*idhhab*) is a command to Musa to go and to command his brother to go with him, while Harun is absent. This is more suitable to the context of the clauses. The clause (﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear..."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]) is then a resumptive clause (*istinaf ibtida'i*, a fresh beginning), and what lies between Allah's address to Musa and the narration of (﴿They said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear..."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 45]) is omitted. The implied sense is: Musa went and met his brother Harun, and conveyed to him the command of Allah with what He had commanded him, and they said, "Our Lord, indeed we fear..." etc.

The clause (﴿indeed he has transgressed﴾) is a reason (*ta'lil*) for the command that they go to him. Thus it is known that the purpose is to restrain him from his transgression.

[Page 225]

The verb *taghā* (transgressed) was written in the Qur'an with its final letter as an inclined *alif* (*alif mumala*), that is, in the form of a *yā'*, to indicate that it derives from *taghiya*, like *radiya*. It is also permissible to write it with a *wāw*, so one says *yatghū*, like *yad'ū*.

Gentle speech (*al-qawl al-layyin*) is speech that indicates meanings of encouragement, presentation, and invitation to comply, by which the speaker shows the addressee that he has such soundness of judgment that he can accept the truth and distinguish between truth and falsehood, while avoiding that the speech include a belittling of the addressee's opinion or ascribing ignorance to him.

So he likened speech containing good meanings to a soft thing (*al-shay' al-layyin*).

*Al-līn* (softness), in its literal sense, is an attribute of bodies: it is the moistness of a body's surface and the ease of its bending. Its opposite is roughness (*al-khushūna*). *Al-līn* is used figuratively for ease of dealing and forgiveness. 'Amr ibn Kulthum said:

"Indeed our spear-shaft, O 'Amr, has refused, against the enemies before you, to bend."

Softness is among the marks of calling to the truth. Allah the Exalted said (﴿And argue with them in the way that is best﴾ [An-Nahl: 125]) and said (﴿It was by a mercy from Allah that you were gentle with them﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 159]). From the gentleness in Musa's call to Pharaoh is His saying (﴿So say, "Would you have a way to purify yourself? And I would guide you to your Lord, so you would fear Him."﴾ [An-Nazi'at: 18–19]) and His saying (﴿And peace is upon those who follow guidance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]). The intent of the calling of the messengers is that guidance be attained, not the display of grandeur and harshness of speech without benefit. So when gentleness does not benefit the one called, and he turns away and is arrogant, harshness may be permitted in admonishing him. Allah the Exalted said (﴿And do not argue with the People of the Book except in the way that is best, except for those of them who have wronged﴾ [Al-'Ankabut: 46]), and Allah the Exalted said about Musa (﴿Indeed, it has been revealed to us that the punishment will be for whoever denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48]).

The expectation (*al-tarajji*) derived from *la'alla* (perhaps) is either an illustration of the matter of Allah in calling Pharaoh by the matter of one who hopes, or it is an announcement to Musa and Pharaoh that they should hope for that,

[Page 226]

so the uttering of the particle of expectation was on their tongues, just as you say to a person when you advise him with something: "Perhaps ease will meet you," while you do not mean that you hope for that, but by requesting a hope from the addressee. Its parallels have occurred in the Qur'an more than once.

*Al-tadhakkur* (being reminded) is from *al-dhikr*, with a *dhāl* that is vowelled with *ḍamma*, meaning consideration (*al-nazar*). That is, perhaps he will consider with the consideration of one who sees clearly, and so he will recognize the truth, or he will fear the descent of punishment upon him and so obey out of fear, not out of insight. Pharaoh was among those who were given to transgression and who believed that he was upon the truth. So *al-tadhkir* (reminding) is that he know that he is upon falsehood, and *al-khashya* (fear) is that he hesitate in this and fear that he is upon falsehood, so he take precaution for himself by adopting what Musa called him to.

Here ends the address of Allah the Exalted to Musa, peace be upon him.

The two sentences are separated because they stand in the position of a dialogue between Musa together with his brother and God, Exalted is He, according to both of the two aspects we mentioned just now; that is, the two of them gathered their resolve, and Musa and Harun resolved to go to Fir'awn, so they whispered to their Lord.

Page 227
(﴿They said: "Our Lord, we fear that he will hasten against us, or that he will transgress."﴾), because most of the thinking about consequences and obstacles occurs at the time of resolving upon an action and beginning to prepare for it. For this reason their command was repeated with the words of God, Exalted is He: (﴿So go to him﴾).

Yafruṭu (يَفْرُطُ) means "he hastens" and "he precedes." It is said: faraṭa, yafruṭu, from the pattern of naṣara. The fāriṭ (الفارِط) is the one who goes ahead of the herd to the watering-place to drink. The meaning is: we fear that he will hasten to punish us, by killing or by other punishments, before we deliver the message to him and establish the proof against him.

And ṭughyān (الطُّغْيان) is making a display of arrogance. It has already been mentioned just now in His words (﴿Go to Fir'awn; indeed he has transgressed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 24]). That is, we fear that his pride will take hold of him, so that he regards our mention of a god other than himself as belittling him and as an attack on his claim to divinity, and so he transgresses, that is, there issues from him what is the effect of pride, such as contempt and humiliation. So the mention of transgression after hastening indicates that the two of them cannot bear that. This is a movement from the stronger to the weaker, because (we fear) is interpreted as having the sense of negation. In negation the weaker is mentioned after the stronger, the reverse of affirmation, unless there is something requiring the reverse.

The complement of (yaṭghā) is omitted. It may be that its omission is due to the indication of its counterpart; it was chosen for omission to preserve the rhyme (fawāṣil). The estimate is: or that he will transgress against us. It is also possible that its complement is not the counterpart of what was mentioned before it, but another complement, since the hypothetical division is an indication of it. For when the complement of (﴿he hastens against us﴾) was mentioned, and hastening included all kinds of punishment, even humiliation by insult, the division by (or) necessarily considered another situation, namely his transgression against one who is beyond his punishment, that is, that he transgress against God by belittling Him, like His words, (﴿I know of no god for you other than me﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]) and His words (﴿that I may look upon the god of Musa﴾ [al-Qasas: 38]). So the complement of yaṭghā is then omitted, to exalt Him from being stated explicitly in this context. The estimate is: or that he will transgress against you, so that he hardens in his disbelief and it becomes difficult to turn him away from it.

Page 228
In guarding against that there is zeal for the side of God, Exalted is He. And in it also there is a guard against the entrenchment of the creed of disbelief in the soul of the transgressor, so that hope for his faith afterwards becomes weaker than it was before, and that is a corruption in the view of religion. Al-ityān (الإتْيان) is arrival and alighting; that is, go and alight with him, because coming is the result of the going commanded in the preceding address. They had already drawn near to Fir'awn's place, since they were in his city, so they were commanded to come to him and call him. The dual of rasūl (رسول) came according to the original in agreement with the description applied to it in singular and otherwise.

Fa'ūl in the sense of maf'ūl admits agreement, as in their saying: nāqah ṭarūqat al-faḥl (a she-camel mounted by the stallion), and non-agreement, as in their saying: waḥshiyyah khalūj, that is, whose young has been torn away from her. Both forms occur in words like rasūl, and both are equally acceptable.

Page 229
Among its coming without agreement is His words, Exalted is He, in Surat al-Shu'ara' (﴿So come to Fir'awn and say: Indeed we are a messenger of the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 16]). Its verification will come there, God willing.

He introduced the particle of consequence (fa) before the request for the release of the Children of Israel, because he made the request for their release like something established and known to Fir'awn, either because the news of their resolve to attend Fir'awn for that request had already spread, or because he made it, given its importance, like something settled. The consequence of that is upon their being two messengers from God openly, because a messenger from God must be obeyed.

They specified the Lord by an attribution to the pronoun of Fir'awn, intending the greatest reach of the call, since God being their Lord is known from their saying (﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾), and His being the Lord of mankind is known all the more, because Fir'awn had taught them that he was the Lord.

The punishment from which they asked him to refrain was that in which Fir'awn would employ the Children of Israel in hard labour in service, because he regarded the Children of Israel as slaves and servants in return for their settling in his land.

The clause (﴿Indeed we have come to you with a sign from your Lord﴾) contains an explanation of the clause (﴿Indeed we are two messengers of your Lord﴾), so the first was a summary and the second an explanation. It also carries the sense of causation, for the confirmation that they are two messengers from God by what God manifests at the hand of one of them of signs of truthfulness. Both purposes require separating the clause from the one before it.

They limited themselves to stating that they were accompanied by a sign, to show that they were prepared to display the sign if Fir'awn wished it. But if he believed without needing the sign to be displayed, his faith would be more perfect. For this reason, in Surat al-A'raf, Fir'awn's words are related: (﴿He said: If you have come with a sign, then produce it, if you are among the truthful﴾ [al-A'raf: 106]). This sign is the transformation of the staff into a serpent, and it was followed by other signs.

Page 230
Limiting the request to the release of the Children of Israel indicates that Musa was sent to rescue the Children of Israel and to form an independent nation, by disseminating among them the law that benefits them and that establishes their independence and authority. He was not sent to address the Copts with the law. Nevertheless he called Fir'awn and his people to monotheism, because it is obligatory on him to change the evil that is among them. Also, because that is a means to his answer to the request for the release of the Children of Israel. This is drawn from what is in this verse, what is in the verse of Surat al-Isra', what is in the verse of Surat al-Nazi'at, and the other verses.

And al-salām (السَّلام) means safety and honour. It is not intended here as a greeting, since there is no specific person to whom the greeting is directed. Nor is Fir'awn's greeting meant, because it occurs at the beginning of an encounter, not in the course of speech. This is like the words of the Prophet ﷺ in his letter to Heraclius and others: "Accept Islam and you will be safe" (ﷺ).

And (ʿalā) indicates firmness, that is, the safety of those who follow the guidance is established for them without doubt. This is a precaution and an introduction to the warning in His words (﴿Indeed it has been revealed to us that the punishment is for whoever denies and turns away﴾). So His words (﴿And peace be upon whoever follows the guidance﴾) is an allusion that Fir'awn should seek the guidance that Musa, peace be upon him, brought.

His words (﴿Indeed it has been revealed to us﴾) are an allusion to warning him of denial before it occurs from him, in order to convey the message in the most complete manner before Fir'awn's opinion on that becomes manifest, so that they do not confront him after his opinion appears with an explicit directing of the warning at him. This is the style of gentle speech which God commanded them to use.

The definition of al-'adhāb (الْعَذَاب) is the definition of genus, so the defined term is in the position of an indefinite, as if it were said: indeed a punishment is for whoever denies.

Unrestricted mention of peace and punishment, without limitation to this world or the Hereafter, is a generalization of glad tidings and warning. God, Exalted is He, said in Surat al-Nazi'at (﴿So God seized him with the punishment of the Hereafter and the former﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 25]) (﴿Indeed in that is a lesson for whoever fears﴾ [al-Nazi'at: 26]).

All of this is the speech of God which He commanded them to convey to Fir'awn, as the following indicates, namely His words (﴿He said: Who then is your Lord, O Musa?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49]), in the manner of relating dialogues. What has been mentioned from the beginning of the story up to here has not occurred in the preceding surahs.

This is the narration of Pharaoh's reply to the message that God commanded Moses and Aaron to deliver to Pharaoh. The verse therefore omits some clauses that the context implies, for the sake of brevity. The implied sentence is: "So they both came to him and said to him what they had been commanded, and he said: 'Who then is your Lord?'" For this reason, Pharaoh's speech is reported as a separate sentence, in the manner of reporting dialogues that we have inferred from the Qur'anic style and explained in Surat al-Baqara and elsewhere.

Pharaoh addressed them both using the dual pronoun, then singled out Moses by directing the address to him, because he knew that Moses was the principal bearer of the message and that Aaron was his follower. Although their speech does not contain this, it must be that Pharaoh knew it from the manner in which they entered upon him and addressed him. Moreover, Moses was well known in Pharaoh's court, since he had been raised by him or by his father, so he had a previous association with the house of Pharaoh, as is shown by Pharaoh's words to him reported in the verse of Surat al-Shu'ara' (﴿He said: "Did We not raise you among us as a child, and you remained among us for years of your life?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 18]), and so on.

Perhaps Moses was the one who took up the speech while Aaron confirmed what he said, by word or by gesture. His attribution of the Lord to the pronoun of both of them is because they both said to him (﴿Indeed, we are two messengers of your Lord﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]).

Pharaoh turned away from saying "Who then is my Lord?" to his words "Who then is your Lord?" (﴿your Lord﴾), turning away from acknowledging being a creature under lordship, even by reporting their words, lest that be heard by his followers and people, who would then suppose that he was uncertain about the knowledge of his Lord, or that he had acknowledged that he had a lord. Moses took up the answer because he was singled out for the question by being addressed, to the exclusion of others.

Moses answered by affirming the lordship of God over all existing things, following the rule of inferring the particular from the universal (istidlal bi-l-kulliyya 'ala al-juz'iyya, deduction from the general to the particular), such that a syllogism (qiyas, a logical inference) is formed from the combination of the two, for Pharaoh is among all things, and so he is included in the generality of "every thing."

"Every thing" is the first object of (a'ta, gave). And (khalqahu, its creation) is its second object.

Khalq (creation) is a verbal noun meaning bringing into existence. The verb "gave" was used to draw attention to the fact that creation and formation are a blessing. Thus it is both an argument for lordship and a reminder of the blessing together.

It is also possible that khalq is meant in the more specific sense, namely creation in a particular form, so that it means "making" (ja'l): the One who gave every existing thing its particular form, and through that creation the genera, species, categories and individuals came into being as effects of it.

It is also possible that "every thing" is the second object of (a'ta), and its first object is (khalqahu), meaning: He gave His creatures what they need, as in His words (﴿So We brought forth thereby the vegetation of every thing﴾ [al-An'am: 99]). The structure of the sentence is apt for both meanings.

The inclusiveness conveyed by "every" (kull) is customary, meaning every thing whose nature it is to be given to by the kinds of creatures and that suits the giver. Or it is inclusiveness intended as distribution, by matching things with "creation," as in the saying: "The people rode their animals."

The meaning is: reflect and consider whether you gave creation or not. There is no doubt that he knows that he did not give every thing its creation. When he reflects, he will know that the Lord is the One who poured out existence and blessings upon all existing things, and so he will believe in Him through the attribute of this characteristic and that knowledge, which leads to the correct belief.

(Thumma, then) denotes sequence in both its temporal and its ranking senses: He created things, then guided them to that for which He created them, and He guided them to the truth after He created them and poured out blessings upon them, in the manner of His saying, may He be exalted (﴿Did We not make for him two eyes?﴾ [al-Balad: 8] ﴿and a tongue and two lips?﴾ [al-Balad: 9] ﴿And We guided him to the two highways?﴾ [al-Balad: 10]), meaning the paths of good and evil, that is, We distinguished between them by clear proofs.

Al-Zamakhshari said in al-Kashshaf: "How excellent is this answer! How concise it is, how comprehensive, and how clear, for one who applies his mind and looks with an eye of fairness and is seeking the truth."

**Ibn 'Ashur's commentary (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah Ta-Ha (20), verses 51–52:**

﴿He said, "Then what is the state of the former generations?"﴾ ﴿He said, "Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record. My Lord neither errs nor forgets."﴾

The word *al-bal* (بال) has a subtle meaning. It is used for a matter of importance, and its verbal noun is *al-balah* (البالَهُ) with the *lam* lightened. God, exalted is He, says: ﴿He has amended their state (bālahum) and forgiven their sins﴾ [Muhammad: 2], meaning their condition. In the hadith, "Every matter of importance (dhi bāl)..." and so on. The word is also used for opinion, as when one says, "such-and-such occurred to my mind" (khaṭara bi-bālī). People also say, "I did not pay it any attention" (mā alqā lahu bālan). The choice of this word here is one of the finer rhetorical features.

Page 234

Pharaoh wanted to dispute with Musa by means of what had happened to the past generations who followed the religion of Pharaoh, that is, the generations of the people of Egypt. He asked, in effect, "What is their state? Do you claim that they all agreed upon misguidance?" This is the manner of one who has no argument: he resorts to stirring confusion by feigning that his opponent's words are implausible. It is similar in meaning to the words of Pharaoh and his chiefs in another verse: ﴿They said, "Have you come to turn us away from what we found our fathers doing?"﴾ [Yunus: 78].

It is also possible that the meaning is that Pharaoh wanted to create confusion against Musa when his argument had prevailed, by turning him to speak about the state of the former generations: "Are they in punishment?" in reference to Musa's words ﴿that the punishment is upon him who denies and turns away﴾ [Ta-Ha: 48]. If he said, "They are in punishment," their descendants would rage and become enemies of Musa. If he said, "They are in peace," Pharaoh's argument would prevail, since he follows their religion. Also, because Musa had informed him of his Lord, and this implied the first creation, it occurred to Pharaoh to ask him about the belief concerning the fate of people after annihilation. So he asked, "What is the state of the former generations?" and "What is their affair, and what is the report about them?" This is a question meant to confound and to create confusion.

Musa's answer, ﴿Their knowledge is with my Lord, in a Record﴾, is suitable for both possibilities. According to the first possibility, Musa turned him away from delving into what is of no benefit in that context, since that context was purely for calling the living, not for investigating the dead who had passed on to the world of recompense. This is like the saying of the Prophet (ﷺ) when he was asked about the children of the polytheists: "God knows best what they used to do."

According to the second possibility, Musa avoided mentioning their state, thwarting Pharaoh's purpose and turning away from occupying himself with something other than the aim for which he had been sent.

The summary is that Musa avoided undertaking debate and contradiction on matters other than those for which he had come, because he had not been sent for that. In this turning away there are many benefits.

Page 235

He had knowledge of the general state of the former generations, but was not aware of the details of their conditions and the conditions of their individuals.

The construct *ʿilmuhā* (عِلْمُها) is an idafa of a verbal noun to its object. The pronoun in *ʿilmuhā* refers back to "the former generations," because a collective noun may have a feminine pronoun.

His words *fī kitāb* (في كتاب) may be understood as the Record being a metaphor for the detailed knowledge, likening it to written matters. It may also be a metonymy for the certainty of knowledge, since written things are established and certain, as in the words of al-Harith ibn Hilliza: "Do the desires overturn what is in the scrolls?"

This meaning is confirmed by His words ﴿My Lord neither errs nor forgets﴾. *Al-dalāl* (الضلال) is error in knowledge, likened to losing the way. *Al-nisyān* (النسيان) is the failure to recall a known matter in the mind of one who knows.

This passage consists of three sentences inserted into the middle of the story of Musa (Moses).

The first sentence is a new, independent sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a fresh opening sentence), in keeping with the Qur'an's habit of varying its style to refresh the listener's attention. It cannot be part of Musa's own speech, because that would not suit the sequence of his words, "so We brought forth with it pairs" (﴿فَأخْرَجْنا بِهِ أزْواجًا﴾). ﴿Who made the earth a cradle for you﴾ (﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأرْضَ مِهادًا﴾) is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: He is the One who made the earth a cradle for you. The pronoun refers to the Lord mentioned in "my Lord" (*rabbi*) earlier in the story, so the meaning is: He is the Lord of Musa.

The definiteness of the two parts of the sentence conveys restriction (*qasr*, exclusivity), meaning: the One who made the earth a cradle, so how can you worship other than Him? This is a true restriction, but it is not intended as a direct refutation of the polytheists. It is a reminder of a blessing, and an allusion that others do not truly deserve divinity.

The majority of readers recite *mihādan* with a kasra on the *mīm*. It is a noun meaning "that which is prepared," like *firāsh* (bedding) and *libās* (clothing). It may also be the plural of *mahd*, which is what is prepared for an infant, on which it is laid and carried. In that case it takes the pattern of *ki'āb*, the plural of *ka'b*. The plural form is understood in light of the many tracts of land.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read *mahdan* with a fatḥa on the *mīm* and a sukūn on the *hāʾ*, meaning like the cradle prepared for an infant. It is a noun derived from the verbal noun of *mahada* (to prepare), with the verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, as *al-khalq* is used in the sense of *al-makhlūq* (the created). This usage then became common and came to mean that which is prepared.

The two readings have one meaning: He made the earth prepared and made easy for walking, sitting and lying down, such that there are no protrusions in it except rarely, and these can be avoided. This is like His words, ﴿And God has made the earth a spread-out carpet for you﴾ (Nuh 71:19), ﴿That you may follow therein roads, spacious ways﴾ (Nuh 71:20).

*Salaka* is a verb derived from *suluk* (going through). *Salk* is entering while passing through and cutting across during travel along a road, a metaphor for the traveller being like a thing that enters into another thing. One says *salaka ṭarīqan* (he took a road). The basic rule for this verb is that it takes one object, the thing entered into, and it is used transitively in the sense of *aslaka* (to cause to pass through). The regular form of its transitivity would be with the causative *hamza*, as in *aslaka al-mismār fī al-lawḥ* (he caused the nail to pass into the board, meaning he made it go through). However, it has become common in speech to use it without the *hamza*, as in His words, ﴿We shall make it enter into a painful punishment﴾ (al-Jinn 72:17). It has also become common for the noun that was originally the second object to be put in the genitive with *fī* (in), as in His words, ﴿What has caused you to enter into Saqar?﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:42), meaning what has caused you to enter Saqar. Also His words, ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:200), in Surat al-Shu'ara'. And His words, ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky and causes it to flow as springs in the earth?﴾ (al-Zumar 39:21), in Surat al-Zumar. Al-A'sha said:

*As the carpenter drives the nail into the door*

That is, the carpenter inserted the nail into the door. So the verb *salaka* came to be used both intransitively and transitively.

As for His words here, ﴿And He made roads for you therein﴾ (﴿وسَلَكَ لَكم فِيها سُبُلًا﴾), it is *salaka* in its transitive sense, meaning *aslaka fīhā subulan*: He made roads go through the earth, that is, He made roads passing and penetrating into it, interspersed. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for their abundance in all directions of the earth.

By "roads" is meant every path on which it is possible to travel, whether it comes from the original creation of the earth, such as plains and sands, or from the effect of human activity, such as hilltops where travel has been repeated until they were trodden and became roads that people follow.

When He had mentioned the blessing of the creation of the earth, He followed it with the blessing of bringing forth plants from it through the water that descends upon it from the sky. This is a blessing that refers to the creation of the heavens, since He brought up its mention for the purpose of that reminder. For this reason He did not say "and We poured water upon the earth," as in the verse, ﴿That We poured water in abundance, then We split the earth in splitting﴾ (Abasa 80:25). This is an eloquent *idmāj* (embedding of one theme within another).

The turn from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in "so We brought forth" (*fa-akhrajnā*) is an *iltifāt* (shift of person). Its beauty here is that, after He had argued against the polytheists with the proof of His sole creation of the earth and His subjugation of the heavens, something they could not deny, the discourse rose to the form of the first person of the one who is obeyed. The One who created the earth and subjected the heavens is worthy of being obeyed by the forces and elements. So He brings forth plants from the earth through the water of the sky. The subjection of the plants is therefore a consequence of the subjection of their origin, which is formed from the water of the sky and the dust of the earth.

Because of attention to this point, this kind of *iltifāt* recurs in the Qur'an when mentioning the growing of plants, as in His words, ﴿And He it is who sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth with it the growth of everything﴾ (al-An'am 6:99), and His words, ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky, and We bring forth with it fruits of diverse colours?﴾ (Fatir 35:27), and His words, ﴿Or who created the heavens and the earth and sent down for you water from the sky, and We caused to grow with it gardens of delightful beauty?﴾ (al-Naml 27:60). Among them is His words in Surat al-Zukhruf, ﴿And He who sends down water from the sky in a measure, and with it We revive a dead land﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:11). Al-Zamakhshari (in al-Kashshaf) drew attention to this, and how excellent is his insight. Its parallels in the Qur'an are numerous.

*Al-azwāj* is the plural of *zawj*. The essential meaning of *zawj* is a name for each of two of one kind, so each of them is a *zawj* in relation to the other, since by the precedence of the first one it becomes a *zawj* to it. Then it became specifically used for the male and female pair of the human species or of animals. He said, ﴿Then load therein of every kind two mates﴾ (al-Mu'minun 23:27), and He said, ﴿And He made of him the two mates, the male and the female﴾ (al-Qiyamah 75:39), and He said, ﴿Dwell, you and your spouse, in the Garden﴾ (al-Baqarah 2:35). Since the consideration of the meaning of unity of type became widespread in it, people extended from this to using the word *zawj* in the sense of a type without the condition that it be second to another. This is by way of *majāz mursal* (metonymy) through the relation of generality. He said, ﴿Glory be to Him who created all the pairs, from what the earth grows, and from themselves, and from what they do not know﴾ (Ya Sin 36:36), and from it is His words, ﴿Then We caused to grow therein of every noble pair﴾ (Luqman 31:10).

In a hadith, "Whoever spends two pairs in the way of God, the gatekeepers of Paradise will hasten to him..." (the hadith continues), meaning whoever spends two kinds, such as food and clothing, or horses and mounts. This general usage is what is intended here, meaning: So We brought forth with it kinds of plants. It was mentioned before in Surat al-Ra'd.

*Al-nabāt* (plants) is a verbal noun used as the name of the thing that grows. Because it was originally a verbal noun, the singular and the plural are the same in it.

*Shattā* is the plural of *shatīt*, on the pattern *fa'lā*, like *marīḍ* and *marḍā*.

*Al-shatīt* means the scattered one, that is, the far apart. Here it means divergence in attributes, of shape, colour and taste. Some of them are suitable for humans and some for animals.

The second sentence, ﴿Eat and pasture your livestock﴾ (﴿كُلُوا وارْعَوْا أنْعامَكُمْ﴾), is a quoted speech (*maqūl qawl*) of an elided verb, in the state of a circumstantial clause (*ḥāl*) from the pronoun in *fa-akhrajnā*. The implied sense is: saying, "Eat and pasture your livestock." The imperative here is for permission, and what is meant by it is a favour. The implied sense is: Eat from them and pasture your livestock from them. This is an instance of matching a plural with a plural for the purpose of distribution.

The verb *ra'ā* is used both intransitively and transitively. One says *ra'at al-dābba* (the animal grazed) and *ra'āhā ṣāḥibuhā* (its owner pastured it). The two are distinguished in the verbal noun: the verbal noun of the intransitive is *al-ra'y*, and the verbal noun of the transitive is *al-ri'āya*. From it is the saying of al-Nabigha:

*I saw you watching over me with a discerning eye*

The third sentence, ﴿Indeed in that are signs for people of understanding﴾ (﴿إنَّ في ذَلِكَ لَآياتٍ لِأُولِي النُّهى﴾), is a parenthetical clause that serves to confirm the argument. After it had been pointed out that the aforementioned creatures show the existence of the Maker and His oneness, and the blessing they constitute for humans to whoever reflects, these signs were gathered together in this sentence, and what all of them contain of numerous signs was stated explicitly. Both the parenthetical insertion and the emphasis require the separation of the sentence. The affirmation of the predicate with the particle *inna* serves to treat the addressees as if they were deniers, because they did not reflect on the indication of those creatures to God's oneness, though they think themselves to be among the people of understanding. Their failure to be guided by those signs was only because they did not regard them as signs. Indeed, what has been mentioned contains many signs that people of intellect perceive through reflection and contemplation, and they become aware of them through being reminded.

*Al-nuhā* is a noun, the plural of *nuhya* (with a *ḍamma* on the *nūn* and a sukūn on the *hāʾ*), meaning intellect. It was called *nuhya* because it is the cause by which the one who possesses it desists from many corrupting and destructive deeds. For this reason it is also called *ʿaql* (intellect) and called *ḥijr* (restraint).

This passage consists of three sentences inserted into the middle of the story of Musa (Moses).

The first sentence is a new, independent sentence (*isti'naf ibtida'i*, a fresh opening sentence), in keeping with the Qur'an's habit of varying its style to refresh the listener's attention. It cannot be part of Musa's own speech, because that would not suit the sequence of his words, "so We brought forth with it pairs" (﴿فَأخْرَجْنا بِهِ أزْواجًا﴾). ﴿Who made the earth a cradle for you﴾ (﴿الَّذِي جَعَلَ لَكُمُ الأرْضَ مِهادًا﴾) is the predicate of an elided subject, meaning: He is the One who made the earth a cradle for you. The pronoun refers to the Lord mentioned in "my Lord" (*rabbi*) earlier in the story, so the meaning is: He is the Lord of Musa.

The definiteness of the two parts of the sentence conveys restriction (*qasr*, exclusivity), meaning: the One who made the earth a cradle, so how can you worship other than Him? This is a true restriction, but it is not intended as a direct refutation of the polytheists. It is a reminder of a blessing, and an allusion that others do not truly deserve divinity.

The majority of readers recite *mihādan* with a kasra on the *mīm*. It is a noun meaning "that which is prepared," like *firāsh* (bedding) and *libās* (clothing). It may also be the plural of *mahd*, which is what is prepared for an infant, on which it is laid and carried. In that case it takes the pattern of *ki'āb*, the plural of *ka'b*. The plural form is understood in light of the many tracts of land.

ʿĀṣim, Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī and Khalaf read *mahdan* with a fatḥa on the *mīm* and a sukūn on the *hāʾ*, meaning like the cradle prepared for an infant. It is a noun derived from the verbal noun of *mahada* (to prepare), with the verbal noun used in the sense of the passive participle, as *al-khalq* is used in the sense of *al-makhlūq* (the created). This usage then became common and came to mean that which is prepared.

The two readings have one meaning: He made the earth prepared and made easy for walking, sitting and lying down, such that there are no protrusions in it except rarely, and these can be avoided. This is like His words, ﴿And God has made the earth a spread-out carpet for you﴾ (Nuh 71:19), ﴿That you may follow therein roads, spacious ways﴾ (Nuh 71:20).

*Salaka* is a verb derived from *suluk* (going through). *Salk* is entering while passing through and cutting across during travel along a road, a metaphor for the traveller being like a thing that enters into another thing. One says *salaka ṭarīqan* (he took a road). The basic rule for this verb is that it takes one object, the thing entered into, and it is used transitively in the sense of *aslaka* (to cause to pass through). The regular form of its transitivity would be with the causative *hamza*, as in *aslaka al-mismār fī al-lawḥ* (he caused the nail to pass into the board, meaning he made it go through). However, it has become common in speech to use it without the *hamza*, as in His words, ﴿We shall make it enter into a painful punishment﴾ (al-Jinn 72:17). It has also become common for the noun that was originally the second object to be put in the genitive with *fī* (in), as in His words, ﴿What has caused you to enter into Saqar?﴾ (al-Muddaththir 74:42), meaning what has caused you to enter Saqar. Also His words, ﴿Thus We have caused it to enter into the hearts of the criminals﴾ (al-Shu'ara' 26:200), in Surat al-Shu'ara'. And His words, ﴿Have you not seen that God sends down water from the sky and causes it to flow as springs in the earth?﴾ (al-Zumar 39:21), in Surat al-Zumar. Al-A'sha said:

*As the carpenter drives the nail into the door*

That is, the carpenter inserted the nail into the door. So the verb *salaka* came to be used both intransitively and transitively.

As for His words here, ﴿And He made roads for you therein﴾ (﴿وسَلَكَ لَكم فِيها سُبُلًا﴾), it is *salaka* in its transitive sense, meaning *aslaka fīhā subulan*: He made roads go through the earth, that is, He made roads passing and penetrating into it, interspersed. This is a metonymy (*kināya*) for their abundance in all directions of the earth.

By "roads" is meant every path on which it is possible to travel, whether it comes from the original creation of the earth, such as plains and sands, or from the effect of human activity, such as hilltops where travel has been repeated until they were trodden and became roads that people follow.

When He had mentioned the blessing of the creation of the earth, He followed it with the blessing of bringing forth plants from it through the water that descends upon it from the sky. This is a blessing that refers to the creation of the heavens, since He brought up its mention for the purpose of that reminder. For this reason He did not say "and We poured water upon the earth," as in the verse, ﴿That We poured water in abundance, then We split the earth in splitting﴾ (Abasa 80:25). This is an eloquent *idmāj* (embedding of one theme within another).

The turn from the third-person pronoun to the first-person pronoun in "so We brought forth" (*fa-akhrajnā*) is an *iltifāt* (shift of person). Its beauty here is that, after He had argued against the polytheists with the proof of His sole creation of the earth and His subjugation of the heavens, something they could not deny, the discourse rose to the form of the first person of the one who is obeyed. The One who created the earth and subjected the heavens is worthy of being obeyed by the forces and elements. So He brings forth plants from the earth through the water of the sky. The subjection of the plants is therefore a consequence of the subjection of their origin, which is formed from the water of the sky and the dust of the earth.
