Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 55:

﴿From it We created you, and into it We will return you, and from it We will bring you forth once more.﴾

It is a fresh sentence, a resumption of a new topic (*isti'naf ibtida'i*). This is an *idmaj* (embedding), a reminder of the first creation, so that it serves as proof of the possibility of the second creation after death. The connection is firm: mentioning the creation of the earth and its benefits calls for completing the mention of what matters most to people about its conditions. Thus the creation of the origin of man from the earth resembles the growth of plants from it, and bringing people out to the gathering (*hashr*) resembles bringing plants out of the earth. God the Exalted said (﴿And God has caused you to grow from the earth as a growth. Then He will return you into it and bring you forth in an emergence.﴾ [Nuh: 17]). The fronting of the three prepositional phrases before their complements is as follows: as for the first and third prepositional phrases, it is to emphasize that the earth is the origin of the first creation and of the second creation. As for fronting (﴿and into it We will return you﴾), it is for the sake of *muzawaja* (pairing) with its two counterparts.

God the Exalted's words (﴿and into it We will return you﴾) indicate that burying the dead in the earth is the legislated method of concealing the dead, whether it is a pit (*shaqq*) or a niche (*lahd*), because both are a return into the earth. As for what some non-religious nations do, such as cremating the dead with fire, or drowning them in water, or placing them in coffins above the ground, this contradicts the sunnah of God and His natural disposition (*fitrah*), because the natural disposition requires that the dead body falls to the earth, so it must be concealed in it. Likewise, the first burial among humans was when one of the two sons of Adam killed his brother, as God the Exalted said in Surat al-'Uqud (﴿Then God sent a crow digging in the earth to show him how to conceal his brother's nakedness. He said, "Woe to me! Was I unable to be like this crow and conceal my brother's nakedness?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 31]). Thus the divine laws brought the obligation of burial in the earth.

*Al-tara* means "a time" (*marrah*), and its plural is *taratat*. The origin of its alif is a waw. Ibn al-A'rabi said: the origin of its alif is a hamza, but when they used it frequently they dropped the hamza. Some of them said: the hamza appears in its plural on the pattern *fi'al*, so they said *ti'ar* with a hamza. It appears that it is a fixed noun (*ism jamid*) that has no derived root from which it comes.

*Al-ikhraj* (bringing forth) refers to bringing them out to the gathering after the frameworks (*hayakil*) of the bodies have been restored inside the earth, as is apparent from His words (﴿and from it We will bring you forth﴾). For this reason, bringing forth was made the "second time" relative to the first creation from the earth. In this there is an allusion that the bringing forth of bodies from the earth is by restoring their creation as they were created the first time. God the Exalted said (﴿As We began the first creation, We will repeat it﴾ [al-Anbiya': 104]).

[Page 242]

A return to the story of Musa (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh. This verse comes between the verses that relate the dialogue between Musa and Pharaoh. It serves as an introduction to restating what took place between Musa and Pharaoh in the dialogue. It is permissible for this sentence to be conjoined (ma'tuf) to the sentence ﴿He said, "Then who is your Lord, O Musa?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49], by considering what is presumed before the conjoined sentence, a statement that was omitted for brevity. Its presumed meaning: "So they came to him and said what We had commanded them to say. He said, 'Then who is your Lord?' etc." The meaning: they came to him and said what We had commanded them, and We showed him all Our signs through Musa (peace be upon him).

It is also permissible for this sentence to be parenthetical (mu'taridah) between what precedes it, and the waw is parenthetical (i'tiradiyyah).

The emphasis of the statement by the oath particle (lam al-qasam) and "qad" (the particle of confirmation) is used to express wonder at Pharaoh's obstinacy in his opposition. Its purpose is to show the severity of his disbelief, and to show that Musa had many signs which Allah displayed to Pharaoh, yet they did not benefit his faith.

It is stated in general terms (ujmilat wa 'ummimat) and not detailed, because the purpose here is to show the severity of his obstinacy in disbelief, unlike the verse in Surat al-A'raf, where the purpose is to show the succession of the signs and their being a victory.

Allah's showing him the signs (irā'ah) means making them manifest to him in such a way that he witnessed them.

The addition of "signs" (ayat) to the Divine Name (damir al-jalalah) here conveys a definiteness to specific, known signs, since the definiteness of a plural by annexation (idafah) comes for the same reasons that definiteness by the article (al-) does: it can denote a known reference ('ahd) or comprehensiveness (istighraq). The intended meaning here is the first, i.e., "We showed Pharaoh Our signs which occurred through Musa," which are those mentioned in His words, ﴿among nine signs to Pharaoh and his people﴾ [An-Naml: 12]. They are: the staff turning into a serpent, the hand turning white, the years of drought, the locusts, the lice, the frogs, the blood, the flood, and the splitting of the sea. His denial continued after all of them, until when he saw the splitting of the sea, he plunged into it, hoping to triumph over the Children of Israel.

The emphasis of "signs" by the emphasizing word "kullaha" (all of them) is for increasing the wonder at his obstinacy. A parallel to it is His words, ﴿And the warners had certainly come to the family of Pharaoh, but they denied Our signs, all of them﴾ [Al-Qamar: 41] in Surat al-Qamar.

[Page 243]

The apparent practice of the exegetes (mufassirun) is that they made the sentence ﴿And We had certainly shown him Our signs﴾ conjoined to the sentence ﴿He said, "Then who is your Lord, O Musa?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49], and the sentence ﴿He said, "Then who is your Lord?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 49] an explanation of the sentence ﴿so he denied and refused﴾. This entails that Pharaoh's resolve to bring the magicians was later than the will to show all the signs, and so they fell into the problem of the validity of the generalization in His words, ﴿All Our signs﴾. How can that be before the magicians' acknowledgment that they had been overcome, when many of the signs appeared only after a long time, such as the years of drought, the blood, and the splitting of the sea? But this interpretation has no basis, because conjunction by the waw does not require sequential order.

[Page 244 begins within the passage below.]

This sentence is linked to the sentence (﴿Pharaoh said, "Then what of the former generations?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 51]) and is Musa's answer to it. Its opening with the verb (qāla, "he said") and its not being conjoined by a conjunction leave no doubt that this is part of the same dialogue.

His saying (﴿"Have you come to us to drive us out of our land with your magic, O Musa?"﴾) implies that Musa had shown him the sign of the staff turning into a serpent and his hand turning white. This is what Pharaoh called magic. He explicitly stated this implication in His saying, may He be exalted, relating their words (﴿He said, "If you take a god other than me, I will surely make you among the imprisoned."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 29] ﴿He said, "Even if I bring you something clear?"﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 30] ﴿He said, "Then bring it, if you are among the truthful."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 31] ﴿So he threw his staff, and suddenly it was a clear serpent.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 32] ﴿And he drew out his hand, and suddenly it was white to the onlookers.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 33] ﴿He said to the chiefs around him, "Indeed, this is a knowing magician.﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 34] ﴿He wants to drive you out of your land with his magic."﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 35]). The verse is in Surat al-Shu'ara'. Its mention is dispensed with here because of what is contained in the sentence (﴿And We had shown him all Our signs﴾ [Ta-Ha: 56]) of the comprehensive generality that includes the sign of the staff turning into a serpent.

His attributing the magic to the pronoun of Musa was intended to belittle the status of that which he called magic. His attributing the bringing of magic of its like to the pronoun of himself was to magnify his own status. The meaning of his bringing magic is: bringing the magicians before him, that is, "we will surely come to you with magic from those whose task is to produce magic," since magic necessarily requires a magician.

The likeness in His saying (*mithlihi*, "its like") is a likeness in the kind of magic, not in its strength.

Pharaoh made the reason for Musa's coming to him to be that his purpose was to drive them out of their land, by analogy with those who rise up with a call against kings, who aim thereby at removing them from kingship and taking their place. The meaning is that Musa's self deceived him, so he supposed that he could uproot Pharaoh from his kingdom. That is: you supposed that displaying extraordinary signs would make the nation obedient to you, so they would make you king over them and you would drive me out of my land. The pronoun of the speaker who is included is therefore used for magnification, not for participation, because nothing had proceeded from Musa that would suggest his driving them out of their land.

It is also permissible that the pronoun of the speaker who is included be used for the group, by way of predominance (*taghlīb*), and Pharaoh placed himself as one of them. By the group he meant the group of the Children of Israel, when Musa said to him (﴿So send with us the Children of Israel﴾ [Ta-Ha: 47]). That is: you came to drive out a part of the nation from our land, and you hope that the whole nation will follow you because of what you display to them of your magic.

[Page 245]

The interrogative in (*aji'tanā*, "have you come to us") is a denial (*inkārī*), and for this reason he based on it the oath concerning his bringing him magic of its like. The oath is one of the methods of displaying anger.

The lām is the lām of the oath, and the nūn is for its emphasis. By confronting Musa's act with its like, Pharaoh intended to remove what occurs in people's souls of believing Musa and that he is upon the truth, so that perhaps this would lead them to revolt against Pharaoh and remove him from the kingship of Egypt.

Upon this he based his request to fix an appointment between himself and Musa, in which he would bring before him those who practise magic like his magic. The word (*maw'id*, "appointment") here may be taken to mean the mīmī verbal noun, that is, the promise (*al-wa'd*), or it may be taken to mean the place of the promise, and this is a concision in speech.

His saying (*makānan*, "a place") is a *badal al-ishtimāl* (inclusive apposition) from (*maw'idan*, "an appointment") in one of its two meanings, because the verb requires a place and a time, so the place was substituted for it.

His saying (﴿we will not fail it﴾) in the reading of the majority is with the verb in the nominative, as an attribute of (*maw'idan*) in view of its verbal-noun meaning. Abu Ja'far read it with the *fā'* of (*nakhlifhu*) jussed, taking *lā* as a prohibition. The prohibition is a warning against failing to keep it.

As for (*siwan*, "equidistant"), Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and al-Kisa'i read it with a kasra on the sīn. 'Asim, Hamza, Ibn 'Amir, Ya'qub and Khalaf read it with a damma on the sīn, and both are dialects. The kasra is in the pattern *fi'al*. Abu 'Ali said: the pattern *fi'al* is rare in adjectives, like the phrase *qawmun 'idan* (a people hostile). Abu 'Ubayda, Abu Hatim and al-Nahhas said: the kasra of the sīn is the high, eloquent dialect, and it is an adjective derived from *al-istiwā'* (evenness). So it is permissible that *al-istiwā'* means the evenness of being in the middle between two directions. Abu 'Ubayda recited for Musa ibn Jabir al-Hanafi:

*"Indeed our father had settled in a land equidistant between Qays 'Aylan's Qays and al-Fizr."*

[Page 246]

ʿAlā) Commentary of Ibn ʿĀshūr (al-Taḥrīr wa al-Tanwīr) on Sūrat Ṭā Hā, verses 60–61:

﴿So Pharaoh withdrew, then gathered his scheme, and then came.﴾ ﴿Mūsā said to them, "Woe to you! Do not fabricate a lie against Allah, lest He destroy you with a punishment. Indeed, he who fabricates has failed."﴾

The consequence of Pharaoh's withdrawal and the gathering of his scheme, after Mūsā's appointment of the appointed time, is an indication that Pharaoh hastened to prepare for this appointment and did not waste the time in readying himself for it.

Al-tawallī (withdrawal) means departing. Here it is used in its literal sense: he departed from that assembly to where he would send messengers to the cities to gather those known for the knowledge of sorcery. This is like His, the Exalted, saying in Sūrat al-Nāziʿāt: ﴿Then he turned his back, striving; then he gathered [the people] and called out﴾ [al-Nāziʿāt: 22].

The meaning of "gathering the scheme" is arranging the method of disputing with Mūsā, preparing stratagems to show the sorcerers' victory over him, and persuading those present that Mūsā is "not upon anything."

This is an ancient method in debates: that the debater strives with all his effort to expose the falsehood of his opponent's proof by every means of deception, vilification and defamation, and anticipates him with what weakens his resolve and confuses his judgment, until his plan is lost.

Thus "gathering" here is used in the sense of preparing one's opinion and thoroughly arranging the matter, like His saying: ﴿So settle upon your plan﴾ [Yūnus: 71], meaning: he gathered his opinion and his plan with which he would scheme against Mūsā. It is also permissible that the meaning is: he gathered the people of his scheme, i.e., he gathered the sorcerers, in the manner of His saying: ﴿So the sorcerers were gathered for an appointed day of a known time﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 38].

Al-kayd (scheming) is concealing that which causes harm until the time of its execution. It has already been discussed under His saying: ﴿Indeed, My plan is firm﴾ [al-Aʿrāf: 183] in Sūrat al-Aʿrāf.

The meaning of ﴿then came﴾ is: then he attended the appointment. The particle "thumma" (then) indicates both real succession and rank, because his attendance at the appointment occurred after the passage of the interval of preparation, and because that attendance after gathering his scheme is more important than the gathering itself, since in it appears the effect of what he had prepared.

The clause ﴿Mūsā said to them﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 43] is a resumptive clause of explanatory resumption, because His saying ﴿then came﴾ provokes a question in the listener's mind: what happened when Pharaoh came to the appointed time? Mūsā intended to open with the sorcerers through admonition.

The pronoun in "lahum" (to them) refers to what is known from His saying ﴿so we will surely bring you a sorcery like it﴾ [Ṭā Hā: 58], i.e., to the people of sorcery. Or the address may be to all of them, since that gathering was in view and hearing of Pharaoh and his retinue; so the referent of the pronoun is what His saying ﴿he gathered his scheme, then came﴾ indicates, i.e., he gathered the men of his scheme.

The address in His saying "Woe to you" (wayḥakum) may be intended in its literal sense of supplication, in which case it is not in line with what he was commanded regarding speaking gently to Pharaoh. Either because the address with this was not directed at Pharaoh, but was directed specifically at the sorcerers indicated by His saying ﴿he gathered his scheme﴾, i.e., Mūsā said to the people of Pharaoh's scheme; or because when he saw that speaking gently to him was not beneficial, since he remained steadfast in his disbelief, he made his speech harsher as a rebuke to him, by a specific command from Allah at that moment, qualifying the general command to speak gently, as permission was given to Muḥammad ﷺ by His saying ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 39] and the verses following in Sūrat al-Ḥajj; or because when he saw that their deception upon those present, that their sorcery was a miracle for them from their gods and from Pharaoh their Most High Lord, and they said ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we are the victors﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 44], he saw it as obligatory upon himself to change the wrong with his tongue to the utmost of his ability, because that change is what befits the station of prophethood.

It is also permissible that the phrase "wayḥakum" is used to express astonishment at a strange situation, i.e., "I marvel at you and warn you," like the Prophet ﷺ's saying to Abū Baṣīr: "Woe to his mother, a kindler of war!" So Mūsā's astonishment is conveyed by the Arabic expression indicating intense wonder.

Al-waylu (woe) is a noun for punishment and evil, and it has no verb.

"Wayḥakum" is in the accusative either by supposing a verb for warning or urging, i.e., "Hold fast to your woe" or "Beware your woe"; or by supposing the vocative particle, as they say: "Yā waylanā" and "Yā waylatanā." It has been discussed under His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79] in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

Al-iftirāʾ is the invention of falsehood. The combination of it with "kadhiban" (a lie) is for emphasis, and it has been discussed under His saying: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 103] in Sūrat al-ʿUqūd.

The fabrication that Mūsā meant is what theyImagined for the people of sorcery-trickery, saying to them: "Look how the rope moved and became a serpent," and similar directing of illusions by presenting them as realities; or their saying: "What we do is confirmation from Allah for us"; or their saying: "Mūsā is a liar and a sorcerer"; or their saying: "Pharaoh is their god," or "the gods of Pharaoh are gods." Their statements of disbelief were varied.

The majority recited ﴿fa-yasḥtakum﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, from saḥatahu, meaning he uprooted it totally; this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Khalaf, and Ruways from Yaʿqūb read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, from asḥatahu; this is the dialect of Najd and Banū Tamīm. Both dialects are eloquent.

The clause ﴿and indeed he who fabricates has failed﴾ is in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿do not fabricate﴾. It is brought as a justification for the prohibition, i.e., avoid lying against Allah, for he who fabricated against Him before you has failed. After he admonished them, forbade them from lying against Allah, and warned them of His punishment, he set for them an example from the perished nations who fabricated lies against Allah and did not succeed in what they fabricated for.

The relative "man" (whoever) is for generality.

The placement of this clause after the preceding one is like the placement of the major premise in a categorical syllogism.

In Mūsā's speech there is a declaration that he does not invent speech against Allah that He has not commanded him, because he knows that He will uproot them with punishment, and he knows the failure of him who fabricates against Allah; and one who knows this does not proceed to it.

The address in His saying "Woe to you" (wayḥakum) may be intended in its literal sense of supplication, in which case it is not in line with what he was commanded regarding speaking gently to Pharaoh. Either because the address with this was not directed at Pharaoh, but was directed specifically at the sorcerers indicated by His saying ﴿he gathered his scheme﴾, i.e., Mūsā said to the people of Pharaoh's scheme; or because when he saw that speaking gently to him was not beneficial, since he remained steadfast in his disbelief, he made his speech harsher as a rebuke to him, by a specific command from Allah at that moment, qualifying the general command to speak gently, as permission was given to Muḥammad ﷺ by His saying ﴿Permission is given to those who are fought against, because they have been wronged﴾ [al-Ḥajj: 39] and the verses following in Sūrat al-Ḥajj; or because when he saw that their deception upon those present, that their sorcery was a miracle for them from their gods and from Pharaoh their Most High Lord, and they said ﴿By the might of Pharaoh, indeed we are the victors﴾ [al-Shuʿarāʾ: 44], he saw it as obligatory upon himself to change the wrong with his tongue to the utmost of his ability, because that change is what befits the station of prophethood.

It is also permissible that the phrase "wayḥakum" is used to express astonishment at a strange situation, i.e., "I marvel at you and warn you," like the Prophet ﷺ's saying to Abū Baṣīr: "Woe to his mother, a kindler of war!" So Mūsā's astonishment is conveyed by the Arabic expression indicating intense wonder.

Al-waylu (woe) is a noun for punishment and evil, and it has no verb.

"Wayḥakum" is in the accusative either by supposing a verb for warning or urging, i.e., "Hold fast to your woe" or "Beware your woe"; or by supposing the vocative particle, as they say: "Yā waylanā" and "Yā waylatanā." It has been discussed under His saying: ﴿So woe to those who write the Book with their own hands﴾ [al-Baqarah: 79] in Sūrat al-Baqarah.

Al-iftirāʾ is the invention of falsehood. The combination of it with "kadhiban" (a lie) is for emphasis, and it has been discussed under His saying: ﴿But those who disbelieve fabricate lies against Allah﴾ [al-Mā'idah: 103] in Sūrat al-ʿUqūd.

The fabrication that Mūsā meant is what theyImagined for the people of sorcery-trickery, saying to them: "Look how the rope moved and became a serpent," and similar directing of illusions by presenting them as realities; or their saying: "What we do is confirmation from Allah for us"; or their saying: "Mūsā is a liar and a sorcerer"; or their saying: "Pharaoh is their god," or "the gods of Pharaoh are gods." Their statements of disbelief were varied.

The majority recited ﴿fa-yasḥtakum﴾ with a fatḥah on the yāʾ, from saḥatahu, meaning he uprooted it totally; this is the dialect of the people of the Ḥijāz. Ḥamzah, al-Kisāʾī, Ḥafṣ from ʿĀṣim, Khalaf, and Ruways from Yaʿqūb read it with a ḍammah on the yāʾ, from asḥatahu; this is the dialect of Najd and Banū Tamīm. Both dialects are eloquent.

The clause ﴿and indeed he who fabricates has failed﴾ is in the place of a circumstantial clause (ḥāl) from the pronoun in ﴿do not fabricate﴾. It is brought as a justification for the prohibition, i.e., avoid lying against Allah, for he who fabricated against Him before you has failed. After he admonished them, forbade them from lying against Allah, and warned them of His punishment, he set for them an example from the perished nations who fabricated lies against Allah and did not succeed in what they fabricated for.

The relative "man" (whoever) is for generality.

The placement of this clause after the preceding one is like the placement of the major premise in a categorical syllogism.

In Mūsā's speech there is a declaration that he does not invent speech against Allah that He has not commanded him, because he knows that He will uproot them with punishment, and he knows the failure of him who fabricates against Allah; and one who knows this does not proceed to it.

[p. 251]

Meaning: the disputing among them over their affair resulted from Musa's admonition. This indicates that some of them had been affected by the admonition to some degree, while others feared defeat. Therefore, some of them called upon the others to consult about what they should do.

"Tanazu'" (disputing) is a form of reciprocal action derived from *naza'*, which means pulling, as in drawing water from a well or pulling a garment off the body. It is used figuratively for difference of opinion, where each holder of an opinion tries to convince the one who disagrees that his own view is correct. Thus *tanazu'* means mutual disagreement.

"Najwa" means secret speech: they withdrew and conferred privately so that they would arrive at a decision that no one else would know about. By making *al-najwa* the object of *asarru* ("they kept secret"), the phrase emphasises the thoroughness of the concealment, as if it were said: "they kept their secret secret," as one says "the poetry of a poet."

This emphasis is increased by the phrase "among them" (*baynahum*), which implies that the secret conference was among a particular group, in which no one else took part.

The clause ﴿They said: Indeed these two are magicians﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion) for the clause ﴿and they kept their secret conference﴾, because keeping a secret conference involves many statements, of which this one is mentioned. It is the decisive statement among them and the opinion on which they settled; it is the essence of the churned-out result of the conference. This is the nature of consultation and the clash of opinions: that it ends in an opinion from which all of them proceed.

The attribution of the statement to the plural pronoun of "them" means: one of them said, "These two are magicians," and then all of them said, "Yes, these two are magicians." The statement is therefore attributed to all of them, that is, it is a saying over which they debated and then settled. Some of them said to others, "Yes, it is so," and they uttered the words on which their opinion had settled, namely their certainty that Musa and his brother were magicians.

Know that all the recognised reciters (*qurra'*) recited with the *alif* in the demonstrative *hadhani* ("these two"), except Abu 'Amr among the ten, and al-Hasan al-Basri among the fourteen. This necessitates certainty that the retention of the *alif* in the word *hadhani* is more widely transmitted (*mutawatir*), regardless of how the word *inna* is pronounced, whether with a doubled or a single *nun*. Most of the famous mutawatir recitations read *inna* with a doubled *nun*, except Ibn Kathir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, who read *in* with a sukun on the *nun*, treating it as a lightened form of the heavy *inna*.

The Mushaf al-Imam (the standard codex) was written only in conformity with the most famous recitations that were heard and transmitted from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions who recited. Memorisation of the Qur'an in the breasts of reciters is older than its writing in the codices, and what was written in the master copies was only from the memory of the memorisers. The Mushaf al-Imam was written only from the collected memorised text of the memorisers, and from what the scribes of revelation wrote during the period of revelation.

As for the recitation of the majority, ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾ with a doubled *nun* in *inna* and with an *alif* in *hadhani* and likewise in *la-sahiran*, the commentators have given several interpretations of it, reaching six. The most evident is that *inna* is a particle of answer, like *na'am* ("yes") and *ajal* ("indeed"). This is one of the uses of *inna*, meaning that they followed what their affair had settled upon after the secret conference, as in the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

*"And the women say: 'Greying has overtaken you, and you have aged.' So I said: 'Inna'"*

meaning: "Indeed" or "Yes." The *ha'* in the line is the *ha' al-sakt* (pausal *ha'*).

Likewise the saying of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr to a Bedouin who asked him for a gift and he did not give it. The Bedouin said, "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said, "Inna, and her rider too." This interpretation is an original idea of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, who mentioned it in his tafsir. He said: "I presented it to our two scholars, our two teachers and our two masters, Muhammad ibn Yazid, meaning al-Mubarrad, and Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad, meaning the famous judge. Both accepted it and said that it was the best they had heard on this matter."

I say: They both spoke truly and verified it. What Ibn Jinni raised against it in refutation is open to question.

In al-Wahidi's concise tafsir, it is related that Isma'il al-Qadi (that is, Ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad) asked Ibn Kaysan about this question. Ibn Kaysan said: "Since no inflection appears in the demonstratives in the singular or in the plural (that is, in their saying *hadha* and *ha'ula'*, since these two are indeclinable), the dual has the status of the singular, because the dual ought not to be altered." Isma'il said to him: "How good this is! If someone had preceded you with this statement, it would have been more comforting to hear it." Ibn Kaysan said to him: "Then let the judge say it, so that it may become comforting." So he smiled.

According to this interpretation, God's saying ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾ is a quotation of the statement of one group among the disputants, namely the group that accepted this opinion, because the particle of answer requires a preceding speech.

The *lam* entered the predicate: either on the assumption that the predicate is a sentence whose subject has been omitted, and the one with the *lam* is the implied subject; the presence of the *lam* indicates that the sentence that occurs as the predicate of the demonstrative is an oath-sentence. Or else it is according to the view of those who permit the *lam* to enter the predicate of the subject outside of poetic necessity.

This recitation has also been interpreted by making *inna* a particle of emphasis, with the inflection of its dual subject following the dialect of Kinana and Bilharith ibn Ka'b, who make the sign of the dual inflection the *alif* in all cases. This is a well-known dialect in Arabic literature, and it has many examples, among them the saying of al-Mutalammis:

*"So he lowered his gaze, lowering as the brave man does; and had he found a passage, the brave man's teeth would have been stopped up."*

Hafs read *in* with a kasra on the hamza and a lightened, sukun *nun* in *in*, treating it as a lightened form of the heavy *inna*. The reasoning for this is that the subject of the lightened *in* is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*damir sha'n*), according to the famous view. The *lam* in *la-sahiran* is the *lam* that distinguishes the lightened *in* from the negative *in*.

[p. 252]

Ibn Kathir read the *nun* of *in* with a sukun as a lightened form of the heavy particle, with the *alif* retained in *hadhani*, and with a doubled *nun* in *hadhani* (written *hadhanni*).

As for the recitation of Abu 'Amr alone, ﴿Indeed these two (*hadhayni*)﴾, with a doubled *nun* in *inna* and with a *ya'* after the *dhal* in *hadhayni*: al-Qurtubi said that it contradicts the Mushaf. I say that this does not discredit it, because it is a sound transmission and agrees with an acceptable interpretation in the Arabic language.

The revelation of the Qur'an in these eloquent usages is one of the aspects of its inimitability, so that its constructions proceed in various modes of meaning while being unified in purpose. Therefore no attention should be paid to what has been reported claiming that writing *inna hadhani* was an error by the scribe of the Mushaf. Their transmission of this from Aban ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Affan from his father, and from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr from 'A'isha, has no sound chain. They supposed that the Muslims took the recitation of the Qur'an from the codices, and this is heedlessness. The Mushaf was written only after the Muslims had recited the Qur'an for more than twenty years in the regions of Islam, and the codices were written only from the memory of the memorisers. The Muslims took the Qur'an only from the mouths of its memorisers before the codices were written, and after that until today. Had there been an error in some of them in the orthography, the reciters would not have followed it; it would have been like the omission of many alifs in numerous words, or like writing the alif of *al-salat*, *al-zakat*, *al-hayat* and *al-riba* with a waw in place of the alif, when they recited them only with their alifs.

The emphasis by the sorcerers that Musa and Harun were two magicians, with the particle *inna*, is to confirm this for those in whom doubt about the validity of their call has crept. They made what Musa displayed of the miracle before Pharaoh into magic, because among them they apply the term magic to extraordinary events (*khawariq al-'adat*), just as the woman who saw water gushing from between the fingers of the Prophet (ﷺ) said to her people: "I have come to you from the most magical of people." This is in the Book of Campaigns of the Sahih of al-Bukhari.

Those who said it may have been some of those who witnessed what Musa brought before Pharaoh's assembly, or some of those to whom this had reached by hearsay and widespread report.

The address in God's saying ﴿that they expel you﴾ is to their chiefs. The basis of accusing the two of this is what preceded in God's saying, when he (Pharaoh) said ﴿Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Musa?﴾ [Ta Ha 20:57]. We add here that this may be part of the secret conference among the sorcerers, meaning: they want to monopolise the craft of magic in your land, so that you will leave the land because the people will neglect you and turn to the magic of Musa and Harun.

*Tariqah* (way, manner) means custom and habit; it has been likened to the road along which the traveller walks, because of the common element of constancy. *Al-muthla* is the feminine of *al-amthal*, an elative form derived from *al-matalah*, which means fine condition. One says: "So-and-so is the best of his people," meaning the nearest of them to good and the finest in condition.

By this they intended to stir up the zeal of some of them out of jealousy for their customs, since every nation has jealousy for its customs, its laws and its morals. For this reason they built upon it the instruction to gather their stratagems and all that they could muster in order to overcome Musa.

The *ba'* in ﴿by your way﴾ is for the transitivity of the verb *yadhhaba*. The meaning is: they cause them to depart, and this is more eloquent in linking the verb to the object than making the object accusative. This was discussed earlier, at God's saying ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:17], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

The majority read ﴿So gather together﴾ (*fa-ajmi'u*) with a hamzat qat' (a full hamza) and with a kasra on the *mim*, as an imperative from *ajma'a amrahu*, meaning when one makes an affair agreed upon and not subject to disagreement.

[p. 256]

Abu 'Amr read *fa-jma'u* with a hamzat wasl (a connective hamza) and a fatha on the *mim*, as an imperative from *jama'a*, like His saying earlier ﴿then he gathered his stratagem﴾ [Ta Ha 20:60]. The word *jam'* (gathering) is applied to mutual support and cooperation, likening a thing that differs to a thing that is scattered. It is the opposite of His saying ﴿and they disputed their affair among themselves﴾. They called their action a *kayd* (stratagem) because they had agreed to show the common people that what Musa had brought was not marvellous, since they would bring something like it or greater, in order to divert people from listening to his call, and thus they would plot against him by nullifying the distinctive quality of what he had brought.

It is evident that the general population had heard of Musa's call and of the miracle God had manifested through his hands, and they had become perplexed about his matter. Because of this the sorcerers took great care to plot against him. This is what God's saying in the verse of Surat al-Shu'ara' relates: ﴿So the sorcerers were gathered for an appointed day known﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:38]; ﴿and it was said to the people: Will you gather?﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:39]; ﴿that we may follow the sorcerers if they are the victors﴾ [al-Shu'ara' 26:40].

They planned to terrify the people and to terrify Musa and Harun by agreeing that they would come, when they advanced to cast their magic, arranged in a row, because that would be more awe-inspiring for them.

Those who wish to persuade the public of themselves have always chosen for this the splendour of appearance, goodness of bearing and majesty of presence. Among this was the sitting of kings upon lion skins, and brave men would sometimes wear tiger skins in war. The verb *tanammaru* (they took on the appearance of tigers) in the line of Ibn Ma'di Karib has been explained in this sense:

*"A people who, when they put on iron, take on the appearance of tigers, with rings and sword-strokes."*

It was also said that this is what is meant by the proverbial saying, "So-and-so put on the tiger's skin for me." And it is established in history, which rests on reports, that the priests of the Copts in Egypt used to wear tiger skins.

The ṣaff (row): it is a verbal noun standing in the sense of the active or passive participle, meaning "lined up" or "arranged in rows," when they are placed one after another in good order, such that they are not jumbled together. For when they stand one behind the other and the rows follow one another, they present a more imposing sight. God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as though they were a solid structure﴾ [al-Saff: 4]. All the sorcerers of the Egyptian lands had been brought at the command of Pharaoh, so they were a great number. Thus ṣaff here refers to the category (jins) rather than a single unit: that is, "come in rows," and it is like His saying: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾ [al-Naba': 38], and His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22].

The word ṣaffan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the subject of "come" (i'tū). The intended meaning is coming to the place where they would cast their magic and sorcery, because the private consultation and conspiracy took place on that day, as indicated by their saying: ﴿And he has indeed succeeded today who gains the upper hand﴾.

The clause ﴿And he has indeed succeeded today who gains the upper hand﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyīl) to the speech, gathering what they intended by their plotting: that success belongs to whoever prevails and emerges dominant in that assembly. So "istaʿlā" is an intensified form of "ʿalā," meaning he rose above his companion and overpowered him. The sīn and tā' serve for emphasis, like "istaʾkhara." They meant success in this world, because they did not believe that such encounters would affect the state of eternal life, although they did believe in the second life.

By this they intended to stir up the zeal of some of them out of jealousy for their customs, since every nation has jealousy for its customs, its laws and its morals. For this reason they built upon it the instruction to gather their stratagems and all that they could muster in order to overcome Musa.

The *ba'* in ﴿by your way﴾ is for the transitivity of the verb *yadhhaba*. The meaning is: they cause them to depart, and this is more eloquent in linking the verb to the object than making the object accusative. This was discussed earlier, at God's saying ﴿God took away their light﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:17], at the beginning of Surat al-Baqarah.

[p. 256]

Abu 'Amr read *fa-jma'u* with a hamzat wasl (a connective hamza) and a fatha on the *mim*, as an imperative from *jama'a*, like His saying earlier ﴿then he gathered his stratagem﴾ [Ta Ha 20:60]. It is the opposite of His saying ﴿and they disputed their affair among themselves﴾. It is evident that the general population had heard of Musa's call and of the miracle God had manifested through his hands, and they had become perplexed about his matter. Because of this the sorcerers took great care to plot against him. Those who wish to persuade the public of themselves have always chosen for this the splendour of appearance, goodness of bearing and majesty of presence. Among this was the sitting of kings upon lion skins, and brave men would sometimes wear tiger skins in war. The verb *tanammaru* (they took on the appearance of tigers) in the line of Ibn Ma'di Karib has been explained in this sense:

*"A people who, when they put on iron, take on the appearance of tigers, with rings and sword-strokes."*

The ṣaff (row): it is a verbal noun standing in the sense of the active or passive participle, meaning "lined up" or "arranged in rows," when they are placed one after another in good order, such that they are not jumbled together. For when they stand one behind the other and the rows follow one another, they present a more imposing sight. God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed, Allah loves those who fight in His cause in a row, as though they were a solid structure﴾ [al-Saff: 4]. All the sorcerers of the Egyptian lands had been brought at the command of Pharaoh, so they were a great number. Thus ṣaff here refers to the category (jins) rather than a single unit: that is, "come in rows," and it is like His saying: ﴿On the Day when the Spirit and the angels stand in rows﴾ [al-Naba': 38], and His saying: ﴿And your Lord comes, and the angels, rank upon rank﴾ [al-Fajr: 22].

The word ṣaffan is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (ḥāl) of the subject of "come" (i'tū). The intended meaning is coming to the place where they would cast their magic and sorcery, because the private consultation and conspiracy took place on that day, as indicated by their saying: ﴿And he has indeed succeeded today who gains the upper hand﴾.

The clause ﴿And he has indeed succeeded today who gains the upper hand﴾ is a concluding remark (tadhyīl) to the speech, gathering what they intended by their plotting: that success belongs to whoever prevails and emerges dominant in that assembly. So "istaʿlā" is an intensified form of "ʿalā," meaning he rose above his companion and overpowered him. The sīn and tā' serve for emphasis, like "istaʾkhara." They meant success in this world, because they did not believe that such encounters would affect the state of eternal life, although they did believe in the second life.

[p. 251]

Meaning: the disputing among them over their affair resulted from Musa's admonition. This indicates that some of them had been affected by the admonition to some degree, while others feared defeat. Therefore, some of them called upon the others to consult about what they should do.

"Tanazu'" (disputing) is a form of reciprocal action derived from *naza'*, which means pulling, as in drawing water from a well or pulling a garment off the body. It is used figuratively for difference of opinion, where each holder of an opinion tries to convince the one who disagrees that his own view is correct. Thus *tanazu'* means mutual disagreement.

"Najwa" means secret speech: they withdrew and conferred privately so that they would arrive at a decision that no one else would know about. By making *al-najwa* the object of *asarru* ("they kept secret"), the phrase emphasises the thoroughness of the concealment, as if it were said: "they kept their secret secret," as one says "the poetry of a poet."

This emphasis is increased by the phrase "among them" (*baynahum*), which implies that the secret conference was among a particular group, in which no one else took part.

The clause ﴿They said: Indeed these two are magicians﴾ is a *badal ishtimal* (substitution of inclusion) for the clause ﴿and they kept their secret conference﴾, because keeping a secret conference involves many statements, of which this one is mentioned. It is the decisive statement among them and the opinion on which they settled; it is the essence of the churned-out result of the conference. This is the nature of consultation and the clash of opinions: that it ends in an opinion from which all of them proceed.

The attribution of the statement to the plural pronoun of "them" means: one of them said, "These two are magicians," and then all of them said, "Yes, these two are magicians." The statement is therefore attributed to all of them, that is, it is a saying over which they debated and then settled. Some of them said to others, "Yes, it is so," and they uttered the words on which their opinion had settled, namely their certainty that Musa and his brother were magicians.

Know that all the recognised reciters (*qurra'*) recited with the *alif* in the demonstrative *hadhani* ("these two"), except Abu 'Amr among the ten, and al-Hasan al-Basri among the fourteen. This necessitates certainty that the retention of the *alif* in the word *hadhani* is more widely transmitted (*mutawatir*), regardless of how the word *inna* is pronounced, whether with a doubled or a single *nun*. Most of the famous mutawatir recitations read *inna* with a doubled *nun*, except Ibn Kathir and Hafs on the authority of 'Asim, who read *in* with a sukun on the *nun*, treating it as a lightened form of the heavy *inna*.

The Mushaf al-Imam (the standard codex) was written only in conformity with the most famous recitations that were heard and transmitted from the time of the Prophet (ﷺ) and his Companions who recited. Memorisation of the Qur'an in the breasts of reciters is older than its writing in the codices, and what was written in the master copies was only from the memory of the memorisers. The Mushaf al-Imam was written only from the collected memorised text of the memorisers, and from what the scribes of revelation wrote during the period of revelation.

As for the recitation of the majority, ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾ with a doubled *nun* in *inna* and with an *alif* in *hadhani* and likewise in *la-sahiran*, the commentators have given several interpretations of it, reaching six. The most evident is that *inna* is a particle of answer, like *na'am* ("yes") and *ajal* ("indeed"). This is one of the uses of *inna*, meaning that they followed what their affair had settled upon after the secret conference, as in the saying of 'Abdullah ibn Qays al-Ruqayyat:

*"And the women say: 'Greying has overtaken you, and you have aged.' So I said: 'Inna'"*

meaning: "Indeed" or "Yes." The *ha'* in the line is the *ha' al-sakt* (pausal *ha'*).

Likewise the saying of 'Abdullah ibn al-Zubayr to a Bedouin who asked him for a gift and he did not give it. The Bedouin said, "May God curse the she-camel that carried me to you." Ibn al-Zubayr said, "Inna, and her rider too." This interpretation is an original idea of Abu Ishaq al-Zajjaj, who mentioned it in his tafsir. He said: "I presented it to our two scholars, our two teachers and our two masters, Muhammad ibn Yazid, meaning al-Mubarrad, and Isma'il ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad, meaning the famous judge. Both accepted it and said that it was the best they had heard on this matter."

I say: They both spoke truly and verified it. What Ibn Jinni raised against it in refutation is open to question.

In al-Wahidi's concise tafsir, it is related that Isma'il al-Qadi (that is, Ibn Ishaq ibn Hammad) asked Ibn Kaysan about this question. Ibn Kaysan said: "Since no inflection appears in the demonstratives in the singular or in the plural (that is, in their saying *hadha* and *ha'ula'*, since these two are indeclinable), the dual has the status of the singular, because the dual ought not to be altered." Isma'il said to him: "How good this is! If someone had preceded you with this statement, it would have been more comforting to hear it." Ibn Kaysan said to him: "Then let the judge say it, so that it may become comforting." So he smiled.

According to this interpretation, God's saying ﴿Indeed these two are magicians﴾ is a quotation of the statement of one group among the disputants, namely the group that accepted this opinion, because the particle of answer requires a preceding speech.

The *lam* entered the predicate: either on the assumption that the predicate is a sentence whose subject has been omitted, and the one with the *lam* is the implied subject; the presence of the *lam* indicates that the sentence that occurs as the predicate of the demonstrative is an oath-sentence. Or else it is according to the view of those who permit the *lam* to enter the predicate of the subject outside of poetic necessity.

This recitation has also been interpreted by making *inna* a particle of emphasis, with the inflection of its dual subject following the dialect of Kinana and Bilharith ibn Ka'b, who make the sign of the dual inflection the *alif* in all cases. This is a well-known dialect in Arabic literature, and it has many examples, among them the saying of al-Mutalammis:

*"So he lowered his gaze, lowering as the brave man does; and had he found a passage, the brave man's teeth would have been stopped up."*

Hafs read *in* with a kasra on the hamza and a lightened, sukun *nun* in *in*, treating it as a lightened form of the heavy *inna*. The reasoning for this is that the subject of the lightened *in* is an omitted pronoun of the matter (*damir sha'n*), according to the famous view. The *lam* in *la-sahiran* is the *lam* that distinguishes the lightened *in* from the negative *in*.

[p. 252]

Ibn Kathir read the *nun* of *in* with a sukun as a lightened form of the heavy particle, with the *alif* retained in *hadhani*, and with a doubled *nun* in *hadhani* (written *hadhanni*).

As for the recitation of Abu 'Amr alone, ﴿Indeed these two (*hadhayni*)﴾, with a doubled *nun* in *inna* and with a *ya'* after the *dhal* in *hadhayni*: al-Qurtubi said that it contradicts the Mushaf. I say that this does not discredit it, because it is a sound transmission and agrees with an acceptable interpretation in the Arabic language.

The revelation of the Qur'an in these eloquent usages is one of the aspects of its inimitability, so that its constructions proceed in various modes of meaning while being unified in purpose. Therefore no attention should be paid to what has been reported claiming that writing *inna hadhani* was an error by the scribe of the Mushaf. Their transmission of this from Aban ibn 'Uthman ibn 'Affan from his father, and from 'Urwa ibn al-Zubayr from 'A'isha, has no sound chain. They supposed that the Muslims took the recitation of the Qur'an from the codices, and this is heedlessness. The Mushaf was written only after the Muslims had recited the Qur'an for more than twenty years in the regions of Islam, and the codices were written only from the memory of the memorisers. The Muslims took the Qur'an only from the mouths of its memorisers before the codices were written, and after that until today. Had there been an error in some of them in the orthography, the reciters would not have followed it; it would have been like the omission of many alifs in numerous words, or like writing the alif of *al-salat*, *al-zakat*, *al-hayat* and *al-riba* with a waw in place of the alif, when they recited them only with their alifs.

The emphasis by the sorcerers that Musa and Harun were two magicians, with the particle *inna*, is to confirm this for those in whom doubt about the validity of their call has crept. They made what Musa displayed of the miracle before Pharaoh into magic, because among them they apply the term magic to extraordinary events (*khawariq al-'adat*), just as the woman who saw water gushing from between the fingers of the Prophet (ﷺ) said to her people: "I have come to you from the most magical of people." This is in the Book of Campaigns of the Sahih of al-Bukhari.

Those who said it may have been some of those who witnessed what Musa brought before Pharaoh's assembly, or some of those to whom this had reached by hearsay and widespread report.

The address in God's saying ﴿that they expel you﴾ is to their chiefs. The basis of accusing the two of this is what preceded in God's saying, when he (Pharaoh) said ﴿Have you come to us to drive us out of our land by your magic, O Musa?﴾ [Ta Ha 20:57]. Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 65–66:

﴿They said: "O Musa, either you throw, or we will be the first to throw."﴾ ﴿He said: "Rather, you throw." And suddenly their ropes and their staffs, because of their sorcery, appeared to him to be moving, [as if] they were slithering.﴾

This story and its meanings have already been discussed in Surah al-A'raf, except that the priority (al-awwaliyyah) is stated explicitly here in one of the two alternatives. So it was explicit that the choice applies to priority in throwing, [and] except that he here stated explicitly that the sorcery they threw was by imagination (takhyil) that their ropes and staffs were serpents moving [along]; because no kind of animal resembles them in shape except snakes and serpents.

The sense of surprise derived from "idha" (suddenly) indicates that they had prepared them for throwing, and they feared that a time would pass in which their properties would disappear, so they hastened to throw them.

The majority (al-Jumhur) read "yukhayyalu" with a yeh (ya') at the beginning of the verb, taking its subject to be the clause "annaha tas'a" (that it was moving). Ibn Dhakwan, from Ibn 'Amir, and Rawh, from Ya'qub, read "tukhayyalu" with a teh (ta') at its beginning, taking the verb to have as its subject the pronoun referring to "hibaluhum wa 'isiyyuhum" (their ropes and their staffs), i.e., they were imagined to him as moving.

And "annaha tas'a" is a substitute (badal) for the implicit pronoun, a substitute of inclusion (badal ishtimal).

This imagining that Musa experienced from the sorcery of the sorcerers was the effect of drugs which they applied to those ropes and staffs. The ropes were of a special kind, and the staffs were of special wood, having in them a potency for those drugs; when they met the rays of the sun, those drugs became agitated, and so the ropes and staffs moved. It is said that they put mercury coating on them. The imagining that befell Musa was not the effect of magic upon his soul, because the soul of a messenger is not affected by illusions; but it is possible that he was affected by influences that affect the body, such as illness. For this reason, the apparent meaning of the hadith of Hisham ibn 'Urwah, from his father, from 'A'ishah, concerning the sorcery of the Prophet (ﷺ), must be interpreted, and single reports (akhbar al-ahad) do not overturn certainties (al-qata'i'). This is not the place to mention it, and I have verified it in my book called al-Nazar al-Fasih 'ala Sahih al-Bukhari.

And "min" in His saying "min sihrihim" (from their sorcery) is causal (lil-sababiyyah), as in His saying, exalted is He, "mimma khati'atihim ughriqu" (because of their sins they were drowned) [Nuh: 25].

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 67–69:

Page 259
﴿So Moses sensed fear within himself.﴾ ﴿We said, "Do not fear. Indeed, it is you who are the superior.﴾ ﴿And throw what is in your right hand; it will swallow up what they have crafted. What they have crafted is only the plot of a magician, and the magician does not succeed, wherever he comes from."﴾

Awjasa (he concealed and sensed): he concealed and perceived. The accusative of (khīfatan) is as an object, meaning he found within himself; a parallel of this has already occurred in His saying, may He be exalted, (﴿So he sensed fear of them in his heart﴾ [Hud: 70]) in Surah Hud.

And (khīfah) is a noun of form (ism hay'ah) of fear, intended to denote the absolute verbal noun; its origin is khawfah, and the waw was changed into a ya' because it came after a kasrah.

The addition of (﴿within himself﴾) here indicates that it was a fear of reflection, whose effect did not appear on his features. Moses feared that the matter of the magicians would become apparent such that what appeared at his hands, the transformation of his staff into a serpent, would be equaled, since they would have equaled him in their action while they would have surpassed him in number; or he feared that God intended to lead the magicians on gradually for a period, letting them prevail over him for a time and granting them respite for what would be their end, so he feared that. This is a station of fear, and it is a lofty station. Similar to it is the station of the Prophet ﷺ on the day of Badr when he said: "O God, I ask You for Your help and Your promise. O God, if You will, You will not be worshipped on earth."

The evidence for this is His saying, may He be exalted, (﴿We said, "Do not fear."﴾). The emphasis of the sentence with the emphatic particle, the reinforcement of its emphasis with the separating pronoun, and the definite article in (al-a'la) are evidence that the fear that had entered him was only the fear that the magicians would prevail in the eyes of the common people, even if only for a time. And although he was certain

Page 260
that God would fulfil for him what He had sent him for, there is no barrier to God granting the disbelievers gradual respite for a short period in order to display the steadfastness of the faith of the believers, as He said to His Messenger ﷺ, (﴿Let not the movement of those who disbelieve through the land deceive you﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 196] ﴿A brief enjoyment﴾ [Ali 'Imran: 197]).

He referred to the staff with (ma), the relative pronoun, to remind him of the day of speech when He said to him, (﴿And what is that in your right hand, O Moses?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 17]), so that he might attain tranquillity in the knowledge that it would return to the state it had attained on that day. For this reason He did not say to him, "And throw your staff."

Al-talaqquf: swallowing up. The majority read (talaqqaf) with a jazm on it as the answer to His saying (wa alqi, "and throw"), while Ibn Dhakwan read (talaqqafu) with a raf' as a new sentence (isti'naf). The majority read (talaqqaf) with a fatha on the lam and a shaddah on the qaf.

Hafs read it with a sukun on the lam and a fatha on the qaf, from laqifa like fariha.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 20, verses 70–71:**

﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate. They said, "We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses."﴾ ﴿[Pharaoh] said, "Have you believed in him before I give you permission? Indeed, he is your chief who taught you magic. I will surely cut off your hands and your feet on opposite sides, and I will crucify you on the trunks of palm trees, and you will surely know whose punishment is more severe and more lasting."﴾

The *fa'* (ف) in ﴿فَأُلْقِيَ﴾ is coordinating (*'atifah*) over an omitted element indicated by His saying ﴿And throw down what is in your right hand﴾ [Ta-Ha: 69]. The implied meaning is: "So he threw it, and it swallowed what they had made," as in His saying, ﴿Strike the sea with your staff, and it split﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63].

*Al-ilqa'* (الإلقاء, casting down) means throwing to the ground. The verb is put in the passive because they had no one to cast them down except themselves. It is as if it were said: "So they cast themselves down prostrate." Their prostration was a public declaration of their acknowledgment that Moses was sent by God. It is also possible that their prostration was an act of glorifying God, the Exalted.

It is also possible that it indicates Moses' victory over them, so they prostrated in honor of him. It is further possible that they intended by it the glorification of Pharaoh, making it an introduction to their statement, ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾, out of fear of his tyranny.

*Sujjad* (سُجَّدٌ) is the plural of *sajid* (ساجد, prostrating).

The clause ﴿قالوا﴾ (they said) may be in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*), meaning: "They were cast down while saying..." It may also be a substitution of inclusion (*badal ishtimal*, بدل اشتمال, a substitute that includes the thing substituted) for the clause ﴿So the magicians were thrown down prostrate﴾, since their prostration included their belief. The ﴿أن﴾ (*an*) may be an independent initiating clause, marking the opening of the dialogue between them and Pharaoh.

They believed in God at that moment because they were certain that what had happened at the hand of Moses was not of the kind of magic, since they were the leaders of magic. So they knew that it was a sign from God. Their expressing the Lord by way of attribution to Aaron and Moses is because God was not known among them on that day except by this relation, since they had lords whom they worshipped, and whom Pharaoh worshipped as well.

The placing of Aaron before Moses here, and the placing of Moses before Aaron in His saying in Surah al-A'raf, ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds, the Lord of Moses and Aaron"﴾ [al-A'raf: 121–122], carries no indication of preference or otherwise, because the coordinating *waw* (و) conveys nothing more than mere joining in the ruling concerned. They knew God as the Lord of these two men, so their speech was related in a manner indicating this. Do you not see that in Surah al-A'raf the words of the magicians were related as ﴿They said, "We have believed in the Lord of the worlds"﴾ [al-A'raf: 121], and that this was not related here? This is because relating reports does not require exhausting everything related; the intent is only the place of lesson in that situation, according to need.

The reason for placing Aaron first here is the rhyme of the verse-end (*al-fasilah*, الفاصلة). The placement occurred in the narration, not in what was narrated, since in the other verse it occurred as ﴿the Lord of the worlds﴾ [al-A'raf: 121] ﴿the Lord of Moses and Aaron﴾ [al-A'raf: 122]. It is also possible that the placement of Aaron in this verse is part of the narration of the magicians' words, so two statements came from them: in one they put the name of Aaron first, considering his seniority in age, and in the other they put the name of Moses first, considering his superiority over Aaron through messengerhood and God's speech. So the difference of expressions is due to the difference of considerations.

It is said: *amana lahu* (آمن له), meaning that faith came into being in him for his sake, just as one says *amana bihi* (آمن به), meaning that faith came into being in him by means of him. The original use of the verb is that it is transitive by itself, because *amanahu* means *saddaqahu* (he confirmed him). But it has almost come to be used in the sense of confirmation only with one of these two particles.

Qalun, Warsh (through the route of al-Azraq), Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr, Abu Ja'far, and Rawh from Ya'qub recited ﴿آمنتم﴾ (*amantum*) with a single hamza followed by a lengthening (*madd*), which is the lengthening arising from easing the original hamza in the verb *amana*, with the sentence being a question.

Warsh (through the route of al-Asfahani), Ibn Kathir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Ruways from Ya'qub recited it with a single hamza, with the sentence being a statement. It is then a statement used for reproach.

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i, Abu Bakr from 'Asim, and Khalaf recited it with two hamzas, also in the form of a question.

When Pharaoh saw the faith of the magicians, he became enraged and sought to punish them. But he knew that punishing them for believing in Moses, after he had opened the door of debate with him, would be a breach of the principles of debate. So for the sake of vengeance against those who believed, he invented a pretext for their declaring faith before seeking Pharaoh's permission. He counted that as an act of audacity against him, and implied that if they had asked his permission, he would have granted it to them. He also deduced from their hastiness in this that they had colluded with Moses beforehand, and so had displayed incapacity when debating him. Pharaoh's aim in this was to convince those present that Moses had not brought anything that could overcome the magicians, thereby introducing doubt into the minds of those who had witnessed the signs. This is a habit from ancient times: a defeated party fabricates a cold excuse. Of this kind is the accusation by those judged against of the judges with bribery, and the accusation by defeated states in wars of their army commanders with treason.

The pronoun in ﴿لَهُ﴾ (*lahu*) refers to Moses, like the pronoun in ﴿إنَّهُ لَكَبِيرُكُمُ﴾ (*innahu lakabirukum*). The meaning of ﴿قبل أن آذن لكم﴾ (*qabla an adhana lakum*) is: before I permit you to believe in him. It is said: *adhina lahu* (أذن له), when he allowed him something.

*Al-taqti'* (التقطيع, cutting) means intense cutting. The intensification relates to the manner, which is what he described by His saying ﴿مِن خِلافٍ﴾ (*min khilaf*, on opposite sides), i.e., varied, namely not cutting on one side only, but from two different sides: the hand is cut, then the foot from the side opposite the cut hand, then the other hand, then the other foot. The apparent meaning is that cutting in this manner was a known mark of cutting criminals, so mentioning this attribute is a narration of the actual practice, not a precaution against cutting in another form, since this attribute has no effect on horror or on severity of pain when it occurs in succession.

As for what came in Islam regarding the punishment of the one who wages war (*al-muharib*, المحارب), it is only the cutting of one limb for each act of brigandage. This is from the mercy in punishment, lest the cut person be deprived of the benefit of his remaining limbs as a result of cutting a hand and then a foot from the same side, or cutting one hand after another while leaving both feet.

The *min* (مِن) in His saying ﴿مِن خِلافٍ﴾ is for the beginning (*ibtida'*), meaning that the cutting begins from the starting point of the opposition between the parts cut. The genitive phrase is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), and a parallel of it has been mentioned before in Surah al-A'raf and in Surah al-Ma'idah.

[Page 265]

*Al-taslib* (التصليب) is an intensification of *al-salb* (الصلب, crucifixion). *Al-salb* is binding the body to an upright post, or nailing it to it with spikes; this was mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' at His saying ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. The intensification also relates to the manner, by the intensity of nailing to the posts. For this reason, the preposition of elevation (*'ala*, على) is replaced with the preposition of location (*fi*, في), likening the firm fixing of the crucified person to the trunk to the firm placement of a thing within its container.

*Al-judhu'* (الجذوع) is the plural of *jidh* (جذع, with a kasrah on the jim and a sukun on the dhal), which is the trunk of the palm tree. This was mentioned before at His saying ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 25]. The verb ﴿لأصلبنكم﴾ (*la-usallibannakum*, I will surely crucify you) is made to govern the preposition *fi* (في, in), even though crucifixion occurs upon the trunk, not inside it, in order to indicate that it is a firm crucifixion resembling the presence of the contained thing within the container. So the preposition *fi* is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*, استعارة تبعية), following from the metaphor in which the meaning of *fi* is applied to the meaning governed by *'ala*.

*Ayyuna* (أيُّنا) is an interrogative about two parties sharing in the severity of punishment. The verb ﴿لتعلمن﴾ (*la-ta'lamunna*, you will surely know) is suspended from its operation (*mu'allaq*, معلّق), because the interrogative occurs at its end. By "the two parties" he meant himself and the Lord of Moses, glory be to Him, because he knew from their words ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾ that what moved them to believe in Him was the admonition Moses had given them when he said to them in Pharaoh's hearing, ﴿Woe to you! Do not invent against God a lie, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]; that is, "You will find My punishment more severe than the punishment you were warned of." This was from his delusion. What shows that this was Pharaoh's intent is that the believers answered his saying, ﴿Whose punishment is more severe and more lasting?﴾ with their saying, ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 73], meaning: better than you and more lasting in effect than your effect. So His reward is better than your pleasure, and His punishment is more severe than your punishment.

The pronoun in ﴿لَهُ﴾ (*lahu*) refers to Moses, like the pronoun in ﴿إنَّهُ لَكَبِيرُكُمُ﴾ (*innahu lakabirukum*). The meaning of ﴿قبل أن آذن لكم﴾ (*qabla an adhana lakum*) is: before I permit you to believe in him. It is said: *adhina lahu* (أذن له), when he allowed him something.

*Al-taqti'* (التقطيع, cutting) means intense cutting. The intensification relates to the manner, which is what he described by His saying ﴿مِن خِلافٍ﴾ (*min khilaf*, on opposite sides), i.e., varied, namely not cutting on one side only, but from two different sides: the hand is cut, then the foot from the side opposite the cut hand, then the other hand, then the other foot. The apparent meaning is that cutting in this manner was a known mark of cutting criminals, so mentioning this attribute is a narration of the actual practice, not a precaution against cutting in another form, since this attribute has no effect on horror or on severity of pain when it occurs in succession.

As for what came in Islam regarding the punishment of the one who wages war (*al-muharib*, المحارب), it is only the cutting of one limb for each act of brigandage. This is from the mercy in punishment, lest the cut person be deprived of the benefit of his remaining limbs as a result of cutting a hand and then a foot from the same side, or cutting one hand after another while leaving both feet.

The *min* (مِن) in His saying ﴿مِن خِلافٍ﴾ is for the beginning (*ibtida'*), meaning that the cutting begins from the starting point of the opposition between the parts cut. The genitive phrase is in the position of a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*), and a parallel of it has been mentioned before in Surah al-A'raf and in Surah al-Ma'idah.

[Page 265]

*Al-taslib* (التصليب) is an intensification of *al-salb* (الصلب, crucifixion). *Al-salb* is binding the body to an upright post, or nailing it to it with spikes; this was mentioned in Surah al-Nisa' at His saying ﴿And they did not kill him, nor did they crucify him﴾ [al-Nisa': 157]. The intensification also relates to the manner, by the intensity of nailing to the posts. For this reason, the preposition of elevation (*'ala*, على) is replaced with the preposition of location (*fi*, في), likening the firm fixing of the crucified person to the trunk to the firm placement of a thing within its container.

*Al-judhu'* (الجذوع) is the plural of *jidh* (جذع, with a kasrah on the jim and a sukun on the dhal), which is the trunk of the palm tree. This was mentioned before at His saying ﴿And shake toward you the trunk of the palm tree﴾ [Maryam: 25]. The verb ﴿لأصلبنكم﴾ (*la-usallibannakum*, I will surely crucify you) is made to govern the preposition *fi* (في, in), even though crucifixion occurs upon the trunk, not inside it, in order to indicate that it is a firm crucifixion resembling the presence of the contained thing within the container. So the preposition *fi* is a subsidiary metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*, استعارة تبعية), following from the metaphor in which the meaning of *fi* is applied to the meaning governed by *'ala*.

*Ayyuna* (أيُّنا) is an interrogative about two parties sharing in the severity of punishment. The verb ﴿لتعلمن﴾ (*la-ta'lamunna*, you will surely know) is suspended from its operation (*mu'allaq*, معلّق), because the interrogative occurs at its end. By "the two parties" he meant himself and the Lord of Moses, glory be to Him, because he knew from their words ﴿We have believed in the Lord of Aaron and Moses﴾ that what moved them to believe in Him was the admonition Moses had given them when he said to them in Pharaoh's hearing, ﴿Woe to you! Do not invent against God a lie, lest He destroy you with a punishment﴾ [Ta-Ha: 61]; that is, "You will find My punishment more severe than the punishment you were warned of." This was from his delusion. What shows that this was Pharaoh's intent is that the believers answered his saying, ﴿Whose punishment is more severe and more lasting?﴾ with their saying, ﴿And God is better and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 73], meaning: better than you and more lasting in effect than your effect. So His reward is better than your pleasure, and His punishment is more severe than your punishment.

[Page 266]

﴿They said, "We will never prefer you over the clear proofs that have come to us, or over He who originated us. So decree whatever you will decree. You can only decree concerning this worldly life. Indeed, we have believed in our Lord, that He may forgive us our sins and the magic you compelled us to practise. And Allah is better and more enduring."﴾

They displayed their contempt for his threat and his punishment, since they had become people of faith and certainty. Such is the way of those who believe in the messengers when the lights of the message shine upon them. Their turning from the ignorance and harshness of disbelief to the wisdom and steadfastness of faith comes swiftly. For us, in 'Umar ibn al-Khattab and others like him who believed in Muhammad ﷺ, there is an example of truthfulness.

Al-īthār (preference) means favouring. It has already been mentioned in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Allah has certainly preferred you over us﴾ [Yusuf: 91], in Surat Yusuf. The preference here, between Pharaoh and the clear proofs that came to them, requires an elided modifier that suits the contrast with "clear proofs." That is, "We will never prefer your obedience or your religion over the clear proofs that came to us, which indicate the obligation to obey Allah, Exalted is He." This fits the conjunction of ﴿He who originated us﴾, meaning: we will not prefer you in lordship over He who originated us.

The relative form was used to hint at the reason, because the Originator is the one deserving of being preferred.

﴿He who originated us﴾ is placed after ﴿the clear proofs that came to us﴾ because the clear proofs are evidence that He who created them intended from them faith in Musa and the rejection of worshipping other than Allah. It also contains an allusion to Pharaoh's call to faith in Allah.

The imperative in His saying ﴿So decree whatever you will decree﴾ is used to express indifference, because ﴿whatever you will decree﴾ has as its referent what he threatened them with, namely cutting off hands and feet and crucifixion. That is, it is all the same to us whether that is partial or total, or whether it does not occur. So we do not seek from you any deliverance from it in return for our obedience. Do what you will do. (Al-qadā' here means execution and fulfilment.) Your punishment does not go beyond this life, while we hope for the enduring reward from our Lord.

﴿This worldly life﴾ is in the accusative as a substitute for the adverbial object (al-maf'ul fihi, the object of time or place), because what is meant by "life" is its duration.

The restriction (al-qasr) derived from ﴿innama﴾ ("only") is the restriction of a described thing to an attribute. That is, you are restricted to deciding in this worldly life and do not go beyond it to deciding in the Hereafter. Thus it is a true restriction.

The sentence ﴿Indeed, we have believed in our Lord﴾ is in the position of a causal clause for what their speech implies.

The meaning of ﴿and the magic you compelled us to practise﴾ is that he compelled them to challenge Musa with their magic. They then knew that their act was false and a sin, because it was used to nullify the divinity of Allah. Therefore it was deserving of a plea for forgiveness.

The sentence ﴿And Allah is better and more enduring﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (al-hal), or is a parenthetical statement at the end of the speech serving as a tadhyil (a concluding remark that reinforces the meaning). The meaning is: Allah is better for us, in that we prefer Him over you. What is meant is the pleasure of Allah, and it is more enduring than you. That is, His reward, whether good or evil, is more enduring than your reward. So let not your saying ﴿and you will surely know which of us is more severe in punishment and more enduring﴾ [Ta-Ha: 71] frighten us. This is a complete answer to his threat.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 74–76:

[p. 268]
﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal, for him is Hell; he will neither die therein nor live.﴾ ﴿And whoever comes to Him as a believer who has done righteous deeds, for those are the high ranks.﴾ ﴿Gardens of perpetual residence, beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein forever. That is the reward of one who purifies himself.﴾

These sentences are a parenthetical insertion between the narration of the story of the magicians and the mention of the story of the Exodus of the Children of Israel. God related them as an admonition and as a confirmation of the statement of the believers from the people of Pharaoh. It has been said that they are part of the speech of those believers, but this is far-fetched, since He did not relate a similar statement from them in the parallel accounts of this story.

Al-mujrim (the criminal) is the doer of a jarimah (crime), which is disobedience and an evil act. In the terminology of the Qur'an, al-mujrim is the disbeliever, as in His saying (﴿Indeed, those who committed crimes used to laugh at those who believed﴾ [al-Mutaffifin: 29]).

The lam in (﴿for him is Hell﴾) is the lam of entitlement, meaning he will certainly arrive there, and his punishment will be continuously renewed therein. So he is neither dead, since he feels the punishment, nor alive, since being in the state of death is easier for him than it. The life that is negated is a particular kind of life, namely the life free of punishment and pain. Thus its negation does not contradict the negation of death, and this is like the saying of 'Abbas ibn Mirdas:

And I was in war one who warded off, yet I was not given anything, nor was I refused.

This is not of the same kind as His saying (﴿It is a cow neither old nor virgin﴾ [al-Baqarah: 68]) nor His saying (﴿an olive tree neither of the east nor of the west﴾ [al-Nur: 35]).

[p. 269]
As for the eternal abiding in the Fire of the people of major sins other than the disbelievers, His saying (﴿he will neither die therein nor live﴾) makes them not included in this verse. There are other proofs that require the eternal abiding of the disbeliever and the non-eternal abiding of the sinning believer. The Mu'tazilah and the Khawarij disputed these with us. This is not the place to mention them, and we have mentioned them in their places in this commentary.

The use of the demonstrative in His saying (﴿So those, for them are the high ranks﴾) serves to draw attention to the fact that they are deserving of what is mentioned after the demonstrative, on account of what preceded the demonstrative.

The meaning of (ʿAdn) [Eden] and the explanation of (﴿beneath which rivers flow﴾) have already been given in His saying (﴿God has promised the believing men and believing women gardens beneath which rivers flow, abiding therein, and pleasant dwellings in gardens of Eden﴾ [al-Tawbah: 72]) in Surah Bara'ah.

Al-tazakki (purification) is purifying oneself from acts of disobedience.
