Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 77:

﴿And We had already revealed to Moses: "Travel by night with My servants, and strike for them a dry path through the sea; you will not fear being overtaken, nor will you be afraid."﴾

The opening of the sentence with the particle of confirmation (harf al-tahqiq) serves to draw attention to the narrative, so that the listeners give it their minds. The change of style at the beginning of this sentence signals that a number of stories have been passed over between the mention of the two narratives. Had it been limited to the conjunctive particle, one would have assumed that the narration of the first story was still continuing, and so one would have supposed that the command to depart came directly after the end of the assembly of the magicians, although many stories mentioned in Surat al-A'raf and elsewhere lie between them. For the departure took place after many signs had appeared, to terrify Pharaoh each time he intended to release the Children of Israel to depart. Then he drew back, until he finally gave them permission, and they departed; then he regretted this and pursued them.

Thus the clause (﴿And We had already revealed to Moses﴾) is independent (ibtida'iyyah), and the waw is a conjunction joining one story to another, not a conjunction joining parts of one story to other parts of it.

And (أسر) (asri) is the imperative of al-sura (السُّرى, travelling by night), with a damma on the sin and a fatha on the ra'. It was mentioned in Surat al-Isra' that it is said: sara and asra. God commanded him thus to avoid Pharaoh's reneging upon them. The idafah in His words "with My servants" is for their honouring and bringing near, and to indicate their deliverance from being enslaved by the Copts, and that they are not slaves of Pharaoh. The verb (فاضرب) (fadrib) here means "to make," as in the saying: "the gold was struck into dinars" (ضُرِبَ الذهبُ دنانيرَ). And in the hadith: "and strike toward me with an arrow along with you" (واضربوا إليَّ معكم بسهم). It is not like His words (﴿أنِ اضْرِبْ بِعَصاكَ البَحْرَ﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 63]) because the verb there is transitive to the sea, whereas here it has taken "a path" as its object.

Yabas (اليَبَس), with a fatha on the ya' and on the ba', and it is also said with a sukun on the ba': it is an adjective meaning "dry" (اليابس). Its origin is a verbal noun, like al-'adam and al-'udm, and it was described by it for emphasis; for this reason it does not take a feminine form, so they say: naqatun yabasun, when her milk has dried up.

(﴿لا تَخافُ﴾) (la takhafu) is in the reading of the majority in the nominative, a promise to Moses. It was limited to the promise to him, excluding the rest of his people, because he was their exemplar: when he was not afraid, they took courage and their certainty grew strong. So it is a statement intended as glad tidings. The clause is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

Hamza alone read (لا تَخَفْ) (la takhaf) as a response to the imperative in His words "fadrib." The word (تَخَفْ) is written in the codices without an alif, so that it may be read in both ways, because of the great number of similar words that have an alif in their middle in the orthography of the Mushaf; the teachers of grammar call this the "deleted" (المحذوف).

As for His words (﴿ولا تَخْشى﴾) (wa la takhsha), there is consensus on reading it with an alif at its end. The explanation for Hamza's reading of it, although he read the conjoined verb with apocopation (jazm), is that the alif may be for lengthening for the sake of the rhyme (al-fawasil), like the alif in (﴿فَأضَلُّونا السَّبِيلا﴾ [al-Ahzab: 67]) and the alif in (﴿وتَظُنُّونَ بِاللَّهِ الظُّنُونا﴾ [al-Ahzab: 10]), or the waw in His words (﴿ولا تَخْشى﴾) is for resumption (isti'naf), not for conjunction.

Al-darak (الدَّرَك), with fatha on both letters, is the verbal noun of al-idrak (overtaking), i.e., you will not fear that Pharaoh will overtake you.

Al-khashyah is intense fear. Its object is omitted to convey generality, i.e., you will not fear anything; and this is a general term intended in a restricted sense, i.e., you will not fear anything of what is feared from an enemy or from drowning.

[p. 272]

The *fa'* here is *fasiha* (an "expressive" fa', which indicates an omitted clause) and it is conjunctive, coordinating with an implied clause that the preceding speech points to. The sense is: "So he set out with them, and Pharaoh followed them." After Pharaoh saw the signs of God's wrath upon him and his people, and became certain that all of this was a confirmation for Musa, he gave Musa and Harun permission to bring out the Children of Israel. Pharaoh's permission had been granted at night, because a great death had struck the Copts on the night of the seventh month of the Coptic months, which is the month of "Barmahat." It is the month that the Jews adopted as the beginning of their year, by a command from God, and they named it "Tishri." So they left the city of "Ra'messes," heading for the shore of the Red Sea. Pharaoh regretted letting them go, so he wanted to catch up with them in order to bring them back to his city. He went out in his chariot, with six hundred select chariots and other chariots carrying his army.

*Atba'* is a synonym of *taba'*. The *ba'* in *bi-junudihi* indicates accompaniment.

*Al-yamm* means the sea. Its "covering" them means its enveloping their bodies, that is, they drowned.

[p. 273 marker follows below]

His saying *ma ghashiyahum* conveys what his saying *fa-ghashiyahum min al-yamm* conveys, since it is known that a coverer covered them. Therefore it is determined that the intent of it is to inspire awe, meaning that the terror of that drowning reached a degree that its description cannot be achieved. Al-Zamakhshari said in *al-Kashshaf*: "It is one of the comprehensive expressions (*jawami' al-kalim*), which, despite their brevity, stand on their own with many meanings." This part of the story has already appeared in Surah Yunus.

The clause *wa-adalla Fir'awnu qawmahu* is in the position of a circumstantial clause (*hal*) relative to the pronoun in *ghashiyahum*.

*Al-idlal* means causing someone to fall into error (*dalal*), which is straying from the path that leads to the destination. It is used most often to mean ignorance and doing what is harmful, and this is what is meant here. The meaning is that Pharaoh caused his people to fall into ignorance and evil outcome, by spreading among them the reversal of realities and compound ignorance. So they did not meet with rectitude in their actions, until their final end was that they were drowned in the sea, because of his obstinacy in denying the call of Musa, upon him be peace.

As for the conjunction of *wa-ma hada* with *adalla*: either it is the conjunction of the more general with the more specific, because the absence of guidance is true by leaving guidance aside without misleading; or it is a verbal emphasis by a synonym, reinforcing the negation of guidance from Pharaoh toward his people, so that his saying *wa-ma hada* is an emphasis of *adalla* by a synonym, like the saying of Allah, Exalted is He, *﴿amwatun ghayru ahya'in﴾* ("dead, not living" [al-Nahl 16:21]), and the saying of al-A'sha:

*"Though you see us barefoot, with no sandals for us, thus indeed we go barefoot and we wear sandals."*

In *al-Kashshaf* it says: "The point of mentioning *wa-ma hada* is a mockery of Pharaoh in his saying *﴿wa-ma uhdikum illa sabila al-rashad﴾* ('And I guide you only to the path of right conduct' [Ghafir 40:29])." Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (*al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir*) on Surah 20, verses 80–82:

﴿O Children of Israel, We have certainly delivered you from your enemy, and We made an appointment with you at the right side of the mount, and We sent down to you the manna and the quail.﴾ ﴿Eat of the good things with which We have provided you, and do not transgress therein, lest My wrath descend upon you. And whoever has My wrath descend upon him has indeed fallen.﴾ ﴿And indeed, I am Most Forgiving toward whoever repents, believes, does righteous deeds, and then remains guided.﴾

These sentences are parenthetical interjections within the narrative, like what preceded them in His saying (﴿Indeed, whoever comes to his Lord as a criminal...﴾ [Ta-Ha 20:74]) and so on. This is an address to the Jews who were in the time of the Prophet (ﷺ), reminding them of other blessings. The great blessing, their deliverance from the enslavement of the disbelievers, is mentioned first.

Al-Jumhur (the majority of readers) read (قَدْ أنْجَيْناكم وواعَدْناكم) with the *nun* of majesty (*nun al-'azamah*, the "we" form).

Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read them (قَدْ أنْجَيْتُكم) and (وَعَدْتُكم) with the *ta'* of the first-person singular speaker.

He reminded them of the blessing of the sending down of the Law (*shari'ah*), which is what His saying (﴿and We made an appointment with you at the right side of the mount﴾) points to. *Al-muwa'adah* (mutual appointment) is a mutual agreement from two sides: We commanded Musa to attend for the private conversation (*munajah*), so that is a promise from God's side of the private conversation, and Musa's compliance with that is a promise from his side. Thus the meaning of *muwa'adah* is complete, as He said in Surat al-Baqarah (﴿And when We made an appointment with Musa for forty nights﴾ [al-Baqarah 2:51]).

It appears that the verse alludes to what came in Chapter 19 of the Book of Exodus: "In the third month after the children of Israel left the land of Egypt, they came to the wilderness of Sinai. There Israel encamped before the mountain. As for Moses, he went up to God, and the LORD called to him from the mountain, saying: 'Thus you shall say to the house of Jacob: You have seen what I did to the Egyptians, and that I bore you on eagles' wings and brought you to Myself. Now therefore, if you will indeed obey My voice and keep My covenant, you shall be a special treasure to Me...'" etc.

The mention of *al-Tur* (the mount) has already occurred in Surat al-Baqarah.

*Janib al-Tur* (the side of the mount) means its slope (*safhuh*). Describing it as "right" (*ayman*) is with regard to the direction of the person facing the rising of the sun. Otherwise, the mountain has no fixed right or left; these are known only by knowing the basic directions, and the basic direction is the sunrise. So it is the southern side (*al-qiblī*) by our terminology. The place of the appointment was made the southern side, and it is not the western side mentioned in Surat al-Qasas (﴿So when he came to it, he was called from the right side of the valley, in the blessed spot, from the tree﴾ [al-Qasas 28:30]), where He said (﴿And you were not on the western side when We decreed to Musa the command﴾ [al-Qasas 28:44]); that is a western side, meaning from the direction of the sunset of the mountain, and it is the side from which Musa perceived a fire.

*Janib al-Tur* is in the accusative (*nasb*) by way of place adverb (*zarfiyyah makaniyyah*), because, owing to its extent, it is like an indefinite place.

The object of *al-muwa'adah* is omitted, and its estimated meaning is "the private conversation" (*munajah*).

The transitive use of (*wa'adnakum*) to the pronoun of the group of the Children of Israel, although it was an appointment with Musa and those with him whom he chose from among his people, is on the basis that the purpose of the appointment is the revelation of the fundamentals of the Law, which become a benefit for the community. So the appointment with those (chosen) was like the appointment with the entire community.

All read (﴿wa nazzalna 'alaykumu﴾) etc. According to the reading of Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf (*qad anjaytukum wa wa'adtukum*) with the *ta'* of the singular, the reading of (*wa nazzalna*) with the *nun* of majesty becomes close to *iltifat* (a shift in grammatical person), though it is not the same as it, because the *nun* of majesty is equivalent to the *ta'* of the speaker.

As for *al-salwa*, it was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah. That occurred in the middle of the second month after their departure from Egypt, as in Chapter 16 of the Book of Exodus.

The clause (*kulu*, "eat") is a omitted quotation (*maqul mahdhuf*). Its estimated form is: "And We said," or "saying." Its counterpart has already been discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

Al-Jumhur read (*ma razaqnakum*) with the *nun* of majesty. Hamzah, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it (*ma razaqtukum*) with the *ta'* of the singular.

*Al-tughyan* is the most extreme arrogance. The meaning of the prohibition against *tughyan* regarding provision is the prohibition against neglecting gratitude for it and little concern for worshipping the Benefactor.

The particle (*fi*), which is for location (*zarfiyyah*), is a subordinate metaphor (*isti'arah tab'iyyah*): it likens the involvement of arrogance with the blessing to the descent of arrogance into it, comparing the abundant blessing to a container surrounding the one who receives it, in the manner of the implicit metaphor (*makniyyah*), and the particle of location is its indicator.

*Al-hulul* means to descend and reside in a place. The reaching of the effects of wrath to them is likened to an army or the like descending upon the dwellings of a people.

Al-Jumhur read (﴿fa yahilla 'alaykum﴾) with a *kasrah* on the *ha'* and they read (﴿wa man yahlil 'alayhi ghadabi﴾) with a *kasrah* on the first *lam*, taking them as verbs from *halla al-dayn*, which is said when the time for paying a debt has arrived. Al-Kisa'i read both verbs with a *dammah*, taking it from *halla bi-l-makan yahullu*, meaning to descend at a place. Thus it is stated in *al-Kashshaf*, and they did not criticize it.

This is one of the things Ibn Malik omitted in his *Lamiyyat al-Af'al*, and its commentator Bahraq al-Yamani did not supplement it in his large commentary. What is found in *al-Misbah* contradicts it and is not relied upon. The apparent meaning of *al-Qamus* is that *halla* in the sense of *nazala* is used both intransitively and transitively, but I have not found any evidence for them in this.

*Hawa* means to fall from a height. It is used here as a metaphor for a destruction from which there is no rising afterward, as they said: "May his mother fall" (*hawat ummuhu*), as an imprecation against him, and as one says: "Woe to his mother" (*waylu ummihi*). From it comes (﴿then his mother is the Abyss﴾ [al-Qari'ah 101:9]). So a specific falling is intended, namely falling from a mountain or a roof, by the indication of the threat.

The sentence (*wa inni la-ghaffarun*, "And indeed, I am Most Forgiving") to its end is a digression (*istitrad*) after the warning against arrogance regarding the blessing, by guiding to that by which arrogance may be remedied if it occurs: through repentance and righteous deeds. The meaning of (*taba*) is: he regretted his disbelief, believed, and did righteous deeds.

His saying (*thumma ihtada*, "then remained guided"): the *thumma* here indicates delay in rank (*tarakhi fi al-rutbah*). It is used metaphorically to indicate the difference between two things in status, just as it was used for the difference between two times in occurrence. The meaning of *ihtada*: he persisted in guidance and remained steadfast upon it. It is like His saying (﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast, there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:13]).

The verses point to what came in the Book of Exodus: "The LORD is a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in goodness, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but He will by no means clear the guilty..."

The apparent meaning of *al-Qamus* is that *halla* in the sense of *nazala* is used both intransitively and transitively, but I have not found any evidence for them in this.

*Hawa* means to fall from a height. It is used here as a metaphor for a destruction from which there is no rising afterward, as they said: "May his mother fall" (*hawat ummuhu*), as an imprecation against him, and as one says: "Woe to his mother" (*waylu ummihi*). From it comes (﴿then his mother is the Abyss﴾ [al-Qari'ah 101:9]). So a specific falling is intended, namely falling from a mountain or a roof, by the indication of the threat.

The sentence (*wa inni la-ghaffarun*, "And indeed, I am Most Forgiving") to its end is a digression (*istitrad*) after the warning against arrogance regarding the blessing, by guiding to that by which arrogance may be remedied if it occurs: through repentance and righteous deeds. The meaning of (*taba*) is: he regretted his disbelief, believed, and did righteous deeds.

His saying (*thumma ihtada*, "then remained guided"): the *thumma* here indicates delay in rank (*tarakhi fi al-rutbah*). It is used metaphorically to indicate the difference between two things in status, just as it was used for the difference between two times in occurrence. The meaning of *ihtada*: he persisted in guidance and remained steadfast upon it. It is like His saying (﴿Indeed, those who say, "Our Lord is Allah," then remain steadfast, there will be no fear upon them, nor will they grieve﴾ [al-Ahqaf 46:13]).

The verses point to what came in the Book of Exodus: "The LORD is a God merciful and gracious, slow to anger, and abundant in goodness, forgiving iniquity and transgression, but He will by no means clear the guilty..."

[p. 277]

﴿And what has hastened you away from your people, O Musa?﴾ ﴿He said: "They are right behind me on my track, and I hastened to You, my Lord, that You may be pleased."﴾ ﴿He said: "Indeed, We have tried your people after you, and al-Samiri has misled them."﴾

This is an conjunction (*'atf*) on the clause ﴿Travel by night with My servants﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77], which comes as an explanation (*tafsir*) of the act ﴿We revealed to Musa﴾ [Ta-Ha: 77]. So His words ﴿And what has hastened you away from your people﴾ are part of what Allah revealed to Musa. The sense is: "and [He said]: what has hastened you..." etc. This refers to what happened to them during Musa's private conversation with Allah at Mount Tur, in the third month after their departure from Egypt. This part of the story is not mentioned in Surat al-A'raf.

*Al-i'jal* means making something hasty.

The interrogative is used here to rebuke. What is understood from the statements of the exegetes (*mufassirun*), and what the verse indicates, is that Musa hastened to leave his people in order to attend the conversation before the appointed time that Allah had set for him, out of his own striving and desire to receive the Law, as Allah had promised him before the Children of Israel surrounded the mountain of Tur. He considered in this only the priority of what was good for himself and for his people. So Allah rebuked him for having neglected to consider what surrounded this action: his distance from his people before Allah had instructed them to observe the covenant and warned them against the deception of one who might be suspected of deceit. Thus he was in the position of Abu Bakr when he entered the mosque, found the Prophet ﷺ bowing, bowed (in place) and walked toward the row, and the Prophet ﷺ said to him: "May Allah increase you in eagerness, but do not repeat it."

Close to Musa's conduct (peace be upon him) is the case of a mujtahid (one who exercises independent legal reasoning) who acts on an indication that has a counter-indication of which he is unaware. That was the cause of his people's being tempted into making an idol to worship.

[p. 278]

The Torah contains nothing indicating more than that the Children of Israel made a calf of gold and took it as a god during Musa's absence, and that the reason for this was their slowness in Musa's return (﴿They said: "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Musa returns to us."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 91]).

His words here, ﴿They are right behind me on my track﴾, indicate that they were traveling behind him and that he had gone ahead of them to the conversation. He excused his haste by saying that he hastened to comply with Allah's command, in an effort to please Him. Then His words, exalted is He, ﴿Indeed, We have tried your people after you﴾ contain a kind of blame for the haste, in that it caused a trial to occur among his people. This was to inform him that he should not exceed what was appointed for him, even if he had been driven by desire for an increase of good.

*Al-athar* (with two fatha vowels) is what a walker leaves on the ground of the marks of a foot, hoof or shoe. It is also said *ithr* (with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the tha'), and both are eloquent forms, as Tha'lab mentioned. So the meaning of their saying "he came upon his trace" is: he came following him closely, near the time of his coming. He likened the one who follows to one who walks on the footprints of those who walked before, before those traces change by other feet. The point of resemblance is following closely, and that no one had preceded him.

The meaning is: "They are walking on the places of my footsteps," that is, following me in reaching the destination. From this is the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: ("I am al-Hashir (the Gatherer), upon whose footsteps people will be gathered"), its implied meaning being: they will be gathered walking on the traces of my footsteps.

The majority of readers recited (*'ala athari*) with two fatha vowels. Ruways, on the authority of Ya'qub, recited it with a kasra on the hamza and sukun on the tha'.

The construction *hum ula'* ("they, these") was used without the particle of alerting (*harf al-tanbih*) at the beginning of the demonstrative (*ism al-isharah*), unlike His words in Surat al-Nisa': (﴿Here you are, you who argued﴾ [al-Nisa': 109]).

[p. 279]

Omitting the alerting particle *ha* from the demonstrative is a permissible usage; less common than it is its use with the alerting particle together with the pronoun without the demonstrative, as in the saying of 'Abd Bani al-Hasḥas:

"Here am I, far from the beloved, O pain."

This was discussed earlier at His words, exalted is He (﴿Here you are, you love them﴾ [Al 'Imran: 119]) in Surat Al 'Imran.

Attributing the trials to Allah is in view of His being the one who decrees them and creates their remote causes. As for their direct attribution, it is the one in His words (﴿and al-Samiri has misled them﴾), because he was the immediate cause of their misguidance, which in turn caused their trial.

Regarding al-Samiri: it appears that its *ya'* is the *ya'* of relative nisba, and that its definition with *al-* is for a known (specific) referent. As for the nisba, its basis in Arabic is that it applies to tribes and clans. So al-Samiri is attributed to the name of an ancestor of a tribe from the Children of Israel or others, whose name resembles the word Samir; and among the ancient names were Shumar and Shamir, which are close to the name Samir, especially with Arabicization.

In Anwar al-Tanzil (of al-Baydawi): "al-Samiri is a nisba to a tribe from the Children of Israel called al-Samira." (End quote.)

We take from al-Baydawi's words that al-Samiri is attributed to a tribe, but his saying "from the Children of Israel" is not correct. For the Samaritans were a community of inhabitants of Palestine in the area of Nablus during the Roman (Byzantine) state. They were in Palestine before Palestine came under the hand of the Children of Israel, and then they mixed with the Israelites and followed the law of Musa (peace be upon him), with differences in their manner from the manner of the Jews. He was not attributed to the city of Samaria near Nablus, because the city of Samaria was built by King Omri, king of the kingdom of Israel, in the year 925 BCE. He made it the capital of his kingdom and named it Shomeron, because he built it on a mountain he bought from a man named Shamer for two talents of silver; it was Arabicized in Arabic as Samirah,

[p. 280]

and the Jews considered it a city of disbelief and tyranny, because Omri, its builder, and his son Ahab had corrupted the religion of the Torah and worshipped the Canaanite idols. Allah commanded the prophet Elijah (Ilyas) to rebuke them both and to rouse opposition against them. Therefore, it did not exist in the time of Musa, nor was its region part of the land of the Children of Israel in the time of Musa (peace be upon him).

It is possible that al-Samiri was attributed to a village called al-Samira from the villages of Egypt, as some of the people of tafsir said, so that he would have been a Coptic youth who infiltrated the Children of Israel because of his attachment to them in Egypt or because of a craft he practiced for them. From Sa'id ibn Jubayr: al-Samiri was from the people of Kirman. This is close to the possibility that al-Samiri is an Arabicized form of Kirmani, with some letters changed, which is common in Arabicization.

It is also possible that the *ya'* in al-Samiri is not a ya' of nisba, but a letter of a noun, like the ya' in 'Ali and Kursi, in which case it would be a原 (original) name or one borrowed into Hebrew, and the *lam* at its beginning would be extra.

Al-Zamakhshari and al-Qurtubi mentioned a mixture of stories: that al-Samiri's name was Musa ibn Zafar (with a fatha on the dotted *za'* and a fatha on the *fa'*), and that he was the son of Musa's maternal aunt or the son of his maternal uncle, and that he disbelieved in the religion of Musa after having been a believer in it. Some of them added details to others which the soul recoils from.

Know that al-Samiriyyun is a designation for a group of Jews, who are also called the Samaritans. They have a distinct doctrine that differs from the doctrine of the Jewish community in the fundamentals of religion. They do not venerate the Holy House (Bayt al-Maqdis), and they deny the prophethood of the prophets of the Children of Israel except Musa, Harun and Yusha' (Joshua). These deviations among them were only remnants of the teachings of heresy that they used to receive in the city of Samaria, which was founded on laxity, a disregard for the fundamentals of religion, and permissiveness in venerating the gods

[p. 281]

of their neighbours, the Canaanites, who were in-laws of their kings. That deviation persisted among them until the time of Jesus (peace be upon him). In the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 10, and in the Gospel of Luke, chapter 9, there is something implying that the town of the Samaritans was deviant from the followers of the Messiah, and that he forbade the Apostles from entering their city.

In the Book of Exodus in the Torah, chapter 32, there occurs a great error, for they claim that Harun made the calf for them when they said to him: "Make for us gods who will walk before us, for we do not know what has happened to Musa on the mountain." I suppose that this is one of the traces of the disappearance of the original Torah after the Babylonian Captivity, and that the one who rewrote it did not handle this story well. And among what we are certain of is that Harun is protected from this, because he is a messenger.

In the Book of Exodus in the Torah, chapter 32, there occurs a great error, for they claim that Harun made the calf for them when they said to him: "Make for us gods who will walk before us, for we do not know what has happened to Musa on the mountain." So he made for them a calf of gold. I suppose that this is one of the traces of the disappearance of the original Torah after the Babylonian Captivity, and that the one who rewrote it did not handle this story well. And among what we are certain of is that Harun is protected from this, because he is a messenger.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 86–87:

﴿So Moses returned to his people, angry and grieved. He said, "O my people! Did your Lord not make you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you, so that you broke your appointment with me?"﴾

Al-ghadab (anger): an emotional agitation of the soul and a surge that arises from perceiving what harms and displeases it, without fear. Its descriptive form is ghadban (angry).

Al-asaf (grief): an emotional state of the soul that arises from perceiving what saddens it and what it dislikes, together with a breaking of the heart. Its descriptive form is asif (grieved). Both emotions gathered in the soul of Moses, because what had happened among his community pained him, and he was not afraid of them. So his emotion concerning their condition was anger. He was also saddened by the occurrence of this while he was in his intimate conversation with God Most High, which he had hoped would be the cause of God's pleasure with his people. But when they did what does not please God, his heart was broken before his Lord.

This is the beginning of the description of Moses standing among his people, and among them were Harun (Aaron) and al-Samiri. He was striking their ears with the rebukes of his admonition. He began by addressing all of his people, and he knew that Harun would not be supporting them; therefore he began by addressing his people, then he turned the address to Harun by saying: "﴿O Harun, what prevented you...﴾" [Ta-Ha 20:92].

The clause "qala ya qawmi" (He said: O my people) is a resumptive explanatory clause (jumla bayaniyya).

Opening the address with "O my people" is a preparation for blame, since reproach directed at people is more fitting when the harm comes from one's own folk; this is shown by his saying "﴿so you broke my appointment﴾".

The interrogative in "﴿Did your Lord not make you a promise﴾" is denunciatory (inkari): they were treated as though they were someone who claimed that God had not made them a good promise, because they acted in a manner consistent with one who holds that claim, so he denounced their claim. It may also be a confirmatory interrogative (taqriri), whose nature is to be on the supposition of negation, as has been mentioned more than once.

The good promise is: His promise to Moses of sending down the Torah, and His appointing him thirty nights for intimate conversation. He had informed them of this, so it is a promise to his people, because it was for their benefit, and because God promised them that He would be their helper against their enemy and their guide on their path. This is what is related in His saying: "﴿And We appointed for you the right side of the Mount﴾" [Ta-Ha 20:80].

The interrogative in "﴿Did the time seem long to you?﴾" is based upon his previous statement "﴿Did your Lord not make you a promise?﴾", and it is a denunciatory interrogative: that is, the time since God's promise to you is not far. The meaning of "long time" is the length of the period, i.e., its distance: the time since your Lord's promise to you has not grown so distant that you should despair of its fulfilment, and so disbelieve and deny the one who conveyed the promise to you, and worship a lord other than the One to whom he who conveyed the promise called you, such that you would have a semblance of an excuse for turning away from worshipping God and forgetting His covenant.

Al-ahd (covenant): knowledge of a thing and remembering it; it is a verbal noun. It may be that it is applied to the object, like the use of "khalq" (creation) for "makhluq" (the created), meaning: what was known to you has grown long and its time has become distant, until you forgot it and acted contrary to it. It may also remain on the original sense of the verbal noun, which is their covenant with God to comply with and act upon the Law. This was mentioned in His saying "﴿Those who break the covenant of God after its confirmation﴾" [al-Baqara 2:27] and His saying "﴿Fulfil My covenant﴾" [al-Baqara 2:40] in Surah al-Baqara.

"Am" (or rather) is a retractive particle (idrab ibtali). The implied interrogative after "am" in "﴿or did you wish that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾" is also denunciatory, since the implied sense is: "Rather, did you wish that wrath should descend upon you?" So your disbelief in that case is nothing but casting yourselves into the wrath of God, like the condition of one who loves that wrath from God should descend upon him.

In His saying "﴿You wished that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you﴾" there is a figurative metaphor (isti'ara tamthiliyya), since it likens their state, in committing the causes for the descent of God's wrath upon them without any motive for doing so, to the state of one who loves that God's wrath should descend upon him; for love has no cause.

His saying "﴿so you broke my appointment﴾" is a consequence of the second denunciatory interrogative. The meaning of "my appointment" is the promise of God through his tongue, and its attribution to his pronoun is because he is the intermediary in it.

The sentence "They said" (قالوا) is not conjoined to what precedes it, because in the discourse it functions as a reply to the words of Musa (peace be upon him). The pronoun in (قالوا) refers to "the people" (القوم).

The one who spoke was in fact some of them, who undertook to answer on behalf of the whole people, and they were their elders and the righteous among them. Regarding his words "by our own will" (بِمَلْكِنا): Nafi', 'Asim and Abu Ja'far read it with a fatha on the mim. Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a kasra on the mim. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a damma on the mim. These are three readings of this word, and their meaning is: by our will and choice, that is, to break your promise. In other words, we did not presume to do so, but al-Samiri deceived them and the common mass of the people overpowered them. This is an admission by the respondents of what their common folk had done.

The corrective qualification (al-istidrak) [a clause that qualifies and corrects what precedes] refers back to what the negation implied, namely that their breaking of the covenant was not intentional misguidance. The clause that follows it is concise, expressing the purpose of disclaiming responsibility for breaking the covenant. The place of the istidrak is his words "So they said: 'This is your god and the god of Musa'" (﴿فَقالُوا هَذا إلَهُكم وإلَهُ مُوسى﴾), and what precedes it is preparation for it. Accordingly the clauses before it were joined with the particle fa, and they offered an excuse that they had been overcome in their judgment by the misleading of al-Samiri. Thus there was incorporated into this excuse a reference to the matter of fashioning the calf which they worshipped, and which deceived them as it was made to appear to them to be their sought-after god, because of how much they had heard from their messenger that God is with them or before them, and because of the longing that stirred in their minds to see Him, exalted is He.

Nafi', Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Amir, Hafs from 'Asim, and Ruways from Ya'qub read "we were loaded" (حُمِّلْنا) with a damma on the ha' and a shadda on the mim with a kasra. That is, "he who loaded us loaded us," or "we loaded ourselves."

Abu Bakr from 'Asim, Hamza, Abu 'Amr, al-Kisa'i, and Rawh from Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the ha' and a fatha on the mim, unshadda'd.

[p. 285]

The "burdens" (الأوزار) are loads. The "ornaments" (الزينة) are jewelry and worked gold and silver. When the Children of Israel were resolved to leave, they had devised a stratagem against the Copts, so that each one borrowed from his Coptic neighbour jewelry of silver and gold and household goods, as is in chapter 12 of the Book of Exodus (سفر الخروج). The meaning is that they feared the loss of that finery, so they resolved to fashion it into one piece or two, so that it could be kept safely in a secure place.

The "casting" (القذف) is throwing. It is intended here to mean throwing into the fire of al-Samiri for melting, as chapter 32 of the Book of Exodus suggests. This is therefore a report of their answer to Musa (peace be upon him), briefly and concisely, in the manner of one who offers a feeble excuse and is ashamed of it, and so cuts his speech short.

* * *

﴿Thus did al-Samiri cast﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87] ﴿so he brought forth for them a calf, a body that had a lowing sound, and they said: "This is your god and the god of Musa, but he forgot."﴾

The apparent state of the consequential fa' (الفاء التفريعية) [the fa' that marks a consequence following from what precedes] is that what follows it is spoken by the speaker of the statement on which it is consequent. The meaning is: just as we cast the ornaments of the people (into the fire), so al-Samiri cast something of the people's ornaments, and so he brought forth for them a calf. The purpose of this comparison is to move on to the story of fashioning the calf they worshipped. The pronouns of the third person in "so he brought forth for them" (﴿فَأخْرَجَ لَهُمْ﴾) and in "they said" refer to persons other than the speakers. The speakers attributed the bringing out and the saying to absent persons, to indicate that the speakers with Musa had not been among those who believed in the divinity of the calf, but that they had flattered the common folk. On this view the passage is a report of what the people said to Musa, and it is part of the excuse with which the respondents answered Musa. The pronoun in "so he brought forth for them" is then an iltifat (shift of grammatical person) which the proponents intended as a disclaimer, that the bringing forth of the calf was for their sake; that is, he brought it forth for those who desired it.

Some exegetes took this whole passage to be from God's side, and this is the view of Abu Muslim. It would then be an interjection and a report to the Messenger (ﷺ) and to the community. But the position of the fa' contradicts this, because the fa' does not, on careful analysis, introduce a fresh beginning; so the fa' is a consequential fa' of one report following on another. The meaning: just as that casting by which we cast what was in our hands of the ornaments of the people, al-Samiri cast what was in his hand into the fire so that it would melt and he could fashion it; so he brought forth for them from that a calf, a body. The verb "cast" (ألقى) narrates a state that is compared with the state of their casting the Copts' worked gold. "Casting" and "throwing" (القذف والإلقاء) are synonyms, and one is likened to the other.

The "body" (الجسد) is a physical form with limbs, whether alive or not, as in God's words: ﴿And We placed upon his throne a body﴾ [Sad: 34]. It is said that it was the half of a child that one of his wives had borne, as is reported in a hadith. Al-Zajjaj said: the "body" is that which does not understand or discern; it is merely the lifeless form, that is, he brought forth for them an image of a calf embodied in its shape, its legs, and its sides, not merely a picture engraved on a plate of silver or gold. In the Book of Exodus it is said that it was of gold.

"Bringing forth" (الإخراج) is making manifest what had been hidden. The expression "bringing forth" indicates that he made it by a concealed stratagem kept from them until he completed it.

The "lowing" (الخوار) is the sound of a cow. The one who made the calf for them was skilled in the tricks by which they used to make idols, placing in their bellies and necks openings like pipes, through which sounds would come out when winds were blown into them by bellows or the like.

[p. 287]

Al-Samiri made for them an idol in the form of a calf, because they had grown accustomed in Egypt to worshipping the calf "Apis" (إيبيس). When they saw what al-Samiri had fashioned in the form of a deity, they recognised it from before, and saw that it surpassed it in having a lowing sound. There became firmly fixed in their confused imaginings that this was the true God, which they expressed by saying: "This is your god and the god of Musa," because they saw it was of gold or silver, and so they imagined it to be superior to the calf "Apis." Since they used to affirm a god hidden from sight, and sought to see him, they said to Musa: "Show us God openly." Then they imagined that this was their sought-after lost object. The story of their taking the calf in the Torah is not consistent with sound reasoning.

The consequential fa' in "so he forgot" (فنسي) may be a consequence following from "so they said: 'This is your god'," a consequence of cause upon effect, in which case the pronoun refers to al-Samiri: al-Samiri said that because he had forgotten what he had received of guidance. Or it may be a consequence of effect upon cause, that is, he said that, and his saying it became the reason for his forgetting the guidance he had, since God set a seal upon his heart through this saying, depriving him of success thereafter.

"Forgetting" (النسيان) is used to mean neglect, as in God's words: ﴿He said: "Thus did Our signs come to you, but you forgot them"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 126], and His words: ﴿those who are heedless of their prayer﴾ [al-Ma'un: 5]. On this view the words "so he forgot" are part of the report and not of what is reported, and the pronoun refers to al-Samiri. On this basis it should be connected to his words "Do they not see?" (﴿أفَلا يَرَوْنَ﴾) and be an interjection. A group of exegetes took the pronoun to refer to Musa, meaning: Musa forgot your god and his god, that is, he neglected him, and went to the mountain seeking him while he was among you. But the position of the consequential fa' weakens this interpretation.

"Forgetting" is sometimes used metaphorically to mean heedlessness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 89:

Page 288
﴿Do they not see that it does not return to them any word, nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit?﴾
It is permissible that this be an interjection (i'tiraด, parenthetical insertion) and not part of the report of the people's speech. It is then placed between the clause ﴿So the Samiri cast [it]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87] and the clause ﴿[Moses] said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, from following me?"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 92–93]. In that case the fa' (the particle "fa", "then/so") serves to connect the speech of one speaker to the speech of another, that is, it connects the report and not the one who reports it, and the reporter is plural. It is also permissible that it be part of the report of those who took it upon themselves to address Moses, peace be upon him, from among his people, namely their elders and righteous ones, so that it becomes known that they were upon insight into monotheism.

The interrogative is a rebuke (istifham inkari), and they are treated as one who does not see the calf, because they did not act in accordance with what sight requires. So their failure to see it, despite its being manifest, is condemned. That is, how do they claim divinity for the calf when they see that it does not speak and cannot bring about benefit or harm?

The seeing here is either visual, used figuratively, or used in the general sense of perception, so it returns to the meaning of belief and knowledge, especially with respect to the clause ﴿nor does it possess for them any harm or benefit﴾, for that is not seen with the eye, unlike ﴿does not return to them any word﴾. The seeing of the absence of both matters is meant as seeing the effect of their absence, through the continuing absence of speech and the absence of their benefit and harm, because the denunciation is directed at their belief that it is their god, which would require that it possess harm and benefit for them.

The meaning of "yarji'u" (returns) is "yaruddu", that is, it answers speech, because that is the locus of the lesson in its lacking the attributes of the rational being: they call upon it, praise it and glorify it, while it is silent, neither thanking them nor promising them a response. It is the nature of one who is perfect, when he hears praise or receives a request, to respond. There is no doubt that in that great throng there were those in need of bringing benefit or repelling harm, and that they asked it for that, but found nothing in it that would benefit them

Page 289
or repel harm from them, such as the harm of an enemy or an illness. They had witnessed its lack of use to them. Moreover, the evidence of its state, namely its lack of movement, bears witness that it is incapable of benefiting or harming, so the denunciation was directed at the failure to see, because its state is something that is seen.
The lam in "lahum" is connected to "yamliku", which is in the sense of "yastati'u" (is able), as was previously mentioned in the words of Allah, exalted is He: ﴿Say, "Do you worship besides Allah that which possesses for you neither harm nor benefit?"﴾ [al-Ma'idah: 76] in Surat al-'Uqud. He placed harm before benefit to definitively cut off their excuse in believing in its divinity, because the excuse of one who fears harm is stronger than the excuse of one who desires benefit. The "an" in His words "alla yarji'u" is a lightened form of "anna" (that), with a suppressed pronoun of the matter (damir sha'n) as its subject, and the clause that follows it is its predicate. So "yarji'u" is in the nominative by the agreement of the readings except for some anomalous readings. "An" is not a verbal (masdariyyah) "an", because the verbal "an" does not occur after verbs of knowledge or verbs of perception.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 20, verses 90–91:**

﴿And Aaron had already said to them before: "O my people, you are only being tested by it, and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, so follow me and obey my command."﴾ ﴿They said: "We will not cease to be devoted to it until Moses returns to us."﴾

The clause is in the position of a circumstantial phrase (ḥāl) relative to the pronoun in "Do they not see" according to both possibilities; that is, how do they not infer, from the fact that the calf does not return speech to them and possesses neither harm nor benefit for them, that it does not deserve divinity, so that they would desist from worshipping the calf?

This is a rational proof (dalālah 'aqliyyah), in the circumstance that Aaron had admonished them and alerted them to this, for he reminded them that it was a trial (fitnah) by which the Samiri had tested them, and that their Lord is the Most Merciful, not that which does not possess benefit for them, let alone mercy. He commanded them to follow his command, and this is an auditory proof (dalālah sam'iyyah).

The emphasis of the statement by the particle of certainty (ḥarf al-taḥqīq) and the oath particle (lām al-qasam) serves to establish the falsity of what is in the Book of the Jews, that Aaron is the one who made the calf for them and that he did not deny their worship of it. The most that can be said is that he was mocking them within himself, and that is a great falsehood in their book.

The noun governed by "qabl" (before) is omitted, indicated by the context, that is: before Moses returns to them and rebukes them. The opening of his address with "O my people" is a preparation for the situation of counsel.

The meaning of ﴿you are only being tested by it﴾: it is nothing but a trial for you, and it is not a lord; and indeed your Lord is the Most Merciful, who shows mercy to you in all circumstances. They answered him that they would not cease to remain devoted to its worship until Moses returns, whereupon he will declare to them plainly that the calf is not their lord.

Aaron arranged his address according to the natural order, for he began by restraining them from falsehood and from worshipping what is not a lord; then he called them to knowing the true Lord; then he called them to following the Messenger, since he was a messenger among them; then he called them to acting by the sharia. Yet they did nothing but insist on continuing their worship of the calf, so they answered Aaron with a resolute reply.

"ʿalayhi" is connected to "ʿākifīn," and it was placed before its complement to strengthen the judgment; or they meant: "We will not cease; we will single it out for devotion and will not be devoted to anything else."

*al-ʿUkūf* (devotion): staying constantly in a place with the intention of drawing near to God and worship; the worshippers of idols would remain by them and circumambulate them.

﴿He said, "O Harun, what prevented you, when you saw them going astray, ﴾ ﴿from following me? Did you then disobey my command?" ﴾ ﴿He said, "O son of my mother, do not seize me by my beard or by my head. I feared that you would say, 'You have caused division among the Children of Israel and did not heed my word.'"﴾

Musa moved from addressing his people to addressing his brother. The clause "﴿He said, 'O Harun'﴾" follows the clause "﴿He said, 'O my people, did your Lord not promise you a good promise?'﴾" [Ta-Ha: 86], and also the clause "﴿They said, 'We did not break our promise to you of our own will'﴾" [Ta-Ha: 87]. There is a occasion for relating his address to Harun after a separation occurred among the parts of the narrative by parenthetical clauses, among them the clause "﴿And Harun had already said to them before this﴾" [Ta-Ha: 90], etc. So this is a digression (istitrad) within the narrative, serving to signal Harun's excuse as mentioned earlier. Musa turned the address to the Samiri, who had been the cause of the people's misguidance. So this sentence follows from the people's words: ﴿Thus did al-Samiri cast [it]﴾ [Ta-Ha: 87], ﴿and brought forth for them a calf﴾ [Ta-Ha: 88], and so on, and it is therefore the beginning of a new address. Perhaps Musa did not speak harshly to him as he had to Harun, because he was ignorant of the religion, so his straying was not surprising. This may also support what has been said: that the Samiri was not from the Children of Israel but was from the Copts or from Kirman, and infiltrated among the Children of Israel. Since Musa was sent to the Children of Israel specifically, and to Pharaoh and his chiefs in order to free the Children of Israel, following Musa's law was not obligatory for non-Israelites, but it was recommended for them because of the guidance it contains. Therefore Musa did not rebuke him, because the people more deserving of rebuke were those who had covenanted with Allah to follow the law.

The meaning of ﴿What is your business?﴾ (ma khatbuka) is: what is your request, i.e., what are you seeking (takhtubu, "you seek"). It is a verbal noun (masdar). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this expression is used most often for unpleasant matters, because al-khatb (the matter) is an unpleasant affair, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So what is your business, O messengers?﴾. So the meaning is: what is this calamity you have brought upon the people, and what was your purpose in what you did.

As for His saying, ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾ up to His saying ﴿so I threw it away﴾: if the words "bassurtu bima lam yabsuru bihi" (I perceived what they did not perceive), "qabadtu qabdatan" (I grasped a handful), "athar" (the track), and "nabadtuha" (I threw it away) are taken in their literal senses, as the majority of exegetes have held, then the meaning would be: I saw what they did not see, i.e., I looked at what they did not look at. This is based on the view that "basura" and "absara" are both verbs of seeing with the eye. However, basura bi-l-shay' literally means "he became perceptive of it" or "perceptive by means of it," i.e., intensely perceptive, so it is stronger than absara, because it is derived from a verb with the vowel ḍamma on the ʿayn, from which the adjectives of quality (al-sifat al-mushabbaha, adjectives expressing a fixed disposition) are derived. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿and she watched him from afar﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], in Surat al-Qasas.

Since the meaning here is clearly about a visible matter, the word must be taken in a figurative sense: basura, which denotes strength of sight, is used metaphorically for strong knowledge, by the relation of generality to specificity (ʿalaqat al-iṭlaq ʿan al-taqyid). This is like His saying: ﴿So your sight today is keen﴾ [Qaf: 22], and just as firm knowledge is called basira in His saying: ﴿I call to Allah with insight﴾ [Yusuf: 108].

It is reported in the language of the Arabs, from al-Lihyani, that one says: "innahu la-basirun bi-l-ashya'" (he is truly perceptive of things), meaning he knows them, and "basurtu bi-l-shay'" means "I knew it." From this is derived His saying: ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾. Al-Akhfash also interpreted it this way, as reported in Lisan al-Arab, and al-Zajjaj affirmed it. So the meaning is: I knew what they did not know, and I became aware of what they were not aware of, as al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) also took it as the first of two interpretations of the verse. Accordingly there are two approaches: either to treat "basurtu" as a metaphor, or to treat it as a literal usage.

The majority read ﴿they did not perceive (yabsuru)﴾ with a yā' (third person), taking the verb's subject as the absent third person. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a tā' (second person), taking it as an address to Musa and those with him.

Al-qabḍa, with a fatḥa on the qāf, means one instance of grasping (al-qabḍ), which is closing the palm over something. So al-qabḍa is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). Its opposite is al-basṭ (opening the palm).

Al-nabdh is throwing down what is in the hand.

Al-athar, literally, is the trace that a walker leaves in the form of the imprint of his foot in sand or dust. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿They are right behind me on my track﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84].

If the words are taken in their literal senses, then the word "al-rasul" must be understood as something other than its commonly known meaning. It must therefore be taken to refer to Jibril, since he is a messenger from Allah to the prophets. The majority of exegetes said: the intended meaning of "al-rasul" is Jibril. They related a story: they said that Allah tested the Samiri, and Allah showed him Jibril riding a horse, and the horse's hoof struck a place which then became green with plants. The Samiri knew that the trace of Jibril, when cast upon an inanimate object, made it alive, so he took a handful of that dust and made a calf, and cast a handful upon it, and it became a body, i.e., alive, having a lowing like the lowing of a calf. He expressed that casting by the word "nabdh" (throwing). But what they mentioned is not found in the books of the Israelites, nor has any report of it come from the Sunnah. It consists only of statements from some of the early generations (al-salaf), and perhaps it spread among the people from the narrations of the storytellers (al-qussas).

If these six words are interpreted in figurative senses, then "basurtu" means "I knew and was guided," i.e., I was guided to knowledge of what they did not know, namely the knowledge of crafting images and forms by which the calf was made, and the knowledge of the trick by which the lowing of the calf was produced. "Qabḍa" would mean a small portion, "athar" would mean teaching, i.e., the law, and "nabadtu" would mean I neglected and rejected, i.e., I had a general knowledge of the guidance of the law but I departed from it by disbelief. In this way the word "al-rasul" can be understood in its common and well-known sense, namely one to whom a law has been revealed by Allah and who has been commanded to convey it. The meaning would then be: by my making the calf for worship, I have rejected following the law of Musa. The meaning is that he acknowledged before Musa that he had made the calf, and acknowledged that he had been ignorant and had gone astray, and he excused himself by saying that his own soul had made it seem fair to him.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani interpreted it in this sense, al-Zamakhshari preferred it by placing it first in mention before the interpretation of the majority, and al-Fakhr (al-Razi) chose it.

Al-taswil means making seem attractive what is not truly attractive.

The comparison in His saying: ﴿and thus my soul made it seem fair to me﴾ is the comparison of a thing with itself, like His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], i.e., thus the making-seem-fair has made it seem fair to me, a making-seem-fair that cannot be described by anything more than that.

Since Musa was sent to the Children of Israel specifically, and to Pharaoh and his chiefs in order to free the Children of Israel, following Musa's law was not obligatory for non-Israelites, but it was recommended for them because of the guidance it contains. Therefore Musa did not rebuke him, because the people more deserving of rebuke were those who had covenanted with Allah to follow the law.

The meaning of ﴿What is your business?﴾ (ma khatbuka) is: what is your request, i.e., what are you seeking (takhtubu, "you seek"). It is a verbal noun (masdar). Ibn 'Atiyyah said: this expression is used most often for unpleasant matters, because al-khatb (the matter) is an unpleasant affair, as in His saying, Exalted is He: ﴿So what is your business, O messengers?﴾. So the meaning is: what is this calamity you have brought upon the people, and what was your purpose in what you did.

As for His saying, ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾ up to His saying ﴿so I threw it away﴾: if the words "bassurtu bima lam yabsuru bihi" (I perceived what they did not perceive), "qabadtu qabdatan" (I grasped a handful), "athar" (the track), and "nabadtuha" (I threw it away) are taken in their literal senses, as the majority of exegetes have held, then the meaning would be: I saw what they did not see, i.e., I looked at what they did not look at. This is based on the view that "basura" and "absara" are both verbs of seeing with the eye. However, basura bi-l-shay' literally means "he became perceptive of it" or "perceptive by means of it," i.e., intensely perceptive, so it is stronger than absara, because it is derived from a verb with the vowel ḍamma on the ʿayn, from which the adjectives of quality (al-sifat al-mushabbaha, adjectives expressing a fixed disposition) are derived. Allah, Exalted, says: ﴿and she watched him from afar﴾ [al-Qasas: 11], in Surat al-Qasas.

Since the meaning here is clearly about a visible matter, the word must be taken in a figurative sense: basura, which denotes strength of sight, is used metaphorically for strong knowledge, by the relation of generality to specificity (ʿalaqat al-iṭlaq ʿan al-taqyid). This is like His saying: ﴿So your sight today is keen﴾ [Qaf: 22], and just as firm knowledge is called basira in His saying: ﴿I call to Allah with insight﴾ [Yusuf: 108].

It is reported in the language of the Arabs, from al-Lihyani, that one says: "innahu la-basirun bi-l-ashya'" (he is truly perceptive of things), meaning he knows them, and "basurtu bi-l-shay'" means "I knew it." From this is derived His saying: ﴿I perceived what they did not perceive﴾. Al-Akhfash also interpreted it this way, as reported in Lisan al-Arab, and al-Zajjaj affirmed it. So the meaning is: I knew what they did not know, and I became aware of what they were not aware of, as al-Zamakhshari (author of al-Kashshaf) also took it as the first of two interpretations of the verse. Accordingly there are two approaches: either to treat "basurtu" as a metaphor, or to treat it as a literal usage.

The majority read ﴿they did not perceive (yabsuru)﴾ with a yā' (third person), taking the verb's subject as the absent third person. Hamza, al-Kisa'i and Khalaf read it with a tā' (second person), taking it as an address to Musa and those with him.

Al-qabḍa, with a fatḥa on the qāf, means one instance of grasping (al-qabḍ), which is closing the palm over something. So al-qabḍa is a verbal noun in the sense of a passive participle (maf'ul). Its opposite is al-basṭ (opening the palm).

Al-nabdh is throwing down what is in the hand.

Al-athar, literally, is the trace that a walker leaves in the form of the imprint of his foot in sand or dust. It was mentioned earlier at His saying: ﴿They are right behind me on my track﴾ [Ta-Ha: 84].

If the words are taken in their literal senses, then the word "al-rasul" must be understood as something other than its commonly known meaning. It must therefore be taken to refer to Jibril, since he is a messenger from Allah to the prophets. The majority of exegetes said: the intended meaning of "al-rasul" is Jibril. They related a story: they said that Allah tested the Samiri, and Allah showed him Jibril riding a horse, and the horse's hoof struck a place which then became green with plants. The Samiri knew that the trace of Jibril, when cast upon an inanimate object, made it alive, so he took a handful of that dust and made a calf, and cast a handful upon it, and it became a body, i.e., alive, having a lowing like the lowing of a calf. He expressed that casting by the word "nabdh" (throwing). But what they mentioned is not found in the books of the Israelites, nor has any report of it come from the Sunnah. It consists only of statements from some of the early generations (al-salaf), and perhaps it spread among the people from the narrations of the storytellers (al-qussas).

If these six words are interpreted in figurative senses, then "basurtu" means "I knew and was guided," i.e., I was guided to knowledge of what they did not know, namely the knowledge of crafting images and forms by which the calf was made, and the knowledge of the trick by which the lowing of the calf was produced. "Qabḍa" would mean a small portion, "athar" would mean teaching, i.e., the law, and "nabadtu" would mean I neglected and rejected, i.e., I had a general knowledge of the guidance of the law but I departed from it by disbelief. In this way the word "al-rasul" can be understood in its common and well-known sense, namely one to whom a law has been revealed by Allah and who has been commanded to convey it. The meaning would then be: by my making the calf for worship, I have rejected following the law of Musa. The meaning is that he acknowledged before Musa that he had made the calf, and acknowledged that he had been ignorant and had gone astray, and he excused himself by saying that his own soul had made it seem fair to him.

Abu Muslim al-Isfahani interpreted it in this sense, al-Zamakhshari preferred it by placing it first in mention before the interpretation of the majority, and al-Fakhr (al-Razi) chose it.

Al-taswil means making seem attractive what is not truly attractive.

The comparison in His saying: ﴿and thus my soul made it seem fair to me﴾ is the comparison of a thing with itself, like His saying: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143], i.e., thus the making-seem-fair has made it seem fair to me, a making-seem-fair that cannot be described by anything more than that.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 97:

﴿He said, "Then go. For you in this life is that you will say, 'No contact.' And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet. And look at your deity to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it and then blow it into the sea with a blowing."﴾

Moses did not add to the punishment of al-Samiri (the Samaritan) beyond expelling him from the community. This was either because he was not one of them, and so he was not subject to the rulings of the Sharia, or because Moses knew that al-Samiri's reform was not to be hoped for. He would then be among those upon whom "the word of punishment" had come into effect, like those about whom God the Exalted said: ﴿Indeed, those upon whom the word of your Lord has come into effect will not believe﴾ [Yunus: 96] ﴿Even if every sign should come to them until they see the painful punishment﴾ [Yunus: 97]. Moses may have been informed of this by revelation or by inspiration, as with the man who fought fiercely alongside the Muslims, of whom the Prophet ﷺ said, "Indeed, he is among the people of the Fire." It is also like the hypocrites about whom God informed Muhammad ﷺ, and the Prophet – upon him be prayers and peace – informed Hudhayfah ibn al-Yaman about some of them.

As for his saying, "Go" (fa-dhhab), the more evident meaning is that it is a command to him to depart and leave the midst of the community. It is also permissible that it be a word of rebuke, like God's saying: ﴿He said, "Go, and whoever follows you among them – indeed, Hell is your recompense"﴾ [al-Isra: 63], and like the words of the poet which Sibawayh quoted in his book without attributing them:

Today you have approached us to satirize and insult us, so go away, what a strange matter are you and the days!

It is also permissible that what is intended is indifference to his condition, like the words of al-Nabhani, one of the poets of al-Hamasah (the anthology of bravery):

If you were a leader, we would have made you a leader, but if you are only a wanderer, then go away and leave us alone.

As for his saying: ﴿Indeed, for you in this life is that you will say, "No contact." And indeed, for you is an appointment you will not fail to meet﴾, it is an announcement of what God punished him with in this world and the Hereafter. He made his portion in his life that he would say, "No contact" – that is, God removed from him the sociability that is in human nature and replaced it with frenzy, whisperings and wildness. So he became distant from mingling with people, living alone, not allowing anyone to approach him. If a person met him, he would say to him, "No contact," fearing that he would touch him, meaning: do not touch me and I will not touch you; or he meant: no approaching me. The word "touch" (massa) is used for approaching, as in His saying: ﴿and do not touch it with harm﴾. This is more suitable to the form of the verb (mufa'alah), meaning: a mutual closeness between us. So he would say this, and this was a dreadful state in which he became an object of mockery.

"Misas" with a kasrah on the mim is the reading of all the readers. It is a verbal noun from massahu (to touch), meaning "massahu". "La" is a negation of the genus (la al-nafy li-l-jins), and "misas" is its noun, built on fathah. As for His saying: ﴿And indeed, for you is an appointment﴾, the lam in "laka" is an ironic metaphor (isti'arah tahakkumiyyah), like His saying: ﴿and if you do evil, it is for themselves﴾ [al-Isra: 7], meaning: then it is upon them. He threatened him with the punishment of the Hereafter and made it an appointment for him, meaning the appointment of gathering and punishment. So "al-maw'id" is a verbal noun, meaning: a promise that will not be broken, ﴿the promise of God. God does not fail in His promise﴾ [al-Rum: 6]. Here it is a threat of the punishment of the Hereafter.

The majority of readers read "lan tukhlafahu" with a fathah on the lam, in the passive voice, because its agent is known, namely God the Exalted, meaning: God will not delay it from you. So "ikhlaf" (failing to fulfil) is used metaphorically for delaying because of its fitting with "maw'id" (appointment).

[Page 299]

Ibn Kathir, Abu 'Amr and Ya'qub read it with a kasrah on the lam, as the imperfect of akhlafa, and its hamzah is for finding (lil-wijdan). One says: akhlafa al-wa'd when he finds the promise broken. Or it may be that al-Samiri is the one who has the power to break the promise, and that he will not break it; this is in the manner of irony, following the irony conveyed by the lam of possession.

After Moses threatened al-Samiri, he explained to him and to those who followed him the error of their worship of the calf, that it does not deserve divinity, because it is for humiliation and impotence. So He said: ﴿And look at your deity to which you remained devoted; we will surely burn it and then blow it into the sea with a blowing﴾. Reasoning by looking (al-nazar) was made an indication that it is a clear proof, which the one who reasons by it needs no more than observation, for the indication of perceptible things is clearer than the indication of intelligibles. He attributed the deity to the pronoun of al-Samiri as mockery of al-Samiri and as belittling him. He described that alleged deity by means of a relative clause (mawsuliyyah), because of what the relative clause (silah) indicates of alerting to error and mistake, meaning: the one who does not deserve to be devoted to.

As for His saying "zalta" (you remained), with a fathah on the zay in the well-known readings, its origin is "zalalta". The first lam was deleted to lighten the succession of two lams. This deletion is rare according to Sibawayh, and according to others it is analogical. The verb "zall" is one of the sisters of "kana", and its original meaning is indicating the attribution of its subject with its predicate during the daytime. Here it is a figurative usage in the sense of "dama" (to persist), by the relation of generality (ʿalaqat al-iṭlaq), based on the fact that most actions take place during the day.

Al-'Ukuf: constant devotion to worship, which was mentioned earlier.

The fronting of the prepositional phrase in His saying ﴿upon it devoted﴾ is for restriction (li-l-takhsis), meaning: the one you chose for worship to the exclusion of others, that is, to the exclusion of God the Exalted.

[Page 300]

The majority read "li-nuharriqannahu" with a damma on the first nun, a fathah on the ha', and a kasrah on the ra' with shaddah. "Tahrik" means intense burning, meaning: we will burn it with a burning that leaves no shape of it. He intended by it that it would be melted by fire until its shape is ruined and it becomes pieces.

Ibn Jammaz, from Abu Ja'far, read "lanuhriqannahu" with a damma on the first nun, a sukun on the ha', and a light ra'. Ibn Wardan, from Abu Ja'far, read it with a fathah on the first nun, a sukun on the ha', and a damma on the ra', because one says: ahraqahu and harraqahu.

"Al-nasf": dispersing and scattering the parts of a hard thing, like a building or dust. By "al-yamm" he meant the Red Sea, called the Sea of Qulzum, and in the Torah called the Sea of Suf (Sea of Reeds). At that time they were encamped on its shore at the foot of Mount Sinai (al-Tur).

"Thumma" (then) indicates graded sequence (al-tarakhi al-rutbi), because blowing away the calf is more severe in its destruction than burning it, and more humiliating to it. He emphasized "lanansifannahu" with the absolute object (al-maf'ul al-mutlaq), to indicate that he does not hesitate in this and does not fear its anger, as they claim that it is a deity.

This sentence is part of the report of Musa's (peace be upon him) speech, so its place is that of a concluding statement (tadhyil) to his admonition. He turned from addressing al-Samiri to addressing the community, turning away from addressing him in contempt of him, and intending to alert them to their error and to teach them the attributes of the true God. He limited himself to two of these attributes: oneness and the comprehensiveness of knowledge. This is because oneness encompasses all the attributes, as has been established in the books of ʿilm al-kalam (scholastic theology, the discipline of rational theology) regarding the indication of the declaration of tawhid (the testimony of God's oneness) upon them.

[p. 301]

As for the comprehensiveness of knowledge, it is a reference to God's knowledge of all existing things, including their deeds, so that they would keep watch over Him in their private affairs.

The verb "wasiʿa" (encompassed) is used figuratively for the meaning of complete encompassing, because a wide vessel encompasses more things than what is smaller than it. "ʿIlman" (in knowledge) is in the accusative as a specification (tamyiz) of the relation of breadth to God, so the meaning is interpreted as: His knowledge encompassed every thing, that is, it does not fall short of comprehending even the most hidden things, as the word "kull" (every), which denotes generality, indicates. A close meaning to this was mentioned earlier, in His saying: ﴿His Kursi encompasses the heavens and the earth﴾ [al-Baqarah: 255], in Surat al-Baqarah.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 99–101:

﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has preceded; and We have certainly given you from Us a reminder.﴾ ﴿Whoever turns away from it will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden.﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever; and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection.﴾

This is a resumptive sentence serving as a concluding remark (tadhyil), which conveys the high regard for the story of the mission of Musa (Moses) and the matters that followed it concerning the Children of Israel, beginning from His saying: ﴿Has the story of Musa reached you?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9] ﴿When he saw a fire﴾ [Ta-Ha: 10]. That is, like these narratives We relate to you the news of the past generations. The demonstrative refers to the story mentioned. What is meant by His saying "naqussu" (We relate) is Our relating, and the present tense was used to evoke the good state in that narration.

Page 302

The comparison refers to comparing it to itself, as a metonymy for the fact that when one wishes to liken and bring it closer to something better known within its own category, the one who wishes this finds no way to make the comparison except by likening it to itself, because nothing else surpasses it in its category so that it could be brought closer by it. This is in the manner of what preceded in His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And thus We have made you a median nation﴾ [al-Baqarah: 143] in Surat al-Baqarah, and its like is numerous in the Qur'an.

The "min" in His saying ﴿of the news of what has preceded﴾ is partitive (tab'idiyyah), and it is an attribute of an omitted noun whose estimate is: narratives from the news of what has preceded. You may also make "min" a noun meaning "some," in which case it is the object of "naqussu."

Al-anba' (the news) means the reports. The relative "ma" has as its referent the periods of time, because reports are attributed to their times, as in the saying of people: the reports of the days of the Arabs, and the middle centuries. All of these, by right, are defined by "ma," which is predominant for non-rational beings. It is known that what is intended is what they contain of the conditions of nations, so if it had been defined by "man," which is predominant for rational beings, that would have been valid. All of this is broad.

His saying ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ is an allusion to the fact that what is narrated of the reports of nations is not intended to fill up a span of time or to entertain the listeners with talk; rather, what is intended by it is admonition and reminder, and the awakening of the insight of the polytheists among the Arabs to the point of consideration in this story, which is the people's turning away from the guidance of their messenger and their submission to the misleading of the misguiders among them. For the allusion to this, He, exalted is He, said: ﴿And We have certainly given you from Us a reminder﴾ ﴿Whoever turns away from it will bear on the Day of Resurrection a burden﴾ ﴿Abiding therein forever﴾.

The indefiniteness of "dhikran" is for magnification, that is, We have given you a great Book. His saying "from Us" is an emphasis on the meaning of "We have given you" and an honouring of the status of the Qur'an, that it is a gift which was stored with Allah, so He singled out with it the best of His servants.

Page 303

Al-wizr (the burden) means the sin. It was made "carried" as a figure for encountering hardship as a result of sin, that is, of the punishment for it. So here there is an omitted genitive whose indicator is the circumstantial clause in His saying "abiding therein," and it is a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun or the pronoun object of the emphatic particle. Their referent is one and the same, but the number was varied between singular and plural out of regard for the word "man" once and for its meaning another time, which is the plural of those who turn away. So He said "man a'rada" (whoever turns away), then He said "khalidin" (abiding). The clause ﴿and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, that is: and being miserable thereby. "Saa'" here is one of the verbs of blame, like "bi'sa," and the subject of "saa'" is a hidden, undefined pronoun which is explained by the specification (tamyiz) that follows it, which is "himlan" (a burden).

Al-himl (with a kasra on the ha') is a noun meaning the thing carried, like al-dhibh meaning the thing slaughtered. The object of the blame is omitted, the indication being the word "wizran" over it. The estimate: and evil is their burden as a burden, their sin. Omitting the object of praise and blame verbs is common, as in His saying: ﴿And We gave to Dawud, Sulayman; an excellent servant; indeed he was ever turning back (to Allah)﴾ [Sad: 30], that is, Sulayman is the one who turns back. The "lam" in His saying "wa saa'a lahum" is the lam of specification (lam al-tabyin), and it specifies the object in meaning, because the original sentence is: the burden was evil to them, so the lam was brought to add specificity to the connection of blame with their burden. So the lam is for clarifying those with whom the evil of the burden is connected.

Al-himl (with a kasra on the ha') is the thing carried, like al-dhibh.
