His saying "from Us" is an emphasis on the meaning of "We have given you" and an honouring of the status of the Qur'an, that it is a gift which was stored with Allah, so He singled out with it the best of His servants.

Page 303

Al-wizr (the burden) means the sin. It was made "carried" as a figure for encountering hardship as a result of sin, that is, of the punishment for it. So here there is an omitted genitive whose indicator is the circumstantial clause in His saying "abiding therein," and it is a circumstantial clause from the relative pronoun or the pronoun object of the emphatic particle. Their referent is one and the same, but the number was varied between singular and plural out of regard for the word "man" once and for its meaning another time, which is the plural of those who turn away. So He said "man a'rada" (whoever turns away), then He said "khalidin" (abiding). The clause ﴿and evil is their burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾ is a second circumstantial clause, that is: and being miserable thereby. "Saa'" here is one of the verbs of blame, like "bi'sa," and the subject of "saa'" is a hidden, undefined pronoun which is explained by the specification (tamyiz) that follows it, which is "himlan" (a burden).

Al-himl (with a kasra on the ha') is a noun meaning the thing carried, like al-dhibh meaning the thing slaughtered. The object of the blame is omitted, the indication being the word "wizran" over it. The estimate: and evil is their burden as a burden, their sin. Omitting the object of praise and blame verbs is common, as in His saying: ﴿And We gave to Dawud, Sulayman; an excellent servant; indeed he was ever turning back (to Allah)﴾ [Sad: 30], that is, Sulayman is the one who turns back. The "lam" in His saying "wa saa'a lahum" is the lam of specification (lam al-tabyin), and it specifies the object in meaning, because the original sentence is: the burden was evil to them, so the lam was brought to add specificity to the connection of blame with their burden. So the lam is for clarifying those with whom the evil of the burden is connected.

Al-himl (with a kasra on the ha') is the thing carried, like al-dhibh.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 102–104:**

﴿On the Day the Trumpet is blown, and We gather the criminals that Day, blue-eyed.﴾ ﴿They will whisper among themselves, "You stayed only ten."﴾ ﴿We know best what they say, when the most exemplary of them in conduct says, "You stayed only a day."﴾

﴿يَوْمَ يُنْفَخُ في الصُّورِ﴾ is a substitute (badal, a grammatical term meaning apposition or replacement) for "the Day of Resurrection" in His words ﴿and it will be a heavy burden for them on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Ṭāhā: 101]. It is a parenthetical insertion (i'tiraḍ) between the clause ﴿And We have given you a Reminder from Us﴾ [Ṭāhā: 99] and what follows it, and between the clause ﴿And thus We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ [Ṭāhā: 113]. It serves as a transition (takhallus, a shift to a new topic) to mention the Resurrection, to remind of it, and to warn of what will befall the criminals on that Day.

The ṣūr is a great horn with a partial obstruction inside it. When the blower blows into it with force, a powerful sound comes out of it. It has been used to announce gatherings for war. This was discussed earlier at His words ﴿His is the word of truth, and His is the dominion on the Day the trumpet is blown﴾ [al-An'ām: 73] in Surah al-An'ām.

Most reciters read ﴿يُنْفَخُ﴾ with the third-person masculine prefix (yā' of absence) in the passive voice, meaning it is blown by a blower, who is the angel assigned to this task. Abū 'Amr alone read ﴿نَنْفُخُ﴾ with the first-person plural nūn of majesty and a ḍamma on the fā'. Attributing the blowing to God is a figurative attribution (majāz 'aqlī, attributing an act to one who commands it rather than the actual doer), like the saying "the governor built the fortress."

The criminals (al-mujrimūn) are the polytheists and the disbelievers.

Zuruq is the plural of azraq, which is one whose colour is blue. Blueness (al-zarqah) is a colour like the colour of the sky after sunset. On a person's skin it is an ugly appearance, because it resembles the colour of a place touched by the burn of fire. The apparent meaning of the expression is that the blueness is the colour of their bodies, which would be like His words ﴿On the Day when some faces turn white and some faces turn black﴾ [Āl 'Imrān: 106]. It has also been said that the intended meaning is the colour of their eyes, because blue eyes are disliked among the Arabs. On this view, the more apparent meaning is that the intention is the intensity of the blueness of the eye, since it is an unusual colour. This is like the words of Bashshār:

*For the miser over his wealth are excuses, blue of eye, upon them are faces black.*

It has also been said that the intended meaning of "blue" is the blind, because blindness gives the eye a bluish colour. This is also possible in Bashshār's verse.

Al-takhāfut is speech spoken in a low voice out of fear or similar causes. Their whispering is due to the terror that fills their hearts on that Day, like His words ﴿And the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful, so you will hear nothing but a whisper﴾ [Ṭāhā: 108].

[Page 305]

The clause ﴿You stayed only ten﴾ explains the clause ﴿they will whisper﴾. They already know that they were dead and turned to dust, and then God revived them, so they become certain of their error, since they used to deny the Resurrection. Perhaps they intended to make an excuse for their mistake in denying revival after the parts of the body had dispersed, exaggerating in their obstinacy. So they claimed that they had remained in the graves only ten nights, and so they had not become dust. This was because what remained in their souls of the impossibility of revival after the joints had scattered. They claimed that their revival was only by the return of the souls to the bodies. Thus, by "staying" (al-labth) is meant remaining in the graves, as in His words, ﴿He said, "How long did you remain on earth, counting years?"﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 112] ﴿They said, "We remained a day or part of a day"﴾ [al-Mu'minūn: 113] in Surah al-Mu'minūn, and His words, ﴿And on the Day the Hour is established, the criminals will swear that they stayed only an hour. Thus they were deluded﴾ [al-Rūm: 55] in Surah al-Rūm.

"Idhā" (when) is an adverb of time, meaning they whisper at a time when the most exemplary of them in conduct says it. Al-amthal means the most superior and excellent. Al-mathāla means excellence, so the phrase refers to the one possessing the best path (al-ṭarīqah al-muthlā). This is because the attribution, in reality, is an explanatory specification (tamyīz, a grammatical term for specifying what is vague).

Al-ṭarīqah means condition, custom, or opinion. Here the intended meaning is opinion, as was mentioned in His words ﴿and they will take away your best way of life﴾ [Ṭāhā: 63] in this same surah. The commentators did not offer, regarding the description of the speaker ﴿You stayed only a day﴾ as "the most exemplary in path," any explanation that satisfies the soul. What I see is that it admits both literal and figurative meaning. If we take it in the literal sense, the meaning is that he was the closest of them to fabricating an excuse for their error in denying the resurrection. They supposed that the resurrection would occur after a long stay in the earth, long enough for the parts of the bodies to disintegrate. When they found their bodies intact, just as they were in the world, some of them said, ﴿You stayed only ten﴾. That statement was an excuse, because during ten nights bodies do change. The one who said ﴿You stayed only a day﴾ was closer to the acceptance of the excuse. So the intended meaning is that he was the most exemplary among them in making excuses, and not that he was correct.

If we take it in the figurative sense, then it is mockery of the speaker for his poor estimate of their stay in the graves. Since both estimates were deeply in error, indicating the ignorance of those who estimated and their confusion about the matter, and indicating ignorance of the great power of God, who determined long periods of time and great nations and who restored them after past centuries, the one who estimated the duration of the stay in the graves as the shortest was the one who went furthest into error. So he was described as "most exemplary in path," in mockery of him and of them together, since all were equal in error.

The clause ﴿We know best what they say﴾ is an intervening parenthesis between the verb ﴿they will whisper﴾ and the temporal clause ﴿when the most exemplary of them says﴾. That is, they say this secretly, and We know it. We report their words on that Day with the report of the All-Knowing, the Truthful.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 105–107:

﴿They ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast.﴾ ﴿And He will leave it a level plain,﴾ ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness.﴾

When the discussion of the Resurrection was mentioned, and what would be revealed to those who denied it of their error regarding their doubt, namely the impossibility of restoring bodies after their parts have been scattered, there was also mentioned one of their doubts, which they used to put to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a question of obstinacy, not a question of seeking guidance. They would deny that this world could come to an end and say: "Where then will these mountains be that we see?" It is narrated that a man from Thaqif asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and the Thaqif were people of mountains, since their homeland was al-Ta'if, and in it is the mountain of Kara. Whether their question was mockery or a request for guidance, Allah informed them of the fate of the mountains, refuting their doubt and teaching the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: Here, that is His saying, "﴿Fa-qul yansifuha﴾" (so say, "He will blow them away"), came with a fa' (fa), whereas every question in the Qur'an is answered with "qul" (say) without a fa', except this one. This is because the meaning is: "If they ask you about the mountains, then say," so the statement contained the meaning of a condition, and He knew that they would ask him about them, so He answered them before the question. These are questions that had preceded, which they had asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and the answer came right after the question.

"Yansifuha nasfa" (He will blow them away with a blast) is emphasized to establish that it is a literal reality and not a metaphor. The sense of the statement is: "And We will gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed..." to its end, and "We will blow away the mountains with a blast, so say that to those who ask you about the mountains."

Al-Nasf: scattering and dispersing, and it has been discussed earlier.

Al-Qa': the easy, flat land.

Al-Safsaf: the level land that has no protrusions.

The meaning of "yadharuha qa'an safsafan" is that they will be crushed in their places and leveled with the earth until they become at the level of its surface, and this happens through an earthquake or the like. Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking, and the mountains are crumbled to powder, becoming dust scattered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:4–6]. The clause ﴿la tara fiha 'iwajan wa la amtan﴾ is a circumstantial clause emphasizing the meaning of "qa'an safsafan," to increase the depiction of the state and thereby intensify its awfulness. The address in ﴿la tara fiha 'iwajan﴾ is to an unspecified person; the Messenger (ﷺ) addresses it to those who asked him.

Al-'Iwaj, with a kasra on the 'ayn and a fatha on the waw: the opposite of straightness. It is also said with a fatha on the 'ayn and the waw likewise, and the two are synonymous according to the correct view among the linguists. This is what 'Amr affirmed and what al-Marzuqi chose in his "Sharh al-Fasih." A group said: the kasra-'ayn form applies to bodies that are not upright, like the earth, and to abstract things like religion. The fatha-'ayn form is used for upright things like a wall or a staff, and this is the apparent meaning of what is in "Lisan al-'Arab" from al-Azhari. Another group said: the kasra-'ayn form is used for meanings, and the fatha-'ayn form for physical entities. This is the weakest view, and it is reported from Ibn Durayd in "al-Jamharah"; al-Zamakhshari followed him in the "Kashshaf" here, and it seems he inclined to the distinction it contains in usage, which is among the subtleties that the researchers incline toward. The author of "al-Qamus" did not turn to it, and the author of the "Kashshaf" strained in interpreting the verse according to this view, against its apparent meaning. It also requires that its use be invalid in every context. This word was discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Kahf, so refer to it there.

Al-Amt: a slight protrusion, i.e., you will not see in it any depression or any protrusion at all.

The meaning: you will not see in the place of its scattering any crookedness or any unevenness.

Allah the Exalted said: ﴿When the earth is shaken with a violent shaking, and the mountains are crumbled to powder, becoming dust scattered﴾ [al-Waqi'ah 56:4–6]. The clause ﴿la tara fiha 'iwajan wa la amtan﴾ is a circumstantial clause emphasizing the meaning of "qa'an safsafan," to increase the depiction of the state and thereby intensify its awfulness. The address in ﴿la tara fiha 'iwajan﴾ is to an unspecified person; the Messenger (ﷺ) addresses it to those who asked him.

It is also said with a fatha on the 'ayn and the waw likewise, and the two are synonymous according to the correct view among the linguists. This is what 'Amr affirmed and what al-Marzuqi chose in his "Sharh al-Fasih." A group said: the kasra-'ayn form applies to bodies that are not upright, like the earth, and to abstract things like religion. Another group said: the kasra-'ayn form is used for meanings, and the fatha-'ayn form for physical entities. This is the weakest view, and it is reported from Ibn Durayd in "al-Jamharah"; al-Zamakhshari followed him in the "Kashshaf" here, and it seems he inclined to the distinction it contains in usage, which is among the subtleties that the researchers incline toward. It also requires that its use be invalid in every context. This word was discussed at the beginning of Surah al-Kahf, so refer to it there.

Al-Amt: a slight protrusion, i.e., you will not see in it any depression or any protrusion at all.

The meaning: you will not see in the place of its scattering any crookedness or any unevenness.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 105–107:

﴿They ask you about the mountains. Say: My Lord will blow them away with a blast.﴾ ﴿And He will leave it a level plain,﴾ ﴿in which you will see no crookedness or unevenness.﴾

When the discussion of the Resurrection was mentioned, and what would be revealed to those who denied it of their error regarding their doubt, namely the impossibility of restoring bodies after their parts have been scattered, there was also mentioned one of their doubts, which they used to put to the Prophet (ﷺ) as a question of obstinacy, not a question of seeking guidance. They would deny that this world could come to an end and say: "Where then will these mountains be that we see?" It is narrated that a man from Thaqif asked the Prophet (ﷺ) about this, and the Thaqif were people of mountains, since their homeland was al-Ta'if, and in it is the mountain of Kara. Whether their question was mockery or a request for guidance, Allah informed them of the fate of the mountains, refuting their doubt and teaching the believers.

Al-Qurtubi said: Here, that is His saying, "﴿Fa-qul yansifuha﴾" (so say, "He will blow them away"), came with a fa' (fa), whereas every question in the Qur'an is answered with "qul" (say) without a fa', except this one. This is because the meaning is: "If they ask you about the mountains, then say," so the statement contained the meaning of a condition, and He knew that they would ask him about them, so He answered them before the question. These are questions that had preceded, which they had asked the Prophet (ﷺ), and the answer came right after the question.

"Yansifuha nasfa" (He will blow them away with a blast) is emphasized to establish that it is a literal reality and not a metaphor. The sense of the statement is: "And We will gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed..." to its end, and "We will blow away the mountains with a blast, so say that to those who ask you about the mountains."

Al-Nasf: scattering and dispersing, and it has been discussed earlier.

Al-Qa': the easy, flat land.

Al-Safsaf: the level land that has no protrusions.

The clause "﴿They will follow the summoner, from whom there is no deviation﴾" is in the sense of a consequence of the clause "﴿He will blow it away﴾" [Ta-Ha 105]. "Yawma'idhin" (on that day) is an adverbial of time governed by "yattabi'una al-da'iya" (they will follow the summoner). The adverb was placed before its governing verb for emphasis on that day, and so that its placement would stand in place of a conjunction in connecting the sentences. The meaning is: they will follow the summoner on the day when your Lord blows away the mountains, that is, when the mountains are blown away they will be called to the gathering, and they will come forth following the summoner to it.

As for "al-da'i" (the summoner), it has been said that it is the angel Israfil, peace be upon him, who calls with the call of compulsion and bringing into being, so the bodies and souls return to them and they hasten toward the place to which they are summoned. It has also been said that the summoner is the Messenger, meaning each people follows its Messenger.

"La 'iwaja lahu" (from whom there is no deviation) is a circumstantial clause (hal) from "al-da'i." The lam, on both opinions regarding what is meant by "al-da'i," indicates purpose: there is no deviation for the sake of the summoner, meaning those summoned do not swerve in their course for the sake of the summoner, but rather they go directly and intently toward his direction. According to the opinion of the one who understood the summoner to be the Messenger, "al-'iwaj" (deviation) may be understood as falsehood, as an allusion to the polytheists who attributed deviation to the Messenger ﷺ, like their saying: ﴿You follow none but a man bewitched﴾ [al-Isra' 47], and similar of their falsehoods, just as He alluded to them in His saying: ﴿He who has sent down the Book upon His servant and has not made in it any deviation﴾ [al-Kahf 1].

Thus the negated verbal noun is intended to negate the category of deviation in following the summoner, such that they do not take any path other than the straight way, or such that they are not led by any path other than the straight way, or such that they know the innocence of their Messenger from deviation. Between His saying ﴿You will not see therein any deviation﴾ [Ta-Ha 107] and His saying "la 'iwaja lahu" there is what is called "mura'at al-nazir" (correspondence of parallels). Just as God made the earth on that day free of crookedness and protrusion, as He said ﴿then they will be on the level surface﴾ [al-Nazi'at 14], so too He made the people's movement upon it without deviation or evasion.

"Al-khushu'" is humility, and in every part of a human being there is a manifestation of humility. The manifestation of humility in the voice is lowering it, so the statement "﴿and you will hear nothing but whispers﴾" is consequently derived from it. "Al-hams" is the faint sound.

[p. 310]

The address in "﴿You will not see therein any deviation﴾" [Ta-Ha 107] and "﴿so you will hear nothing but whispers﴾" is addressed to an unspecified person, meaning no observer will see and no listener will hear. The clause "﴿and the voices will be humbled﴾" is in the position of a circumstantial clause from the pronoun in "yattabi'una," and attributing humility to voices is a rational metaphor (majaz 'aqli), since humility belongs to the owners of the voices; or humility is used metaphorically for the lowering and hushing of the voice, and this humility arises from the terror of the situation. The clause "﴿On that day intercession will not benefit﴾" is, like the clause "﴿On that day they will follow the summoner﴾," in the sense of a consequence of "﴿and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful﴾." That is: people will not speak among themselves except in whispers, and they will not dare to intercede for anyone whose benefit concerns them. The purpose of this is that the majesty of God and the fear of Him will prevent anyone from mediating before Him to benefit anyone except by His permission. In this there is a discouragement to the polytheists from finding intercessors for themselves with God.

The exception "﴿except for one whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾" from the general scope of intercession is considered in light of the fact that intercession requires an intercessor, since the verbal noun in it carries the sense of a verb and so requires an agent. That is: except that one whom the Most Merciful has permitted to intercede should intercede. Thus it is a complete exception (istithna' tamm) and not an incomplete one (mufarragh).

The lam in "adhina lahu" (permitted for him) is the lam of transitivity of the verb "adhina," like His saying: ﴿Pharaoh said: Have you believed in Him before I gave you permission?﴾ [al-A'raf 123]. The explanation of this is what occurs in the hadith of intercession, the saying of the Prophet ﷺ: "Then it will be said to me: Ask, and you will be given; intercede, and your intercession will be accepted."

His saying "﴿and whose word He approves﴾" refers back to "﴿whom the Most Merciful has permitted﴾," who is the intercessor. The lam that enters upon that pronoun is the lam of causation, meaning the Most Merciful approves the intercessor's word for the sake of the intercessor, that is, as an honor to him, like His saying: ﴿Did We not expand for you your breast?﴾ [al-Sharh 1].

[p. 311]

For God does not permit the intercessor to intercede except when He intends to accept his intercession. Thus permission to intercede and its acceptance become a sign of the intercessor's honor before God the Exalted. The genitive phrase is connected to the verb "radiya" (approved). "Qawlan" is in the accusative as the object of the verb "radiya," since this "radiya" is transitive to the thing approved both directly and with the preposition bi.

The clause "﴿He knows what is before them and what is behind them﴾" is a resumptive explanatory clause (istinaf bayaniyya) answering a question that might arise, asking about what necessitates God's approval of the servant for whom permission to intercede is given. It is explained in a general way that the permission for this follows what God's knowledge of all His servants and their apparent deeds requires. He expressed apparent deeds by "what is before them," since the nature of what is before a person is to be visible, and He expressed hidden inner states by "what is behind them," since the nature of what is placed behind a person is to be concealed. This was already mentioned in the Verse of the Throne, so it is a metonymy (kinaya) for the apparent and the hidden things. That is: He permits whomever He wishes to honor from among His close servants to intercede for groups, as in the hadith: "There will come out of the Fire whoever had in his heart the weight of a grain of faith"; or to intercede in a particular situation, as in the hadith of the Great Intercession at the place of standing for all people, to hasten their reckoning. The clause "﴿and they cannot encompass Him in knowledge﴾" is a concluding clause (tadhyil) for the statement, [emphasizing] the greatness of God's knowledge and the insignificance of human knowledge, similar to what occurred in the Verse of the Throne.

The clause "﴿And faces will be humbled before the Living, the Self-Subsisting﴾" is conjoined to the clause "﴿and the voices will be humbled before the Most Merciful﴾," meaning humility appears in voices and submission in faces. "Al-'ana'" is abasement, and its root meaning is capture, and "al-'ani" is the captive. Since the captive is afflicted with abasement in his face, submission is attributed to the faces by way of rational metaphor, and the whole clause is an image (tamthil) of the state of the criminals about whom the discourse concerned, from His saying: ﴿And We will gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed﴾ [Ta-Ha 102]. So the lam in "al-wujuh" (the faces) is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning "their faces," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hellfire is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at 39], meaning for them. As for the faces of the people of obedience, they are faces on that day, smiling and joyful. It is permissible to take the definiteness in "al-wujuh" as generic. "'Anat" is used in the sense of "khada'at," meaning all people submitted in reverence to God the Exalted.

"Al-Hayy" is the one for whom the attribute of life is established, and it is a state that belongs to the most exalted of existing things, and it is a power of the existent by which the persistence of its essence and the occurrence of its perception are maintained forever or for some duration. True life is the life of God the Exalted, because it is essential, not preceded by its opposite nor ending.

"Al-Qayyum" is the one who manages the affairs of people, an intensive form of "al-qayyim," meaning the one from whom no management of any affair escapes. "Al-Hayy al-Qayyum" [al-Baqarah 255] was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause "﴿And he has failed who carried injustice﴾" is either a parenthetical clause at the end of the discourse that provides the reason, if the definiteness in "al-wujuh" was made a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning the faces of the criminals; the meaning being: since everyone who carried injustice has failed. Or it is a precautionary qualification (ihtiras) to clarify the difference in the outcome of the abasement of faces: whoever carried injustice has failed on that day and his abasement continues. And whoever did righteous deeds, that fear will return to him as security and joy. "Al-zulm" here is the injustice done to oneself. The clause "﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer…﴾" etc. is a conditional clause expressing the counterpart of the content of the clause "﴿And he has failed who carried injustice﴾." This counterpart is phrased in the form of a conditional to affirm the promise, and "fa-la yakhafu" (then he will not fear) is the response of the condition. Its being joined with "fa" is a sign that the clause is not suitable to follow the conditional particle, so it is necessarily either that the "la" in it is prohibitive, or that the statement is intended as a resumption. The implied sense is: then he does not fear.

[p. 312]

The majority read "fa-la yakhafu" in the nominative form, with an alif after the kha', considering the clause a resumption not intended as the response; as if the absence of his fear were a settled matter, because he is a believer and does righteous deeds. The meaning of "﴿then he will not fear injustice﴾" is that he will not fear the punishment of the wrongdoers, because he is secure from it through his faith and his righteous deeds.

In this case "al-hadm" means slight diminution, and its conjunction with "al-zulm" according to this interpretation is a precautionary addition (ihtiras).

"Al-'ana'" is abasement, and its root meaning is capture, and "al-'ani" is the captive. Since the captive is afflicted with abasement in his face, submission is attributed to the faces by way of rational metaphor, and the whole clause is an image (tamthil) of the state of the criminals about whom the discourse concerned, from His saying: ﴿And We will gather the criminals on that day blue-eyed﴾ [Ta-Ha 102]. So the lam in "al-wujuh" (the faces) is a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning "their faces," like His saying: ﴿Indeed, Hellfire is the refuge﴾ [al-Nazi'at 39], meaning for them. As for the faces of the people of obedience, they are faces on that day, smiling and joyful. It is permissible to take the definiteness in "al-wujuh" as generic. "'Anat" is used in the sense of "khada'at," meaning all people submitted in reverence to God the Exalted.

"Al-Hayy" is the one for whom the attribute of life is established, and it is a state that belongs to the most exalted of existing things, and it is a power of the existent by which the persistence of its essence and the occurrence of its perception are maintained forever or for some duration. True life is the life of God the Exalted, because it is essential, not preceded by its opposite nor ending.

"Al-Qayyum" is the one who manages the affairs of people, an intensive form of "al-qayyim," meaning the one from whom no management of any affair escapes. "Al-Hayy al-Qayyum" [al-Baqarah 255] was discussed in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause "﴿And he has failed who carried injustice﴾" is either a parenthetical clause at the end of the discourse that provides the reason, if the definiteness in "al-wujuh" was made a substitute for the genitive complement, meaning the faces of the criminals; the meaning being: since everyone who carried injustice has failed. Or it is a precautionary qualification (ihtiras) to clarify the difference in the outcome of the abasement of faces: whoever carried injustice has failed on that day and his abasement continues. And whoever did righteous deeds, that fear will return to him as security and joy. "Al-zulm" here is the injustice done to oneself. The clause "﴿And whoever does righteous deeds while he is a believer…﴾" etc. is a conditional clause expressing the counterpart of the content of the clause "﴿And he has failed who carried injustice﴾." This counterpart is phrased in the form of a conditional to affirm the promise, and "fa-la yakhafu" (then he will not fear) is the response of the condition. Its being joined with "fa" is a sign that the clause is not suitable to follow the conditional particle, so it is necessarily either that the "la" in it is prohibitive, or that the statement is intended as a resumption. The implied sense is: then he does not fear.

[p. 312]

The majority read "fa-la yakhafu" in the nominative form, with an alif after the kha', considering the clause a resumption not intended as the response; as if the absence of his fear were a settled matter, because he is a believer and does righteous deeds. Ibn Kathir read it in the jussive form, with the alif after the kha' dropped, considering the statement a prohibition used in the sense of negation. It was written in the Mushaf without an alif, so it allowed both readings. Al-Tibi noted that the majority agrees with His saying: ﴿And he has failed who carried injustice﴾ in that both clauses are declarative. Ibn Kathir's reading indicates there is no hesitation in the occurrence of his security from injustice and diminution. That is, in the majority's reading there is a verbal specificity, and in Ibn Kathir's reading there is a semantic specificity. The meaning of "﴿then he will not fear injustice﴾" is that he will not fear the punishment of the wrongdoers, because he is secure from it through his faith and his righteous deeds.

"Al-Hadm" is diminution, meaning they will not be reduced from their recompense that they were promised in anything, like His saying: ﴿And indeed We will give them their portion in full, undiminished﴾ [Hud 109]. It is permissible that "al-zulm" here means severe diminution, as in His saying: ﴿and had not wronged anything from it﴾ [al-Kahf 33], meaning he does not fear the nullification of his deed. In this case "al-hadm" means slight diminution, and its conjunction with "al-zulm" according to this interpretation is a precautionary addition (ihtiras).

[Page 314]

This is connected to the statement ﴿Thus We relate to you some of the news of what has already passed﴾ [Taha: 99]. The purpose is the same, which is to honour the Qur'an. It began by honouring the Qur'an in part, through its stories, and then honoured it as a whole, in a manner resembling a concluding statement (tadhyil), because of the general meaning contained in his words ﴿We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾. The demonstrative "Thus" (kadhalika) points in the same way as in his words ﴿Thus We relate to you﴾ [Taha: 99], meaning: just as you have heard it, it cannot be explained more clearly than that. "Qur'anan" is a circumstantial accusative (hal) from the pronoun in "anzalnahu," and "Qur'an" is a verbal noun used as a name (tasmiyah bil-masdar). What is meant is the recited, that which is read. "Qur'an" became a proper name by dominance (ghalabah) for the revelation sent down to Muhammad (ﷺ) in specific words, which he is obliged to recite in worship and which cannot be matched by producing even a single chapter like it. It was named "Qur'an" because it was arranged in a style that makes its recitation easy. Here the derivational meaning (al-ma'na al-ishtiqaqi) is considered before the dominance of the name, namely what the root (q-r-') conveys of ease of recitation. This is due only to the eloquence of its composition and the harmony of its letters. The indefiniteness (tankir) of "Qur'an" conveys perfection, meaning the most perfect of what is read.

"Arabiyyan" is an adjective of "Qur'anan." This description conveys praise, because the Arabic language is the most eloquent of languages and the finest in fluency and coherence. It also contains an indirect expression of favour toward the Arabs, and a ridicule of the polytheists among them, since they turned away from it and denied it. God the Exalted says: ﴿Indeed We have sent down to you a Book in which is your reminder. Then will you not reason?﴾ [al-Anbiya: 10].

Tasrif (variation, diversification) means arranging things in varied ways and refining them. It has already been discussed under His words ﴿See how We vary the verses, yet they turn away﴾ [al-An'am: 46] in Surat al-An'am, and His words ﴿And We have certainly diversified in this Qur'an so that they may remember﴾ [al-Isra': 41] in Surat al-Isra'. Mentioning the warning (wa'id) here serves as a threat, and it is because of its connection to His words before it: ﴿And he has failed who carries injustice﴾ [Taha: 111]. Taqwa is fear, and it is used as a metonym (kinayah) for obedience to God, meaning: We did this in hope that they would believe and obey. "Dhikr" here means remembrance (tadhakkur), meaning: We did this in hope that they would believe and obey. "Dhikr" here means remembrance (tadhakkur), that is, the Qur'an produces in them remembrance and reflection on what they ought to choose for themselves.

He expressed it with "yuhdithu" (produces) to signal that remembrance was not among their affairs before the Qur'an was sent down. Therefore the Qur'an brought into existence in them a remembrance that had not been there before. Dhu al-Rummah said:

"When she ran with ease in the rope-like path, as if she were the brightness of dawn, we produced thanks to her Creator."

"La'alla" expresses hope. That is, the state of the Qur'an is that it brings people close to taqwa and remembrance, in such a way that the condition of the One who sent it down and commanded what is in it is depicted as the condition of one who hopes, so he utters the particle set for expressing hope. Thus the particle "la'alla" is a subordinate metaphor (isti'arah tab'iyyah), which indicates a figurative metaphor (tamthiliyyah makniyyah). The meaning of "la'alla" in the Qur'an has already been discussed under His words ﴿O mankind, worship your Lord, who created you and those before you, that you may become righteous﴾ [al-Baqarah: 21] in Surat al-Baqarah.

The clause ﴿So exalted is God, the King, the Truth﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) between the clause "And thus We sent it down" and the clause ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾. This is a declaration of praise for God, who sent down the Qur'an, and for the favour of this Qur'an, and it is an instruction to thank Him for what He has made clear to His servants of the means of reform, and for guiding them to it through encouragement and warning, and for addressing them with the most eloquent speech and the finest style. It is therefore a consequence (mufarra') of what came before, from His words ﴿And thus We sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an﴾ to the end. The consequence indicates that this sending down, this diversification, and these means of reform all arise from beautiful effects, all of which show His exaltedness and greatness, and that He is the true King who governs the affairs of His creatures in the most perfect manner and by the most effective ways of governance.

In describing Him as "the Truth" there is a hint that the kingship of others who are named kings is never free from deficiency, as God the Exalted says: ﴿The sovereignty that Day is truly for the Most Merciful﴾ [al-Furqan: 26]. In a hadith: "God says, 'I am the King; where are the kings of the earth?'" That is, bring them forward: do you find any of them who disputes this? It is like the words of the caliph Mu'awiyah when he addressed the people of Medina: "O people of Medina, where are your scholars?"

[Page 316]

Combining the Name of Majesty (Allah, the proper name of God) with His name "al-Malik" (the King) indicates that His greatness and majesty are deserved by His essence, through the name that comprises all attributes of perfection, and it is the name that denotes the exclusivity and perfection of divinity. Then "al-Haqq" (the Truth) follows it, to indicate that His actions clearly show that His kingship is a true kingship, in which there is no disposal except what the requirement of wisdom demands.

"Al-Haqq": the One in whose kingship there is no trace of incapacity or submission to anyone else. Within this there is an indirect expression that the kingship of others is false.

Also, in making this a consequence of the sending down of the Qur'an there is an indication that the Qur'an is the law (qanun) of that King, and that what he brought is the complete governance that guarantees the welfare of the affairs of those who follow it in this world and the Hereafter. The clause ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ follows from what was mentioned before of the honouring of the Qur'an and what it includes of the various means of reforming people. Since the Prophet (ﷺ) was eager for the goodness of the community and intensely concerned for its salvation, there arose in his noble heart, right after hearing those verses, a desire or request for more of the Qur'an to be sent down and for it to come quickly, in order to admonish people and reform them sooner. So God taught him to leave the matter to Him, for He knows best what suits the general condition of the community. The meaning of ﴿before its revelation is completed to you﴾ is: before the revelation of what has been decreed to be revealed to you is completed, that is, before its sending down is carried out, for that is what is suitable. What is forbidden is asking for haste, or a strong desire in the soul that resembles impatience, not the mere love of increase. The Prophet (ﷺ) said concerning the story of Musa with al-Khidr (peace be upon him): "We wished that Musa had been patient until God related to us their story." 

[Page 317]

It is possible that the meaning of "haste with the Qur'an" is haste in reciting it at the moment Jibril delivers its verses. From Ibn 'Abbas: The Prophet would hurry ahead of Jibril and recite before Jibril had finished, out of eagerness to memorize and fear of forgetting. So God sent down ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an﴾, the verse. This is what Ibn 'Abbas said concerning His words ﴿Do not move your tongue with it to hasten it﴾ [al-Qiyamah: 16], as in Sahih al-Bukhari. On these two interpretations, "the completion of its revelation" means its completion and its end, that is, the end of the portion that was about to be sent down.

From Mujahid and Qatadah: its meaning is: do not hasten in reciting what has been sent down to you to your companions, and do not dictate it to them until its meanings become clear to you. On this interpretation, "the completion of the revelation" means the completion of its meanings. On both explanations, the placement of His words ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ is to be considered.

The majority recited "yuqda" with a ya' at its beginning in the passive voice, and "wahyuhu" in the nominative as its deputy subject (na'ib al-fa'il). Ya'qub recited it with the first-person plural of majesty (nun al-'azamah), with a kasrah on the dad, a fathah on the last letter of "naqdi," and "wahyahu" in the accusative. The conjunction of the clause ﴿And say: My Lord, increase me in knowledge﴾ indicates that what is forbidden is a specific haste, and that the motive for haste is praiseworthy. In this there is gentleness toward the Prophet (ﷺ), since after forbidding him to hasten, which he desired, it grants him permission to ask for an increase of knowledge. That is the summation of every increase, whether it comes by the sending down of the Qur'an or by other revelation and inspiration, or by ijtihad in legislation and understanding. It indicates that his desire to hasten was a good desire, like the words of the Prophet (ﷺ) to Abu Bakr when he entered the mosque and found the Prophet bowing. He did not wait to reach the row, but bowed and crept toward the row while bowing. The Prophet said to him: "May God increase your eagerness, but do not repeat it."

[Page 318]

﴿And We had already made a covenant with Adam before, but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve.﴾

Since the story of Musa (peace be upon him) with Pharaoh and his people contains a lesson for those who deny and obstinately oppose, those who denied and opposed the Prophet (ﷺ), and that was the purpose of relating it, as we pointed out a little earlier at His words: ﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has passed. And We have given you from Us a reminder. Whoever turns away from it will bear a burden on the Day of Resurrection﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99], it seems that the Prophet (ﷺ) desired more of these stories containing lessons, hoping that his people would awaken from their misguidance, as we pointed out shortly before at His words: ﴿And do not hasten with the Qur'an before its revelation is completed to you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. This story was followed by the story of Adam (peace be upon him) and what Satan made to appear to him, in order to fulfil the benefit of His words: ﴿And say, "My Lord, increase me in knowledge"﴾ [Ta-Ha: 114]. So the sentence is a conjunction (ʿaṭf) of one story upon another, and the connection is as you have heard.

The statement is conjoined to the sentence ﴿Thus do We relate to you the news of what has passed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 99]. The opening of the sentence with the particle of affirmation (ḥarf al-taḥqīq) and the oath particle (lām al-qasam) is merely to draw attention to the story, alerting to the intention of drawing a parallel between the two stories in respect of neglecting the covenant. In the first story there is the neglect of the Children of Israel regarding God's covenant, as He said in it: ﴿Did your Lord not promise you a good promise? Did the time seem long to you, or did you desire that wrath from your Lord should descend upon you?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86]. In the story of Adam there is also neglect of the covenant. And in the fact that this was from the work of Satan, as He said in the first story: ﴿Thus did my soul prompt me﴾ [Ta-Ha: 96], and He said in this one: ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾ [Ta-Ha: 120]. And in that both stories involve forgetting what must be preserved and remembered, He said in the first story: "so he forgot," and in this story: ﴿but he forgot, and We found in him no resolve﴾.

[Page 319]

Accordingly, His words "from before" (min qablu) have the phrase that is added to "qablu" omitted, and its estimated form is: "from before the sending of Musa," or "from before what has been mentioned." The construction of "qablu" on a dammah is a sign of the omission of the noun to which it is attached while its meaning is intended. What has been mentioned is either the covenant of Musa, which is in His words: ﴿And I have chosen you, so listen to what is revealed﴾ [Ta-Ha: 13], and His words: ﴿So do not let one who does not believe in it and follows his desire turn you away from it, lest you perish﴾ [Ta-Ha: 16]; or it is the covenant of God with the Children of Israel, which Musa (peace be upon him) reminded them of when he returned to them angry and grieved, and that is what is in His words: ﴿Did the time seem long to you?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 86], and what follows.

By "the covenant made to Adam" is meant the covenant made with him in the Garden, in which he was caused to forget.

Forgetting (nisyān) is here applied to neglecting to act upon the covenant deliberately, as in His words in the story of the Samiri: "so he forgot" [Ta-Ha: 88]. It is therefore disobedience (iṣyān), which is what His words require: ﴿And he said, "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the immortal."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 20] ﴿And he swore to them, "Indeed, I am to you among the sincere advisers."﴾ [Al-A'raf: 21], and what follows. This has already passed in Surat al-A'raf. This covenant is the one clarified in the verse by His words: ﴿Then We said, "O Adam, indeed this is an enemy to you and to your wife."﴾ [Ta-Ha: 117], and what follows.

Resolve (ʿazm) is the firm determination to act and the absence of hesitation regarding it. It is a struggle against what the impulse calls for of refraining from it, either because its performance is difficult or because one prefers its opposite. His words ﴿And if they resolve upon divorce﴾ [Al-Baqarah: 227] have already passed in Surat al-Baqarah. What is meant here is resolve to comply with the command and to dismiss what makes non-compliance appealing. He, exalted, said: ﴿And when you have resolved, then rely upon God﴾ [Al-Imran: 159], and He said: ﴿So be patient as the messengers of resolve were patient﴾ [Al-Ahqaf: 35]. They are Nuh, Ibrahim, Isma'il, Ya'qub, Yusuf, Ayyub, Musa, Dawud, and ʿIsa, peace be upon them. The negation of finding resolve in Adam is used to mean the non-existence of resolve as one of his attributes regarding what he was charged with; it is a figurative representation (tamthil) of the state of seeking its presence in him, by the state of one who searches for someone's resolve and does not find it with him after searching.

[p. 320]

﴿And when We said to the angels, "Prostrate to Adam," they prostrated, except Iblis; he refused.﴾

This is an explanation of the sentence ﴿And We had already taken a covenant from Adam before﴾ [Ta-Ha: 115] through to its end. The apparent requirement (muqtadā al-ẓāhir) was that this sentence should not be joined by the conjunction "wa" (and), but rather stand separately (fasl). Its being joined by "wa" is therefore an emphasis on it, so that it becomes an independent story (qiṣṣa mustaqilla) and draws the attention of the listeners' minds to it. The "wa" thus joins the story of Adam to the story of Musa, coordinating it with His saying: ﴿Has there reached you the report of Musa, when he saw a fire﴾ [Ta-Ha: 9]. ﴿So let him not drive you both out of the Garden, so that you become wretched. Indeed, it is for you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked. And indeed, you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun.﴾

The consequence of wretchedness was attributed to Adam alone, rather than to his wife, for brevity, because in the wretchedness of one of the spouses is the wretchedness of the other, given their mutual involvement in existence, with an allusion to the fact that the male's wretchedness is the origin of the woman's wretchedness, along with what this contains of observing the rhyme (fasila).

The clause ﴿Indeed, it is for you that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾ is a justification for the wretchedness resulting from the forbidden expulsion from the Garden. Since he was enjoying in the Garden the comfort of living, with food, clothing, drink, and a moderate climate suited to his temperament, expulsion from it would necessarily entail the loss of all that.

"Tadha" is the present tense of "dha" (ḍaḥiya), like "radiya," when the heat of the sun strikes a person at the time of forenoon (al-duha). Its verbal noun is al-ḍaḥw, and the heat of the sun at that time is the beginning of its intensity. The meaning: nothing will afflict you that is contrary to your temperament. So the restriction to the negation of al-ḍaḥw here is a sufficiency, i.e., "nor will you be scorched." Adam did not know hunger, nakedness, thirst, or ḍaḥw through direct experience, but he knew them by their realities within God's teaching him all the names, as was mentioned in Surat al-Baqarah. And in this report were gathered the basic essentials of human sustenance in livelihood, as an allusion to the fact that self-sufficiency from them will be the goal of a human's striving in his future life; for the states that accompany creation are indications of the characteristics of the Creator in His constituent qualities, as occurred in the hadith of the Night Journey regarding the Prophet's ﷺ success in choosing milk over wine, when it was said to him: "If you had chosen wine, your community would have gone astray." He combined the negation of hunger and clothing in His saying ﴿that you will not hunger therein, nor be naked﴾, and combined the negation of thirst and bodily pain in His saying ﴿you will not thirst therein, nor be exposed to the sun﴾, because of the affinity between hunger and nakedness: hunger is the emptiness of the inner body of what protects it from suffering, which is food; and nakedness is the emptiness of the outer body of what protects it from suffering, which is the sting of heat and the pinch of cold. The affinity between thirst and the heat of the sun is that the former is the pain of inner heat, and the latter is the pain of outer heat. This required that thirst not be paired with hunger, and that nakedness not be paired with the pain of heat, although the apparent requirement would be to join each pair of counterparts in both cases, since joining counterparts is among the stylistic methods of rhetorical embellishment in speech according to its outward form, were it not that something arose here that necessitated separating the counterparts.

Among this kind of separation of counterparts is a delightful literary anecdote that took place between Sayf al-Dawla and Abu al-Tayyib al-Mutanabbi. al-Ma'arri mentioned it in summary in his "Mu'jiz Ahmad," his commentary on the Diwan of Abu al-Tayyib, and al-Wahidi elaborated it in his commentary on the Diwan. It is that when Abu al-Tayyib recited to Sayf al-Dawla his qasida whose opening line is:

"According to the worth of people of resolve come resolutions"

he said, in the midst of it, describing an encounter between Sayf al-Dawla and the Byzantines at the frontier of al-Hadath:

"You stood firm, and there was no doubt in death for one who stands firm, while your face was radiant and your smile was beaming.
Heroes pass by you wounded in defeat, as if you were in the eyelid of destruction while it sleeps."

Sayf al-Dawla then took the poem back from him. After that, when he recited these two verses to him, Sayf al-Dawla said to him: "The first halves of the two verses do not fit their second halves, and you should have said:

"You stood firm, and there was no doubt in death for one who stands firm, while your face was radiant and your smile was beaming.
Heroes pass by you wounded in defeat, as if you were in the eyelid of destruction while it sleeps."

You, in this, are like Imru' al-Qays in his saying:

"As if I had never ridden a horse for pleasure, nor embraced a maiden with anklets,
nor poured out the wine-skin of the aged wine, nor said to my horses: 'Charge again after the stampede.'"

The proper arrangement of the speech, according to what the scholars of poetry have said, is that the second half of the first verse should belong to the second, and the second half of the second verse to the first, so that the speech is sound: riding horses would then accompany the command to the horses to charge, and pouring out wine would accompany the pleasure, along with embracing the maiden. Abu al-Tayyib said: "May God perpetuate the might of the Amir. If it is correct that the one who corrected Imru' al-Qays is more knowledgeable than him in poetry, then Imru' al-Qays erred and I erred. My master knows that the cloth is not known to the cloth-merchant in the same way as to the weaver, because the cloth-merchant knows only its whole, while the weaver knows its whole and its details, for he has taken it out from the amatory genre into the genre of the cloth." Imru' al-Qays only joined the pleasure of women with the pleasure of riding for the hunt, and joined generosity in buying wine for guests with courage in confronting enemies. As for me, when I mentioned death, I followed it with mention of destruction (al-radaa) for its affinity with it; and since the face of the defeated man cannot be other than gloomy, and his eye other than weeping, I said:

". . . . . . . . . .
your face was radiant and your smile was beaming,
to bring together opposites in meaning."

The meaning of this is that Imru' al-Qays departed from the requirement of the outward form by joining two things of well-known affinity, and joined two things of subtle affinity; and that Abu al-Tayyib departed from the requirement of joining counterparts, separating them in order to follow a more inventive method, namely the method of antithesis (tibaq) through contrast (tadadd), which is more ancient in the craft of rhetorical embellishment (badi'). The favor upon Adam with these blessings was framed within the context of the negation of their opposites, so that his hearing would be struck with the names of the kinds of misery, as a warning against them, so that he would avoid whoever seeks to bring him to ruin through them.

Nafi' and Abu Bakr, from 'Asim, read ﴿wa-innaka la tazma'u﴾ with the hamza of "inna" pronounced with a kasra, as a coordination of one clause with another. The rest read ﴿wa-annaka﴾ with the hamza pronounced with a fatha, coordinating it with ﴿allā tajū'a﴾ as the coordination of a single word with a single word, meaning: for you is the negation of hunger and nakedness, and the negation of thirst and exposure to the sun. Emphasis of all of them is achieved under both readings through "inna" and its sister particle, and there is variety between the two styles.

His saying, ﴿Then Satan whispered to him﴾, has been mentioned similarly in al-A'raf. The fa' (then) indicates that the content of this clause follows the content of the preceding clause in sequence. The verb "waswasa" (whisper) is construed here with the preposition "ila" (to), and in Surat al-A'raf with the lam, as in ﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. This is based on how the object is attached to that verb in the speaker's intention, for it is an intransitive verb that cannot do without a transitive particle. Its construction here with "ila" is based on the whisper reaching Adam and arriving at him, while its construction with the lam in al-A'raf is based on the whisper being for the sake of both of them. The clause ﴿saying, "O Adam"﴾ explains the clause ﴿﴿Then Satan whispered to them both﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]﴾. This verse is an example of the clause that explains another in the science of ma'ani (the science of meanings in rhetoric). This speech was a thought that Satan cast into the soul of Adam through the means of whispering, which is covert speech, either with words that Satan uttered secretly to Adam so that the angels would not notice and warn Adam against the plot of Satan, in which case the application of "speech" to it is literal; or by a mere inclination that Satan intended, as he whispers to people in this world, in which case the application of "speech" to it is metaphorical based on resemblance.

And "hal adullука" (shall I direct you) is an interrogative used in the sense of offering, which is the most suitable of the figurative meanings of the interrogative, due to its closeness to its literal meaning.

The opening with the vocative is so that he may give attention to it.

The tree is the one from which God forbade him to eat, to the exclusion of all the trees of Paradise. The prohibition concerning it is not mentioned here, though it is mentioned in the story in Surat al-Baqara. This offer precedes the enticement to eat from it that is related in God's saying in Surat al-A'raf: ﴿He said, "Your Lord has forbidden you from this tree only lest you become angels or become of the eternal"﴾ [al-A'raf: 20]. Satan did not direct him to the tree of eternity; rather, he deceived him and directed him to another tree, as evidenced by the fact that Adam was not made eternal. So there arose in Adam the delusion that if he ate from the tree to which Satan directed him, he would be eternal in life.

Guidance (dalala) is directing to a desired thing that is not apparent to the one seeking it, and the directing to the tree is for the purpose of eating its fruit. He called it here "the tree of eternity" in general terms, to arouse desire to know its specifics, until he would attend to it; then he specified it for him right after, as indicated by God's saying: "So they both ate from it." This has made clear the firm establishment of the love of life in the natural disposition of human beings.

And "al-mulk" (kingdom) is freedom from the authority of another, and it gives Adam the illusion that he would become the owner of Paradise, disposing of it freely without being commanded by any commander.

The word "bala" (decay) is used figuratively for cessation, because when a garment decays, its wearing has ended.

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 121–122:

﴿So they both ate from it, and their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden. And Adam disobeyed his Lord, and so he went astray.﴾ ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of what precedes it, and there is an omitted clause that the context indicates. That is: Adam acted upon the whispering of Satan, so he ate from the tree, and Hawwa' (Eve) ate with him.

The restriction of Satan's enticement to Adam, while he intended that both Adam and Hawwa' eat, is because he knew that a woman's following of her husband is rooted in her natural disposition. The meaning of ﴿their private parts became apparent to them, and they began to cover themselves with leaves from the Garden﴾ has already been mentioned in Surat al-A'raf.

His saying ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾ is coordinated (ma'tuf) upon "So they both ate from it," meaning they both ate together. Adam deliberately opposed the prohibition of God the Exalted against eating from that tree. The attribution of disobedience to Adam alone, without his wife, indicates that Adam was an example (qudwah) for his wife, so when he ate from the tree, his wife followed him. In this regard God the Exalted said: ﴿O you who have believed, protect yourselves and your families from a Fire﴾ [al-Tahrim: 6].

Al-ghiwayah (error) is the opposite of rushd (right guidance); it is a corrupt action or a false belief. The attribution of disobedience to Adam is evidence that he was not a prophet (nabi') on that day, and that he was in a world other than the world of obligation (taklif), and error was likewise. So disobedience and error on that day meant departing from compliance in upbringing (tarbiyah), like the disobedience of some members of a family to the command of its elder; it was only grave because it was disobedience to the command of God.

There is no basis in this verse for permitting sin upon the prophets, nor for prohibiting it, because that world was not a world of obligation.

The clause ﴿Then his Lord chose him, accepted his repentance, and guided him﴾ is a parenthetical insertion (mu'taridah) between the clause "And Adam disobeyed his Lord" and the clause ﴿He said: Go down from it, all of you﴾ [Ta-Ha: 123], because the choosing and the acceptance of repentance occurred after Adam and his wife were punished with expulsion from the Garden, as in Surat al-Baqarah. This is what fits the consequence of expulsion from the Garden following upon the disobedience, rather than following upon the repentance. The benefit of this parenthetical insertion is to hasten the explanation of Adam's final state, which was one of righteousness.

Al-ijtiba' (choosing) is al-istifa' (selection). It was discussed at the words of God the Exalted: ﴿And We chose them and guided them to a straight path﴾ [al-An'am: 87] in al-An'am, and at His saying: ﴿He chose him and guided him to a straight path﴾ [al-Nahl: 121] in al-Nahl.

Al-hidayah (guidance) is directing toward benefit. When it is mentioned together with al-ijtiba' in the Qur'an, what is meant by it is prophethood, as in these three verses.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 20, verses 123–127:**

﴿He said: "Go down from it, all of you, some of you as enemies to others."﴾

This is an explanatory resumption (*isti'naf bayani*), because the report that Adam disobeyed and went astray prompts the listener to ask what the consequence of that was. The pronoun in "He said" refers back to "his Lord" in the words of God, ﴿And Adam disobeyed his Lord﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:121). The address is to Adam and Iblis. The command "Go down" (*ihbitaa*) is a command of creation (*amr takwin*), because the two of them are unable to descend to the earth except by a creative command from God, since their dwelling in the Garden was by His creative decree, may He be exalted.

"All of you" (*jami'an*) appears to be a noun denoting the totality of all the individuals to which "all" applies. It seems to be a singular noun that indicates plurality, like *fariq* (group). For this reason, it is used the same way for masculine and feminine, and for singular and plural. God the Exalted says: ﴿So scheme against me all together﴾ (Hud 11:55). It is in the accusative as a circumstantial qualifier (*hal*). Here it is a circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "Go down." The clause ﴿some of you as enemies to others﴾ is a second circumstantial qualifier of the pronoun in "Go down." Thus, the ones commanded to descend from the Garden are Adam and Iblis, while Hawwa' (Eve) follows her husband.

The address in "some of you" (*ba'dukum*) is to Adam and Iblis. It was addressed with the plural pronoun because what is intended is the enmity between their offspring, since they are the origin of two kinds: the kind of humans and the kind of devils.

* * *

[Page 329]

﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me, whoever follows My guidance will neither go astray nor be wretched. And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed he will have a constricted life, and We will gather him on the Day of Resurrection blind.﴾ ﴿He will say: "My Lord, why have You gathered me blind, when I was seeing?" He will say: "Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; likewise today you are forgotten." And thus We recompense those who transgress and do not believe in the signs of their Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.﴾

The clause ﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ is a consequence of the command to descend from the Garden to the world. It announces that they will encounter in this world a way of life different from the one they had in the Garden, because they were placed in a mixed world, where good is blended with evil and realities with illusions, after they had been in a world of pure realities and unmixed good. In this there is an announcement of a state that befell the human essence in its nature, which had been prepared for it from the origin of its composition.

The address in "comes to you" (*ya'tiyannakum*) is to Adam in his capacity as the origin of the human race, to inform him that a community will come forth from him. This address does not include Iblis, because he has been created upon evil and misguidance, since God had informed him of this when he refused to prostrate to Adam. Therefore God does not obligate him to follow guidance, because requiring guidance from one whom God has informed will remain in misguidance would be pointless, and the act of the Wise, may He be exalted, is free of such pointlessness. This is not like the command given to Abu Jahl and his like to accept Islam, because people like Abu Jahl are not certain to be unbelievers, and it is not reported in the Sunnah

[Page 330]

that the Prophet (ﷺ) invited Satan to Islam, nor the devils. As for the hadith related by al-Daraqutni: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but that a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him." They said: "And you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "And I too, but God helped me, so he submitted." This does not imply that he invited him to Islam; rather, God inspired his companion to command him to good. By "companion" is meant a devil who accompanies him, and by "guidance" is meant guidance towards good.

In this verse there is God's charge to Adam and his offspring to follow the messengers of God and the divine revelation. From this it is known that the seeking of guidance is innate in the human constitution, to the extent that many scholars of Islam said: the knowledge of the One God is present in the intellects or widespread across generations and eras, and for this reason the polytheists were not excused during the periods of interval (*fatrah*) in which no messengers came to the peoples. This is a great matter, which the scholars of theology (*'ilm al-kalam*) have explored thoroughly, and we have clarified it in the treatise *al-Nasab al-Nabawi*.

The first two clauses have already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah. As for His words, "﴿will neither go astray﴾," their meaning is that whoever follows the guidance that comes from God through His messengers will be safe from being touched by any misguidance. This is derived from the implication of the verb in the context of negation as general, like the generality of an indefinite noun in a negative context; that is, he will not be touched by misguidance in this world. This is unlike one who follows what contains guidance coming from other than God, for even if he gains guidance in some circumstances, he will not be safe from falling into error in other circumstances. This is the situation of followers of non-divine laws, that is, man-made laws. Their framers, though they exhaust their efforts seeking the truth, are not safe from falling into errors due to heedlessness, conflicting proofs, being swayed by established customs, or currying favor with leaders or peoples whom they see as beneficial to please. An example is Socrates, the master of the wise men of the Greeks, who used to employ the device of expressing enjoining good in Athens in the form of stories told through the tongues of animals. Yet he was not safe from submitting to flattering the masses: though he did not regard their gods as divine, before his death he ordered a rooster to be sacrificed to Utarid, the lord of wisdom. Their situation differs from the situation of the messengers, who receive revelation from the Knower of the Unseen, who neither errs nor forgets. God strengthened them and protected them from flattering the people of desires, and formed them with a special formation suited to what was already in His knowledge of His purpose for them, and He firmed their hearts to bear hardship, so that they do not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of God. Whoever looks at man-made laws with the eye of a wise person will find that they include considerations of illusions and customs.

The wretchedness negated in His words "﴿nor be wretched﴾" is the wretchedness of the Hereafter, because whoever is safe from misguidance in this world is safe from wretchedness in the Hereafter.

This is indicated by the contrast with its opposite in His words: "﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed he will have a constricted life﴾," since He ordered that the disruption of his condition in this world and the Hereafter follows from turning away from God's guidance. Here "life" (*ma'ishah*) means the duration of life, that is, the span of existence.

*Dank* (constricted): it is the verbal noun of *dhanuka* (from the pattern *karuma*), *dhanakatan* and *dhankan*. Because it is a verbal noun, its form does not change with the change of the thing it describes, so it is used here to describe *ma'ishah*, which is feminine. *Dank* means narrowness; one says "a *dank* place," meaning a narrow place. It is used metaphorically for hardship of affairs in life. 'Antarah said:

*If they pursue, I will charge; if they close in battle, I will press on; and if they descend into a constricted place, I will descend with them.*

That is, into a narrow place, meaning there is hardship for the one who descends into it. Here it means hardship of condition, from disturbance and confusion of mind. The meaning is that the focal points of his concern and the aims of his gaze are directed toward devising means and ways to obtain his aims. He is consumed with increase and fearful of decrease, not attentive to perfections, nor at peace with the virtues he strives for. God places him in that state while he is unaware. Some of them appear to people to be in a good condition and enjoying a comfortable life, but their souls are not at rest.

[Page 331–332]

God made His punishment on the Day of Gathering to be that he will be blind, as a representation of his sensory state on that day through his spiritual state in this world, which is the state of not looking into the means of guidance and salvation. That meaning is a sign of God's wrath against him and His removal of him from His mercy. Thus the first "blind" is figurative, and the second "blind" is literal. The clause "﴿He will say: 'My Lord, why have You gathered me blind?'﴾" is an independent resumption (*istinaf ibtida'i*), while the clause "﴿He will say: Thus Our signs came to you...﴾" falls within the course of dialogue, so it is separated and not conjoined.

In this verse is evidence that God made known to humankind from the day of its creation the warning against misguidance and polytheism, so this became settled in the natural disposition (*fitrah*). To the extent that many scholars of Islam said that associating partners with God is deserving of punishment for the peoples who live in the interval between the laws. A group of the People of the Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah, all together, said that knowledge of God is obligatory by reason. There is no doubt that the purpose of mentioning it in the Qur'an is to alert those addressed by the Qur'an to beware of turning away from the remembrance of God, and to warn them with a consequence like their state.

The reference in "﴿Thus Our signs came to you﴾" returns to the blindness implied in His words "﴿why have You gathered me blind﴾." That is: like that state about whose cause you asked, you had forgotten Our signs when they came to you, and you used to turn away from looking at the signs when you were called to them. Likewise, the state of your punishment was a fitting recompense for it.

It has become clear from the structure of the verse that it contains three *ihtibak*s (a rhetorical device in which something is omitted in one part and mentioned in another, and vice versa). The supplied sense of the first is: "We will gather him blind on the Day of Resurrection, and We will forget him," that is, We will remove him from Our mercy. The supplied sense of the second and third is: "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them and became blind to them; likewise today you are forgotten and gathered blind."

Forgetting in both places is used as a metaphor or metonymy for being deprived of the portions of mercy. The clause "﴿And thus We recompense those who transgress...﴾" etc. is a concluding appendix (*tadhyil*). It may be part of the report of what God says to the one who is gathered blind on the Day of Resurrection, intended as rebuke and punishment for him, so the *waw* is conjunctive, joining this clause to the one before it. It may also be a concluding appendix to the story and not part of the address to the one who is gathered blind, intended as admonition to the listeners so that they beware of coming to a similar end. In that case the *waw* is parenthetical, because a concluding appendix is a parenthetical remark at the end of speech. The parenthetical *waw* goes back to the conjunctive *waw*, except that it conjoins a whole statement to another whole statement, not to a part of the preceding statement. The meaning is: "And We recompense those who transgress with a similar recompense," that is, those who disbelieved and did not believe in the signs of their Lord.

Transgression (*israf*) is: erroneous belief, not believing in the signs, obstinately denying them and rejecting them. The referent of "thus" (*kadhalika*) is the content of His words "﴿then he will have a constricted life﴾," that is: "And likewise We recompense in this world those who transgressed and did not believe in the signs." He follows it with "﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾." This may be a concluding appendix to the story and not part of God's address to the one He gathered blind on the Day of Resurrection. Here the meaning of "the punishment of the Hereafter" is the counterpart of the punishment of this world, which is implied by "﴿then he will have a constricted life﴾" etc., and the *waw* is parenthetical. It may also be that the sentence is part of God's address to the one He gathers blind, in which case "the punishment of the Hereafter" means the punishment that the addressed one is undergoing, that is: more severe than the punishment of this world and more lasting, because it lasts longer.

The clause ﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ is a consequence of the command to descend from the Garden to the world. It announces that they will encounter in this world a way of life different from the one they had in the Garden, because they were placed in a mixed world, where good is blended with evil and realities with illusions, after they had been in a world of pure realities and unmixed good. In this there is an announcement of a state that befell the human essence in its nature, which had been prepared for it from the origin of its composition.

The address in "comes to you" (*ya'tiyannakum*) is to Adam in his capacity as the origin of the human race, to inform him that a community will come forth from him. This address does not include Iblis, because he has been created upon evil and misguidance, since God had informed him of this when he refused to prostrate to Adam. Therefore God does not obligate him to follow guidance, because requiring guidance from one whom God has informed will remain in misguidance would be pointless, and the act of the Wise, may He be exalted, is free of such pointlessness. This is not like the command given to Abu Jahl and his like to accept Islam, because people like Abu Jahl are not certain to be unbelievers, and it is not reported in the Sunnah

[Page 330]

that the Prophet (ﷺ) invited Satan to Islam, nor the devils. As for the hadith related by al-Daraqutni: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but that a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him." They said: "And you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "And I too, but God helped me, so he submitted." This does not imply that he invited him to Islam; rather, God inspired his companion to command him to good. By "companion" is meant a devil who accompanies him, and by "guidance" is meant guidance towards good.

In this verse there is God's charge to Adam and his offspring to follow the messengers of God and the divine revelation. From this it is known that the seeking of guidance is innate in the human constitution, to the extent that many scholars of Islam said: the knowledge of the One God is present in the intellects or widespread across generations and eras, and for this reason the polytheists were not excused during the periods of interval (*fatrah*) in which no messengers came to the peoples. This is a great matter, which the scholars of theology (*'ilm al-kalam*) have explored thoroughly, and we have clarified it in the treatise *al-Nasab al-Nabawi*.

The first two clauses have already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah. As for His words, "﴿will neither go astray﴾," their meaning is that whoever follows the guidance that comes from God through His messengers will be safe from being touched by any misguidance. This is derived from the implication of the verb in the context of negation as general, like the generality of an indefinite noun in a negative context; that is, he will not be touched by misguidance in this world. This is unlike one who follows what contains guidance coming from other than God, for even if he gains guidance in some circumstances, he will not be safe from falling into error in other circumstances. This is the situation of followers of non-divine laws, that is, man-made laws. Their framers, though they exhaust their efforts seeking the truth, are not safe from falling into errors due to heedlessness, conflicting proofs, being swayed by established customs, or currying favor with leaders or peoples whom they see as beneficial to please. An example is Socrates, the master of the wise men of the Greeks, who used to employ the device of expressing enjoining good in Athens in the form of stories told through the tongues of animals. Yet he was not safe from submitting to flattering the masses: though he did not regard their gods as divine, before his death he ordered a rooster to be sacrificed to Utarid, the lord of wisdom. Their situation differs from the situation of the messengers, who receive revelation from the Knower of the Unseen, who neither errs nor forgets. God strengthened them and protected them from flattering the people of desires, and formed them with a special formation suited to what was already in His knowledge of His purpose for them, and He firmed their hearts to bear hardship, so that they do not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of God. Whoever looks at man-made laws with the eye of a wise person will find that they include considerations of illusions and customs.

The wretchedness negated in His words "﴿nor be wretched﴾" is the wretchedness of the Hereafter, because whoever is safe from misguidance in this world is safe from wretchedness in the Hereafter.
