He will say: "Thus Our signs came to you, but you forgot them; likewise today you are forgotten." And thus We recompense those who transgress and do not believe in the signs of their Lord. And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting.﴾

The clause ﴿So if guidance comes to you from Me﴾ is a consequence of the command to descend from the Garden to the world. It announces that they will encounter in this world a way of life different from the one they had in the Garden, because they were placed in a mixed world, where good is blended with evil and realities with illusions, after they had been in a world of pure realities and unmixed good. In this there is an announcement of a state that befell the human essence in its nature, which had been prepared for it from the origin of its composition.

The address in "comes to you" (*ya'tiyannakum*) is to Adam in his capacity as the origin of the human race, to inform him that a community will come forth from him. This address does not include Iblis, because he has been created upon evil and misguidance, since God had informed him of this when he refused to prostrate to Adam. Therefore God does not obligate him to follow guidance, because requiring guidance from one whom God has informed will remain in misguidance would be pointless, and the act of the Wise, may He be exalted, is free of such pointlessness. This is not like the command given to Abu Jahl and his like to accept Islam, because people like Abu Jahl are not certain to be unbelievers, and it is not reported in the Sunnah

[Page 330]

that the Prophet (ﷺ) invited Satan to Islam, nor the devils. As for the hadith related by al-Daraqutni: that the Prophet (ﷺ) said: "There is none of you but that a companion from the jinn has been assigned to him." They said: "And you, O Messenger of God?" He said: "And I too, but God helped me, so he submitted." This does not imply that he invited him to Islam; rather, God inspired his companion to command him to good. By "companion" is meant a devil who accompanies him, and by "guidance" is meant guidance towards good.

In this verse there is God's charge to Adam and his offspring to follow the messengers of God and the divine revelation. From this it is known that the seeking of guidance is innate in the human constitution, to the extent that many scholars of Islam said: the knowledge of the One God is present in the intellects or widespread across generations and eras, and for this reason the polytheists were not excused during the periods of interval (*fatrah*) in which no messengers came to the peoples. This is a great matter, which the scholars of theology (*'ilm al-kalam*) have explored thoroughly, and we have clarified it in the treatise *al-Nasab al-Nabawi*.

The first two clauses have already been explained in Surat al-Baqarah. As for His words, "﴿will neither go astray﴾," their meaning is that whoever follows the guidance that comes from God through His messengers will be safe from being touched by any misguidance. This is derived from the implication of the verb in the context of negation as general, like the generality of an indefinite noun in a negative context; that is, he will not be touched by misguidance in this world. This is unlike one who follows what contains guidance coming from other than God, for even if he gains guidance in some circumstances, he will not be safe from falling into error in other circumstances. This is the situation of followers of non-divine laws, that is, man-made laws. Their framers, though they exhaust their efforts seeking the truth, are not safe from falling into errors due to heedlessness, conflicting proofs, being swayed by established customs, or currying favor with leaders or peoples whom they see as beneficial to please. An example is Socrates, the master of the wise men of the Greeks, who used to employ the device of expressing enjoining good in Athens in the form of stories told through the tongues of animals. Yet he was not safe from submitting to flattering the masses: though he did not regard their gods as divine, before his death he ordered a rooster to be sacrificed to Utarid, the lord of wisdom. Their situation differs from the situation of the messengers, who receive revelation from the Knower of the Unseen, who neither errs nor forgets. God strengthened them and protected them from flattering the people of desires, and formed them with a special formation suited to what was already in His knowledge of His purpose for them, and He firmed their hearts to bear hardship, so that they do not fear the blame of any blamer in the cause of God. Whoever looks at man-made laws with the eye of a wise person will find that they include considerations of illusions and customs.

The wretchedness negated in His words "﴿nor be wretched﴾" is the wretchedness of the Hereafter, because whoever is safe from misguidance in this world is safe from wretchedness in the Hereafter.

This is indicated by the contrast with its opposite in His words: "﴿And whoever turns away from My remembrance, indeed he will have a constricted life﴾," since He ordered that the disruption of his condition in this world and the Hereafter follows from turning away from God's guidance. Here "life" (*ma'ishah*) means the duration of life, that is, the span of existence.

*Dank* (constricted): it is the verbal noun of *dhanuka* (from the pattern *karuma*), *dhanakatan* and *dhankan*. Because it is a verbal noun, its form does not change with the change of the thing it describes, so it is used here to describe *ma'ishah*, which is feminine. *Dank* means narrowness; one says "a *dank* place," meaning a narrow place. It is used metaphorically for hardship of affairs in life. 'Antarah said:

*If they pursue, I will charge; if they close in battle, I will press on; and if they descend into a constricted place, I will descend with them.*

That is, into a narrow place, meaning there is hardship for the one who descends into it. Here it means hardship of condition, from disturbance and confusion of mind. The meaning is that the focal points of his concern and the aims of his gaze are directed toward devising means and ways to obtain his aims. He is consumed with increase and fearful of decrease, not attentive to perfections, nor at peace with the virtues he strives for. God places him in that state while he is unaware. Some of them appear to people to be in a good condition and enjoying a comfortable life, but their souls are not at rest.

[Page 331–332]

God made His punishment on the Day of Gathering to be that he will be blind, as a representation of his sensory state on that day through his spiritual state in this world, which is the state of not looking into the means of guidance and salvation. That meaning is a sign of God's wrath against him and His removal of him from His mercy. Thus the first "blind" is figurative, and the second "blind" is literal. The clause "﴿He will say: 'My Lord, why have You gathered me blind?'﴾" is an independent resumption (*istinaf ibtida'i*), while the clause "﴿He will say: Thus Our signs came to you...﴾" falls within the course of dialogue, so it is separated and not conjoined.

In this verse is evidence that God made known to humankind from the day of its creation the warning against misguidance and polytheism, so this became settled in the natural disposition (*fitrah*). To the extent that many scholars of Islam said that associating partners with God is deserving of punishment for the peoples who live in the interval between the laws. A group of the People of the Sunnah and the Mu'tazilah, all together, said that knowledge of God is obligatory by reason. There is no doubt that the purpose of mentioning it in the Qur'an is to alert those addressed by the Qur'an to beware of turning away from the remembrance of God, and to warn them with a consequence like their state.

The reference in "﴿Thus Our signs came to you﴾" returns to the blindness implied in His words "﴿why have You gathered me blind﴾." That is: like that state about whose cause you asked, you had forgotten Our signs when they came to you, and you used to turn away from looking at the signs when you were called to them. Likewise, the state of your punishment was a fitting recompense for it.

It has become clear from the structure of the verse that it contains three *ihtibak*s (a rhetorical device in which something is omitted in one part and mentioned in another, and vice versa). The supplied sense of the first is: "We will gather him blind on the Day of Resurrection, and We will forget him," that is, We will remove him from Our mercy. The supplied sense of the second and third is: "Thus Our signs came to you, and you forgot them and became blind to them; likewise today you are forgotten and gathered blind."

Forgetting in both places is used as a metaphor or metonymy for being deprived of the portions of mercy. The clause "﴿And thus We recompense those who transgress...﴾" etc. is a concluding appendix (*tadhyil*). It may be part of the report of what God says to the one who is gathered blind on the Day of Resurrection, intended as rebuke and punishment for him, so the *waw* is conjunctive, joining this clause to the one before it. It may also be a concluding appendix to the story and not part of the address to the one who is gathered blind, intended as admonition to the listeners so that they beware of coming to a similar end. In that case the *waw* is parenthetical, because a concluding appendix is a parenthetical remark at the end of speech. The parenthetical *waw* goes back to the conjunctive *waw*, except that it conjoins a whole statement to another whole statement, not to a part of the preceding statement. The meaning is: "And We recompense those who transgress with a similar recompense," that is, those who disbelieved and did not believe in the signs of their Lord.

Transgression (*israf*) is: erroneous belief, not believing in the signs, obstinately denying them and rejecting them. The referent of "thus" (*kadhalika*) is the content of His words "﴿then he will have a constricted life﴾," that is: "And likewise We recompense in this world those who transgressed and did not believe in the signs." He follows it with "﴿And the punishment of the Hereafter is more severe and more lasting﴾." This may be a concluding appendix to the story and not part of God's address to the one He gathered blind on the Day of Resurrection. Here the meaning of "the punishment of the Hereafter" is the counterpart of the punishment of this world, which is implied by "﴿then he will have a constricted life﴾" etc., and the *waw* is parenthetical. It may also be that the sentence is part of God's address to the one He gathers blind, in which case "the punishment of the Hereafter" means the punishment that the addressed one is undergoing, that is: more severe than the punishment of this world and more lasting, because it lasts longer.

[Page 334]

﴿Has it not become clear to them how many generations We destroyed before them, through whose dwellings they walk? Indeed, in that are signs for people of understanding.﴾

This is a consequence (tafri') of the warning mentioned earlier in His words: ﴿Thus do We recompense whoever transgresses and does not believe in the signs of his Lord﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:127). The interrogative of denunciation and wonder (istifham inkari ta'jibi) is treated as a consequence of the announcement of the penalty, a life of constriction for whoever turns away from the Tawhid of God, because that penalty necessarily follows from it. It expresses wonder at the heedlessness of the polytheist addressees regarding what befell the nations similar to them in associating partners with God and in turning away from the Books of God and the signs of the messengers. Accordingly, the pronouns of the third-person plural refer to a known party from the context of rebuke, warning and admonition, as indicated by His words ﴿through whose dwellings they walk﴾. This phrase can only be a circumstantial clause (hal) describing a people who were alive at that time.

The word "guidance" (al-hidaya) here is a metaphor (isti'ara) for instruction in intellectual matters, treating the intellectual as if it were sensory. Its meaning therefore returns to the sense of making clear (al-tabyin). This is why its verb takes the preposition lam, as in His words ﴿Has it not become clear to those who inherit the land after its people…﴾ (al-A'raf 7:100) in Surat al-A'raf. The clause ﴿how many generations We destroyed before them﴾ suspends (mu'allaqa) the verb yahdi from acting on its object, because an interrogative particle follows it. That is, has it not informed them of the answer to "how many generations We destroyed before them", meaning the multitude of generations We destroyed. The subject of yahdi is a pronoun understood from the context, namely the pronoun for the Divine Name (Allah). The meaning is: "Has God not made clear to them the answer to 'how many did We destroy?'" It is also permissible for the subject to be the content of the clause "how many did We destroy". The meaning would then be: "Has this question not made itself clear to them?", with the object of yahdi omitted, treating the verb as intransitive, that is, "it results in clarity for them." The clause ﴿through whose dwellings they walk﴾ is a circumstantial clause (hal) from the pronoun governed by the preposition lam, because the absence of clarity in that condition is more strange and more deserving of wonder.

[Page 335]

By "the generations" are meant 'Ad and Thamud. The Arabs used to pass by the dwellings of 'Ad on their journeys to Yemen, Najran and what surrounded them, and by the dwellings of Thamud on their journeys to al-Sham. The Prophet (ﷺ) and the Muslims also passed by the abodes of Thamud on their march to Tabuk. The clause ﴿Indeed, in that are signs for people of understanding﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:54) serves as a causal explanation (ta'lil) for the denunciation and wonder at their heedlessness regarding the destruction of those generations. The particle of emphasis (harf al-ta'kid) serves to draw attention to the information and to signal the causal explanation. "Al-nuha", with a damma on the nun and a shortened vowel, is the plural of nuhya (with a damma on the nun and a sukun on the ha'), meaning intellect. The word nuha is also sometimes used in the singular with the meaning of intellect. In this there is an implicit allusion (ta'ridh) to those who were not guided by those signs, that they lack intellects, as in His words ﴿They are only like cattle; rather, they are further astray in way﴾ (al-Furqan 25:44).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verses 129–130:

﴿And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable, and an appointed term.﴾ ﴿So be patient over what they say, and glorify your Lord with praise before the rising of the sun and before its setting, and during the hours of the night glorify Him, and at the ends of the day, that you may be pleased.﴾

The clause "﴿And were it not for a word﴾" is coordinated with the clause "﴿Did it not guide them﴾" [Ta-Ha: 128], in terms of what it contains of warning, threat, and admonition through the earlier generations, that they deserve that there befall them the like of what befell those. So when they had been deceived by their own souls into denying the threat, because of the delay in the descent of the punishment upon them, and they were saying ﴿When is this promise, if you are truthful?﴾ [Yunus: 48], He followed their threat with an alert to what removes their delusion: that the cause of the delay is a word that preceded from God concerning it, for wisdoms that He knows. This is in the sense of His saying:

Page 336
﴿And they say, "When is this promise, if you are truthful?"﴾ [Yunus: 48] ﴿Say, "For you is an appointment of a Day from which you will not remain back an hour, nor will you precede [it]."﴾ [Saba: 30]. And "the word" is used here for what its nature is to be indicated by verbal words of meanings, and it is what the Ash'aris call the inner speech (al-kalam al-nafsi), which returns to God's knowledge of what He will bring forth to people of the matter of creation or the matter of legislation, or of admonition. His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And were it not for a word that preceded from your Lord, it would have been inevitable﴾ was mentioned earlier in Surat Hud. So "the word" here is meant to be what God knew of postponing the descent of the punishment upon them. God, in His wisdom, granted Quraysh respite and did not hasten the punishment for them, because He willed that Islam be spread through those among them who would believe and through their descendants. In this there is an honour for the Prophet Muhammad (ﷺ), by facilitating the means for the survival and spread of his law, since it is the final law. God singled out from among them with the punishment of the sword and captivity those who were most fierce in denial and aversion, as a wisdom from Him, Exalted is He, as He said, ﴿And God would not punish them while you are among them, and God would not punish them while they seek forgiveness﴾ [al-Anfal: 33] ﴿And what is [the matter] with them that God should not punish them while they bar [people] from al-Masjid al-Haram﴾ [al-Anfal: 34]. And "al-lizam" with a kasra on the lam is the verbal noun of lazama, like al-khisam, used as a verbal noun for the second form of the verb lazima, for the purpose of intensifying the meaning, as if it were attained by a number of people. It is also permissible that the pattern fi'al be in the sense of fa'il, like "lizaz" in the saying of Labid:

"From us is a lizaz whose cutting-off is hideous"
and "sidad" in the saying of al-'Arji:

"They abandoned me, and what a youth they abandoned, for a day of hideous calamity and a closing of a breach"

That is, the severe destruction would have been inevitable for them.

Page 337
So "lizaman" is in the accusative as the predicate of "kana," and its subject is a pronoun referring back to the destruction derived from "how many We destroyed," meaning: the destruction by which those before them of the generations were destroyed—namely annihilation—would have been inevitable for them.

"And an appointed term" is coordinated with "a word." The implied sense: "And were it not for a word and an appointed term at which the destruction occurs, their destruction would have been inevitable." What is meant by the term is what will be revealed to them of the descent of the punishment, either in this world, by its befalling some of their men—and this is the great seizing on the day of Badr—or in the Hereafter, which is what will befall those among them who die as disbelievers. Its meaning is found in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Say, "My Lord would not care for you were it not for your supplication. But you have denied, so it will be inevitable"﴾ [al-Furqan: 77]. It appears that it became widespread in the era of the Companions that the name "al-Lizam" was interpreted as a punishment with which God threatened the polytheists of Quraysh. And it was said: it is the punishment of the Day of Badr. In the Sahih of al-Bukhari, from Ibn Mas'ud, who said: "Five have passed: the smoke, the moon, the Romans, the great seizing, and al-lizam ﴿so it will be inevitable﴾" [al-Furqan: 77]. By this he intends to refute that al-lizam is something awaited at the end of the world. There is nothing in the Qur'an that requires interpreting al-lizam by this, as you know.

Upon this is grounded the command of the Messenger of God (ﷺ) to be patient over what they say of denial and of threat, because the descent of the punishment upon them is delayed. The meaning: so do not seek to hasten the punishment for them, and be patient over their denial and the like, which the relative pronoun in His saying "﴿what they say﴾" encompasses. And He commanded him to devote himself to the practice of purifying his own soul and the purification of his family through prayer, and to turning away from what God has withheld from the disbelievers through the comfort of life, and He promised him that the good end belongs to the God-fearing.

So "glorification" (al-tasbih) here is used for prayer, because it includes the glorification of God and His exaltation above imperfection. The "ba'" in His saying "bi-hamdi rabbika" is for accompaniment, which is the accompaniment of the doer with his act, meaning: glorify while praising your Lord; so the position of the prepositional phrase is the position of a circumstantial clause (hal).

Page 338
The times mentioned are the times of prayer: the time of Subh before the rising of the sun; and two times before its setting, which are Zuhr and 'Asr, and it was said the intended one is the 'Asr prayer. As for Zuhr, it is His saying "and the ends of the day," as will come.
The "min" in His saying "min a'na'i al-layl" is for beginning, related to the verb "fa-sabbih," and these are the times of Maghrib and 'Isha'. All of this is from the general (mujmal) matter which the mutawatir Sunnah has clarified. The fa' was introduced upon "fa-sabbih" because when the prepositional phrase was placed before it for emphasis, it resembled the placement of conditional particles which convey the sense of time. So the verb was treated as the response of a condition, as in his (ﷺ) saying: "fa-fihima fa-jahid" (in them [the parents], so strive), and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And of the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory act for you﴾ [al-Isra': 79], which was discussed earlier in Surat al-Isra'. The reason for the emphasis on the hours of the night is that the night is a time when souls incline to rest, so it is feared they will be lax in performing the prayer during it.

"Ana'i al-layl" means its hours. It is the plural of inin—with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the nun, and a ya' at its end. It is said: inw, with a waw at its end; and it is said: ina, with an alif at its end, shortened. And it is said: anaa', with a fatha on the hamza at its beginning and a long vowel at its end. The plural of these is "anaa'" on the pattern af'al.

His saying "﴿and the ends of the day﴾" in the accusative is coordinated with His saying "﴿before the rising of the sun﴾." The "tarf" of a thing is its extremity. It was said: the intended meaning is the beginning of the day and its end, and these are the times of Subh and Maghrib, so this is coordination of a part upon the whole, for emphasis on the part, like His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. And it was said: the intended meaning is the extremity of the sun's course along the arc of the horizon, which is the sun's course reaching the middle of the horizon, expressed as the zawal (declination), and these are two extremities: the extremity of the end and the extremity of the zawal, and this is

Page 339
the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half of the arc, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]. On this interpretation it is fitting that the mention of the two extremities together for a single prayer time indicates that its time is what lies between leaving one of the two extremities and entering the other extremity, and that is a precise portion.

On both interpretations, the day has two extremities, not "atraf" (more than two), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]. The plural in His saying "﴿and the ends of the day﴾" is the use of a plural noun for a dual, which is permitted in Arabic when there is no risk of confusion, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then your hearts have certainly deviated﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. What made it good here is the matching of plural with plural in His saying "﴿and of the night glorify﴾."

The Jumhur read "﴿that you may be pleased﴾" with a fatha on the ta', in the active voice, meaning: hoping that you will attain from God's reward what your soul is pleased with. It is also possible that the meaning is: perhaps in that required measure of prayers is what your soul is pleased with, without an increase in what is obligatory, out of kindness to you and to your community. This is clarified by his (ﷺ) saying: "And the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer."

Al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "tur-da" with a damma on the ta', meaning: your Lord will please you, and it allows both meanings.

All of this is from the general (mujmal) matter which the mutawatir Sunnah has clarified. The fa' was introduced upon "fa-sabbih" because when the prepositional phrase was placed before it for emphasis, it resembled the placement of conditional particles which convey the sense of time. So the verb was treated as the response of a condition, as in his (ﷺ) saying: "fa-fihima fa-jahid" (in them [the parents], so strive), and His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿And of the night, perform tahajjud with it as a supererogatory act for you﴾ [al-Isra': 79], which was discussed earlier in Surat al-Isra'. The reason for the emphasis on the hours of the night is that the night is a time when souls incline to rest, so it is feared they will be lax in performing the prayer during it.

"Ana'i al-layl" means its hours. It is the plural of inin—with a kasra on the hamza, a sukun on the nun, and a ya' at its end. It is said: inw, with a waw at its end; and it is said: ina, with an alif at its end, shortened. And it is said: anaa', with a fatha on the hamza at its beginning and a long vowel at its end. The plural of these is "anaa'" on the pattern af'al.

His saying "﴿and the ends of the day﴾" in the accusative is coordinated with His saying "﴿before the rising of the sun﴾." The "tarf" of a thing is its extremity. It was said: the intended meaning is the beginning of the day and its end, and these are the times of Subh and Maghrib, so this is coordination of a part upon the whole, for emphasis on the part, like His saying: ﴿Guard the prayers and the middle prayer﴾ [al-Baqarah: 238]. And it was said: the intended meaning is the extremity of the sun's course along the arc of the horizon, which is the sun's course reaching the middle of the horizon, expressed as the zawal (declination), and these are two extremities: the extremity of the end and the extremity of the zawal, and this is

Page 339
the end of the first half and the beginning of the second half of the arc, as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]. On this interpretation it is fitting that the mention of the two extremities together for a single prayer time indicates that its time is what lies between leaving one of the two extremities and entering the other extremity, and that is a precise portion.

On both interpretations, the day has two extremities, not "atraf" (more than two), as He, Exalted is He, said: ﴿And establish the prayer at the two ends of the day﴾ [Hud: 114]. The plural in His saying "﴿and the ends of the day﴾" is the use of a plural noun for a dual, which is permitted in Arabic when there is no risk of confusion, as in His saying, Exalted is He, ﴿Then your hearts have certainly deviated﴾ [al-Tahrim: 4]. What made it good here is the matching of plural with plural in His saying "﴿and of the night glorify﴾."

The Jumhur read "﴿that you may be pleased﴾" with a fatha on the ta', in the active voice, meaning: hoping that you will attain from God's reward what your soul is pleased with. It is also possible that the meaning is: perhaps in that required measure of prayers is what your soul is pleased with, without an increase in what is obligatory, out of kindness to you and to your community. This is clarified by his (ﷺ) saying: "And the coolness of my eyes has been placed in prayer."

Al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr from 'Asim read "tur-da" with a damma on the ta', meaning: your Lord will please you, and it allows both meanings.

[p. 340]

His command to be patient over what they say is followed by a prohibition against admiring the luxury enjoyed by those among the polytheists who live in wealth and with children, while they are in a state of disbelief in God, by [the fact] that

That is for wisdoms known to God, Exalted is He, among them the establishment of proof against them, as He, Exalted, said: ﴿Do they reckon that by what We extend to them of wealth and children, We are hastening to them in good things? Rather, they do not perceive.﴾ [al-Mu'minun: 55].

The mention of "spouses" (al-azwaj) here indicates families and households, meaning: We gave enjoyment to them and their spouses through what We gave them of pleasures. Each spouse is given enjoyment in the other spouse according to what is pleasing in the eyes of each of the good qualities of their partner, and what accompanies that of shared good qualities between the two spouses, such as children, fine clothing, dwellings, and servants. "Stretching the eyes" (madd al-‘aynayn) is used to mean prolonged gazing out of wonder, not out of admiration; it is likened to stretching the hand to take hold of a desired thing. A parallel of this has already occurred at the end of Surat al-Hijr. "Zahrah," with a fatha on the zay and a sukun on the ha', is the singular of "zahr," which is the blossom of trees and plants, and it is used metaphorically for an attractive, dazzling adornment, because the sight of a blossom beautifies the plant and pleases the viewer. So "zahrat al-hayah" means the adornment of life, that is, the adornment of the affairs of life, such as clothing, livestock, gardens, women, and children, as in His saying: ﴿So it is the enjoyment of the life of this world and its adornment﴾ [al-Qasas: 60]. The phrase ﴿zahrata al-hayat al-dunya﴾ is in the accusative as a circumstantial state (hal) of the relative pronoun in His saying: ﴿what We gave enjoyment to pairs of them﴾.

The majority of readers read "zahrah" with a sukun on the ha'. Ya'qub read it with a fatha on the ha', and this is a dialect form.

"Li-yaftinahum" (that We may test them) is connected to "matta'na" (We gave enjoyment). "Fi" (in) is used for figurative location, meaning that their trial may occur within it, so in every kind of that enjoyment there is a trial suited to it. The lam is used for the figurative purpose (illah majaziyyah) which is the outcome of a thing, like His saying: ﴿So the family of Pharaoh picked him up, that he might become for them an enemy and a sorrow﴾ [al-Qasas: 8].

[p. 341]

God gave them enjoyment of the splendour of this world for many causes, linked in a chain to the systems of social life, and so it became for them a trial in their religion, and the outcome was made to stand in the position of the motive. "Fitnah" is the disturbance of the soul and the confusion of the mind from fear, or anticipation, or the twisting of affairs, and they were never free of that. Because of their polytheism, God casts into their hearts grief and anticipation, and their trial in the Hereafter is evident. So the "fi" of location here is like that in the verse of Sabrah ibn ‘Amr al-Faqa'si:

We favour with them our equals, and we demean them, and we drink with their prices, and we gamble.

And like His saying: ﴿and provide for them therein and clothe them﴾ [al-Nisa': 5] in Surat al-Nisa'. The clause ﴿but the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting﴾ is a concluding statement (tadhyil), because His saying "Do not strain your eyes toward..." up to its end implies that what appears to the viewer of their fine appearance is mixed with, and concealed by, a trial in the soul, a misery in life, and a punishment for it in the Hereafter. So it is concluded with the statement that the provision made easy by God for the believers is better than that and more lasting in this world, and its benefit remains in the Hereafter due to what accompanies it in this world of gratitude. So the idafah (possessive construction) of "provision of your Lord" is an idafah of honour; otherwise all provision is from God. But because the provision of the disbelievers was mixed with, and surrounded by, the condition of its owners, through God's anger against them, and because of the accountability upon its owners in this world and the Hereafter for their ingratitude for the blessing, it was made as if its attribution to God were denied, and God's provision was made to be that which is free from the association of ingratitude and its consequences.

"Khayr" here is a comparative (tafdil), and the quality of being better is a relative reality (haqiqah i‘tibariyyah) that differs according to its aspects. Among them: something that is good for its possessor in the immediate sense but evil for him in the ultimate sense; among them, a good mixed with evils and trials; and a pure good free of that; and among them, what suits one strongly, and what suits one weakly. So the comparison is in terms of the abundance of safety from bad consequences and trials, as with what is accompanied by contentment. Thus the comparison of goodness comes in a general form that becomes clear through reflection.

"Wa-abqa" (more lasting) is a comparative over what the disbelievers were given enjoyment of, because in the provision of the disbelievers there is some permanence, and this too, its permanence, becomes evident through reflection on what surrounds it and its consequences.

**Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on Surah 20, verse 132:**

﴿And enjoin prayer upon your family, and be steadfast in it. We do not ask you for provision; We provide for you. And the good outcome belongs to righteousness.﴾

The mention of "family" (ahl) here corresponds to the mention of "spouses" (azwaj) in His words: ﴿to what We have given enjoyment to some pairs of them﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131]. For a man's family includes his spouses. The meaning is: your enjoyment, and the enjoyment of your family, is prayer, so do not turn your attention to the glitter of this world. And a man's family are the best of those to whom he belongs.

Among the effects of acting on this verse in the Sunnah is what is in Sahih al-Bukhari (the collection of Imam al-Bukhari): that Fatimah, may Allah be pleased with her, heard that captives had been brought to the Prophet ﷺ, so she came complaining to him about what she suffered from the hand-mill, asking him for a servant from among the captives. But she did not find him. So 'Aisha informed the Messenger of Allah ﷺ of that. The Prophet ﷺ came to them while she and 'Ali were already lying down in their bed. He sat at the edge of the bed and said to her and to 'Ali: "Shall I not tell you of something better for you than what you asked for? Glorify (tusabbihan), praise (tahmadan), and magnify (tukabbiran) Allah thirty-three times after every prayer. That is better for you than a servant."

Allah commanded His Messenger with something greater than what He commands his family, namely that he be steadfast in prayer. The word al-istibar (steadfastness) means restraint (al-inhibas), and it is the reflexive form of sabarahu, meaning "when he restrained him." It is used figuratively (majaz) for increasing one's prayer in the supererogatory prayers (nawafil, voluntary acts of worship beyond the obligatory). Allah says: ﴿O you wrapped in garments, stand [in prayer] at night, except a little﴾ [al-Muzzammil: 1], the verses that follow, and He says: ﴿And from the night, pray with it as a supererogatory act for you﴾ [al-Isra': 79].

The clause ﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾ is an interjection (mu'taridah) between the one before it and the clause ﴿We provide for you﴾, and it was placed as a preparation (tamhid) for this latter clause.

The word "asking" (al-su'al) here means an imposed demand (al-talab al-taklifi), i.e., "We have only obligated you with worship," because worship is gratitude to Allah for the favours He has bestowed upon creation, and Allah does not seek from them any other recompense. This is a refutation of what people have become accustomed to, namely paying levies (jibayat) and land tax (kharaj) to kings, tribal chiefs, and armies. On this meaning is His saying: ﴿I did not create jinn and humankind except that they should worship Me. I do not want provision from them, nor do I want them to feed Me. Indeed Allah is the Provider, the Possessor of strength, the Firm﴾ [al-Dhariyat: 56-58]. Therefore the clause ﴿We provide for you﴾ explains the clause ﴿And the provision of your Lord is better and more lasting﴾ [Ta-Ha: 131]. The meaning is: the provision of your Lord is better, and it is driven toward you.

The primary address of this discourse is the Prophet ﷺ, and it includes his family and the believers, because the reason given in this clause is shared in its ruling by all Muslims.

The clause ﴿And the good outcome belongs to righteousness﴾ is coordinated (atf) upon the clause ﴿We do not ask you for provision﴾, the reason for which is his command to be steadfast in prayer. That is, "We have asked you for righteousness and the outcome."

The true meaning of "outcome" (al-aqibah) is whatever follows a matter and occurs at its end, whether good or evil, but its use has predominantly been for matters of good. So the meaning is: righteousness will come at its end with good outcomes. The particle "lam" here indicates possession (lam al-milk), to confirm the intention of good from the outcome, because the function of the lam of possession is to indicate attaining the desired matter. This applies in particular to the good outcome of the Hereafter, though the outcome may also be a good in this world for those who are righteous.

This clause is a concluding statement (tadhyil) for what it contains of general meaning. That is, the outcome belongs only to righteousness. Therefore this clause was sent forth in the manner of a proverb (mathal).

Commentary of Ibn 'Ashur (al-Tahrir wa al-Tanwir) on surah 20, verse 133:

﴿And they say, "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?" Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾

This is a return to emphasizing the status of the Qur'an, and that it is the greatest of the miracles (mu'jizat). It is the theme from which the discourse moved to other relevant themes, starting from His saying: ﴿And thus We have sent it down as an Arabic Qur'an, and We have diversified in it [some] warning, that they may fear Allah or it may renew for them remembrance﴾ [Ta-Ha: 113]. The connection for the transition is what is contained in His saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. So here there is mention of some of the outrageous things they said, about which Allah commanded His Messenger to be patient in His saying: ﴿So be patient over what they say﴾ [Ta-Ha: 130]. Among their sayings, by which they intend obstinacy and arrogance, is that they said: "Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord, so that we would believe in his message?", as the Exalted said: ﴿So let him bring us a sign like that which the earlier [messengers] were sent with﴾ [al-Anbiya: 5].

Law (lawla) is a particle of urging (tahdid).

The clause ﴿Has there not come to them the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ is in the position of a circumstantial clause (hal), and the waw is for the circumstantial (li-l-hal). That is, they said this while the clear proof of what is in the former scriptures had come to them. The interrogation is one of denial (istifham inkari); by it is denied the negation of a sign coming to them, which is what their urging them to bring a sign implies.

Al-bayyina: the proof (al-hujja).

The former scriptures (al-suhuf al-ula): the books of the earlier prophets, as in His saying: ﴿Indeed, this is in the former scriptures, the scriptures of Abraham and Moses﴾ [al-A'la: 18].

Page 345
Al-suhuf is the plural of sahifa, which is a piece of paper, or of parchment, or a cloth on which something is written. Since a book is a collection of sheets, the word suhuf was applied to books.

The reason for choosing "suhuf" here over "kutub" is that every scripture contains knowledge, and all of it is contained in the Qur'an, so every part of the Qur'an is a sign and proof. This clear proof is Muhammad (ﷺ) and his book, the Qur'an; because the Messenger is promised in the earlier books; and because the Qur'an confirms what is in those books of the reports of the prophets, of admonitions, and of the foundations of legislation. He came with it as an unlettered messenger (ummi), who was not of the People of the Book, and who did not grow up among a people of learning and engagement with history, while bringing reports of their past that are clearer than the break of dawn, which the People of the Book could not deny. The Exalted said: ﴿Those to whom We gave the Book recognize it as they recognize their sons. But indeed, a party of them conceal the truth while they know﴾ [al-Baqarah: 146]. They were not able to verify much of it, because of the division that befell them, the disappearance of the foundations of their books, and the rewriting of many of them in meaning according to corrupt interpretations.

As for the Qur'an, what it contains of the signs of truthfulness and right guidance, and what distinguishes it from the rest of the books in eloquence and fluency reaching the limit of inimitability (i'jaz), is what the proof was established by directly against the Arabs and, by inference, against others. This is like His saying: ﴿Those who disbelieved among the People of the Book and the polytheists were not going to desist until there came to them the clear proof﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 1], ﴿a messenger from Allah, reciting purified scriptures﴾ [al-Bayyinah: 2].

Nafi', Hafs, and Ibn Jammaz from Abu Ja'far read "ta'tihim" with the taa' of the feminine imperfect. The rest read it with the yaa' of the masculine, because the feminization of "bayyina" is not real (ghayr haqiqi), and the original form of attribution is masculine, since the masculine is not a marker; rather, it is the default in speech.

[Page 346]

﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it, they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we could follow Your signs before we were humiliated and disgraced?"﴾

It appears that the clause ﴿And if We had destroyed them with a punishment before it﴾ is conjoined to the clause ﴿Has there not come to them clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133]. The meaning proceeds by escalating argument against them: they are misguided because they deferred belief in what Muhammad (ﷺ) brought and made it conditional on his bringing them a sign from their Lord. What they are engaged in, namely associating partners with God, is clear error. Habits and preoccupation with the affairs of the religion of polytheism have veiled them from perceiving its corruption. Associating partners with God alone is therefore sufficient to make them deserving of punishment. But God, in His mercy, did not call them to account for it until He had sent to them a messenger to awaken their minds. The coming of the messenger with this is therefore sufficient for the intellects to infer the corruption of what they are upon. How, then, after this, do they ask that the messenger bring them a sign of his truthfulness in what he calls them to, namely the abandonment of polytheism? Even if one grants, for the sake of argument, that the clear evidence that came to them is not itself a sign, their excuse has been invalidated at its root. That excuse is their saying: ﴿Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger so that we could follow Your signs?﴾

This is like His saying, exalted is He: ﴿And this is a Book We have sent down, blessed, so follow it and fear God that you may be shown mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 155]; ﴿lest you say, "The Book was only sent down to two groups before us, and we were indeed unaware of their study"﴾ [al-An'am: 156]; ﴿or lest you say, "If the Book had been sent down to us, we would have been better guided than they." Now there has come to you clear evidence from your Lord, and guidance and mercy﴾ [al-An'am: 157].

The pronoun in His saying "from before it" (min qablihi) refers either to the Qur'an, which is the subject of the discourse, or to the messenger, in view of his being described as "clear evidence," or to the coming of the clear evidence derived from ﴿Has there not come to them clear evidence of what is in the former scriptures?﴾ [Ta-Ha: 133].

In this verse there is evidence that belief in the oneness of the Creator of creation is required by reason, were it not for the veiling of error and desire. There is also evidence that the coming of messengers serves to awaken intellects and natural dispositions (fitrah), and that God does not call the people of the interval (ahl al-fatrah, those who lived in the period between messengers) to account for associating partners with Him until He sends them a messenger. And there is evidence that the Quraysh were a people of the interval before the mission of Muhammad (ﷺ).

The meaning of ﴿they would have said: "Our Lord, why did You not send to us a messenger"﴾ is that they would say this on the Day of Reckoning, after God had destroyed them with the destruction decreed, because destruction by a punishment in this world entails that they are punished in the Hereafter.

"Lawla" (لَوْلا) is a particle of urging (taḥḍīḍ), used here to express blame or argument, since the time of sending has passed. The sense is: "Why did You not send to us a messenger?" The word "fa-nattabi'a" (فَنَتَّبِعَ, "so that we could follow") is in the accusative as a response to the particle of urging, considering that the event would have occurred in the past.

Al-dhull (الذُّلُّ) is humiliation. Al-khizy (الخِزْيُ) is exposure, that is, humiliation through punishment.

The disgrace (khizy) lies in their being gathered together with the criminals, as Ibrahim (peace be upon him) said: ﴿and do not disgrace me on the day they are resurrected﴾ [al-Shu'ara': 87].

[Page 348]

This is a reply to their saying: ﴿Why does he not bring us a sign from his Lord?﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:133). What lies between them is an interjection. The meaning is: each party is waiting. You are waiting with regard to faith, meaning you are delaying faith until a sign comes to you from my Lord, while we are waiting for the punishment of this world or the punishment of the Hereafter to come upon you. The clause "fa-tarabbasu" (so wait) follows from this. The root of the imperative verb is used with the sense of continuation, by context, like the verse ﴿O you who believe, believe in God and His Messenger﴾ (al-Nisa' 4:136), meaning: persist in your waiting.

[Page 349]

The imperative form here is used for warning. This is called al-mutaraka (mutual disengagement), meaning: we leave you and your waiting, because we are certain of your evil end. A similar meaning is found in God's words: ﴿So turn away from them and wait; indeed they are waiting﴾ (al-Sajda 32:30). Something close to this is also found in His words: ﴿Say: Are you waiting for us except for one of the two best outcomes? And we are waiting for you that God will afflict you with a punishment from Himself or by our hands. So wait; indeed we are waiting with you﴾ (al-Tawba 9:52). The tanwin on "kullun" (each) is the tanwin of compensation for an omitted genitive that is understood from the context, as in the verse of al-Fadl ibn 'Abbas al-Lahabi:

Each has an intention to hate his companion,
by God's blessing we shall move you and you shall move us.

Al-tarabbus means waiting. It is of the form tafa''ul from al-rabs, and it is waiting for the occurrence of an event, whether good or bad. It has already been discussed in the commentary on Surat Bara'a. Following on from the mutual disengagement, they are informed that in the future they will know which of the two parties are the people of the straight path and which are the guided. This is an allusion that the believers are the people of the straight path and the guided, because such words are not said in a context of argument and disengagement except by one who is certain that he is in the right. The verb "ta'lamun" (you will know) is suspended from operating because of the interrogative that follows it.

Al-sirat means the path. Here it is used metaphorically for religion and belief, as in His words: ﴿Guide us to the straight path﴾ (al-Fatiha 1:6).

"Al-sawiyy" is on the pattern fa'il in the sense of maf'ul, meaning the path that has been made level (al-sirat al-musawwa), and it is derived from al-taswiya (levelling). The meaning allows that they will know this in this world, when Islam spreads and the Muslims prevail. In that case, those who will know this are those among the disbelievers addressed at the time of the revelation of the verse who remain alive, whether among those who did not embrace Islam, such as Abu Jahl,

[Page 349 continued]

and the chieftains of the polytheists who witnessed the victory of the religion at the Battle of Badr, or among those who embraced Islam, such as Abu Sufyan and Khalid ibn al-Walid, and those who witnessed the glory of Islam. It also allows that they will know this in the Hereafter with the certainty of certainty.

The conclusion of this surah has come as one of the most eloquent conclusions of speech, because it announces the end of the argument and the folding up of the carpet of contention.

Among its beauties is that it contains something resembling "radd al-ajuz 'ala al-sadr" (the return of the end to the beginning), because it looks back to the opening of the surah, which is His words: ﴿We did not send down the Qur'an upon you to make you wretched, but as a reminder for those who fear﴾ (Ta-Ha 20:2). The conclusion indicates that he has conveyed all that he was sent with of guidance and proof. When they do not take guidance from it, it is sufficient for him, for the relief of his heart, that he has discharged the message and the reminder. They were not among those who fear, so He leaves them and their misguidance until it becomes clear to them that it is the truth.

Surat al-Anbiya' (The Prophets)

The early scholars named it "Surat al-Anbiya'" (The Surah of the Prophets). In Sahih al-Bukhari, it is related from 'Abd Allah ibn Mas'ud who said: "Bani Isra'il, al-Kahf, Maryam, Ta-Ha and al-Anbiya' are among the first old ones (al-'ataq al-ula), and they are of my earliest possessions (tilad)." No other name for it is known besides this.

The reason for naming it Surat al-Anbiya' is that in it are mentioned the names of sixteen prophets, together with Maryam. No surah of the Qur'an contains such a number of prophets' names, except the surah of al-An'am. In al-An'am the names of eighteen prophets are mentioned, in His words: ﴿And that was Our argument, which We gave to Abraham against his people﴾ (al-An'am 6:83) up to His words: ﴿and Jonah and Lot﴾ (al-An'am 6:86). So if this Surat al-Anbiya' was revealed before Surat al-An'am, then it preceded it in being named by reference to the prophets. Otherwise, the fact that Surat al-An'am is specialised in discussing the rulings concerning livestock (al-an'am) required it to be named by that name, so Surat al-Anbiya' was more worthy than the rest of the surahs of the Qur'an of this name. Nevertheless, it is an established truth that the reason for a naming does not necessarily require it.

It is Meccan by consensus. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Qurtubi relate the consensus (ijma') on this. Al-Suyuti in al-Itqan mentions an exception: His words:

[Page 6]
﴿Do they not see that We come to the land, reducing it from its extremities? Are they the victors?﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:44), but he did not attribute it to any speaker. Perhaps he took it from a narration from Muqatil and al-Kalbi, from Ibn 'Abbas, that the meaning of "naqsuha" (reducing it) is by conquering lands, on the basis that the sight in the verse is ocular vision, that the land is the land of the Hijaz, and that the reduction is the reduction of the authority of polytheism from it. All of this is neither definite nor the preferred view. Its explanation will come in its proper place. Its explanation has already been given in the parallel verse in Surat al-Ra'd, which is also Meccan. So the more probable view is that Surat al-Anbiya' is entirely Meccan.

It is the seventy-first surah in the order of revelation. It was revealed after Ha-Mim al-Sajda and before Surat al-Nahl, so it is among the last surahs revealed before the Hijra. It is possible that it was revealed after the conversion of those of the people of Medina who embraced Islam, as His words indicate: ﴿And they conspired in secret, those who did wrong: "Is this not merely a human being like you? Will you then approach magic while you see?"﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:3), as will be explained. However, what Ibn Ishaq related from Ibn 'Abbas, that His words in Surat al-Zukhruf: ﴿And when the son of Mary is cited as an example, behold, your people turn away from it﴾ (al-Zukhruf 43:57), refer to the example that Ibn al-Za'ba'ra gave when His words were revealed: ﴿Indeed you and what you worship besides God are fuel for Hell﴾ (al-Anbiya' 21:98), as will come, implies that Surat al-Anbiya' was revealed before Surat al-Zukhruf. Surat al-Zukhruf is counted as the sixty-second in revelation. The number of its verses in the counting of the people of Medina, Mecca, Syria and Basra is one hundred and eleven, and in the counting of the people of Kufa it is one hundred and twelve.

The themes mentioned in these surahs are: warning of the Resurrection and affirmation of its occurrence, and that because its occurrence is certain, it is near.
And establishing the proof for it by the creation of the heavens and the earth from non-existence, and the creation of existing things from water.

And warning against denying the Book of God and His Messenger.
And reminding that this Messenger, peace be upon him, is nothing but like the messengers before him, and he brought only what the messengers before him brought.

And mentioning many reports about the messengers, peace be upon them.

And praising the status of the Qur'an, that it is a blessing from God upon those addressed, and the status of the Messenger of Islam, peace be upon him, and that he is a mercy to the worlds.

And reminding them of what befell the earlier nations as a consequence of their denial of their messengers, and that God's promise to those who denied is certain, and that its delay should not deceive them, for it will surely come.

And warning them not to be deceived by its delay as those before them were deceived, until it overtook them suddenly. And he mentioned among the signs of the Hour the opening of Gog and Magog.

And reminding them of what is in the creation of the heavens and the earth of indications of the Creator.

And an allusion that behind this life there is another life, more perfect and more firm, so that every soul may be recompensed for what it earned, and the truth may triumph over falsehood.

Then, what is in that creation of proofs of the Creator's oneness, since this order cannot be upheld by a plurality of gods.

And the glorification of God, exalted is He, above partners and offspring, and the argument for God's oneness.

And that which compels one to do what one does not want.

And that all created things are destined for annihilation.

[Page 8]
He followed this with reminding them of the greatest blessing upon them, which is the blessing of preservation.
Then the discourse turned to the mention of the messengers and prophets.

And the comparison of their circumstances and the circumstances of their nations with the circumstances of Muhammad, peace be upon him, and the circumstances of his people.

And how God gave victory to the messengers over their peoples and answered their supplications.

And that all the messengers brought the religion of God, which is one religion in its fundamentals, which the misguided have fragmented into pieces.

And He praised the messengers and those who believed in them.

And that the final outcome belongs to the believers, in the best of this world and the best of the Hereafter, and that God will judge between the two parties with truth, and will help His messengers in conveying His law.
